statement: For each odd integer p≥3, determine the number of distinct real roots of $f_p(x)=(x-1)(x-2)\cdots(x-p+1)+1$.
solution: For p=3 the quadratic is always positive. For p=5, putting t=(x−5/2)² gives f₅(x)=(t−5/4)², so there are two distinct roots. Let p≥7. The product can be negative only on the (p−1)/2 intervals (1,2),(3,4),…,(p−2,p−1). On each, its absolute value is zero at the endpoints and has strictly concave logarithm: the second derivative is −Σ1/(x−j)²<0. It therefore increases to one maximum and then decreases, so it crosses level one at most twice. At the midpoint j+1/2 of any such interval, the product of the distances to the integer roots is at least (1/2)²(3/2)²(5/2)²=225/64>1: among the ordered distances, the first six are at least these six, and every remaining distance exceeds one. Thus there are exactly two crossings per interval, or p−1 real roots.
ratingReason: The exceptional small cases behave differently. For larger degrees, a uniform midpoint estimate must be combined with strict logarithmic concavity to control the exact number of crossings.

title: Two rows with many matching colours
statement: Every cell of a $5\times2008$ board is coloured red or blue. What is the largest integer $N$ such that two rows always agree in at least $N$ columns?
solution: The answer is 804. A column with $r$ red cells contributes $\binom r2+\binom{5-r}2\ge4$ agreements among the ten row pairs. Thus some pair has at least $\lceil4\cdot2008/10\rceil=804$ agreements. For sharpness, use 200 copies of each of the ten column patterns with exactly two red cells. Every pair agrees in exactly four of the ten patterns, so initially has 800 agreements. Append any eight different such patterns. A pair can gain at most four agreements, hence no pair exceeds 804.
ratingReason: Double-counting agreements gives the lower bound; a balanced collection of the ten two-red column patterns attains the rounded bound.

statement: Let $\sigma=\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots, a_{n}\right)$ be a permutation of $(1,2,3, \ldots, n)$. A pair $\left(a_{i}, a_{j}\right)$ is said to correspond to an inversion of $\sigma$, if $i<j$ but $a_{i}>a_{j}$. (Example: In the permutation $(2,4,5,3,1)$, there are 6 inversions corresponding to the pairs $(2,1)$, $(4,3),(4,1),(5,3),(5,1),(3,1)$.) How many permutations of $(1,2,3, \ldots n)$, $(n \geq 3)$, have exactly two inversions?
solution:
In a permutation of $(1,2,3, \ldots, n)$, two inversions can occur in only one of the following two ways:
(A) Two disjoint consecutive pairs are interchanged:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& (1,2,3, \ldots, j-1, j, j+1, \ldots, k-1, k, k+1, k+2, \ldots, n) \\
& \quad \longrightarrow (1,2, \ldots, j-1, j+1, j, j+2, \ldots, k-1, k+1, k, k+2, \ldots, n)
\end{aligned}
$$
(B) Each block of three consecutive integers can be permuted in any of the following 2 ways:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& (1,2,3, \ldots, k, k+1, k+2, \ldots, n) \longrightarrow (1,2, \ldots, k+2, k, k+1, \ldots, n) \\
& (1,2,3, \ldots, k, k+1, k+2, \ldots, n) \longrightarrow (1,2, \ldots, k+1, k+2, k, \ldots, n)
\end{aligned}
$$
Consider case (A). For $j=1$, there are $n-3$ possible values of $k$; for $j=2$, there are $n-4$ possibilities for $k$ and so on. Thus the number of permutations with two inversions of this type is
$$
1+2+\cdots+(n-3)=\frac{(n-3)(n-2)}{2}
$$
In case (B), we see that there are $n-2$ permutations of each type, since $k$ can take values from $1$ to $n-2$. Hence we get $2(n-2)$ permutations of this type.
Finally, the number of permutations with two inversions is
$$
\frac{(n-3)(n-2)}{2}+2(n-2)=\frac{(n+1)(n-2)}{2}
$$
ratingReason: Classify exactly two inversions as two separated adjacent swaps or a cyclic shift of three consecutive entries.

statement: Three cards carry integers $0<p<q<r$. In each round they are shuffled and dealt one each to players $A,B,C$, who receive that many counters and keep all previous counters. After at least two rounds, their totals are $20,10,9$, respectively. In the last round $B$ receives $r$. Who received $q$ in the first round?
solution:
The total is $39$, so the number $t\geq2$ of rounds divides $39$. Since $p+q+r\geq6$, we have $t\leq6$, leaving $t=3$ and $p+q+r=13$.

Player $A$'s total requires $r\geq7$. Player $B$ receives $r$ last and at least $p$ in each earlier round, so $r+2p\leq10$. Thus $p=1$ and $r$ is seven or eight. The possibilities are $(p,q,r)=(1,5,7)$ or $(1,4,8)$.

The first is impossible: all three card values are odd, so a total after three rounds must be odd, whereas $A$ has 20. Hence the cards are $1,4,8$.

The totals force $A$ to receive $8,8,4$; $B$ to receive $1,1,8$; and $C$ to receive $4,4,1$. Since $B$ gets eight last, the final deal is $(A,B,C)=(4,8,1)$. Both earlier deals are $(8,1,4)$. Therefore $C$ received $q=4$ in the first round.
ratingReason: Use the total count to fix the number of rounds, then extremal individual totals restrict the three card values to two possibilities. The last-round condition then determines both earlier deals.
notes: Official released statement checked; worked exposition independently written and mathematically assessed.

statement: Triangle ABC satisfies AB=1 and angle ABC=120°. The perpendicular at B to AB meets AC at D, where DC=1. Determine AD.
solution: Put B=(0,0), A=(1,0), D=(0,d) with d>0, and l=√(1+d²)=AD. The condition DC=1 places C beyond D at $(-1/l,d(1+1/l))$. Since BC makes angle 120° with the positive horizontal axis, its vertical coordinate is √3 times the negative of its horizontal coordinate. Hence d(l+1)=√3. Squaring and substituting d²=l²−1 gives $(l−1)(l+1)^3=3$, or $l^4+2l^3−2l−4=0$. This factors as $(l+2)(l^3−2)=0$. As l>0, $AD=\sqrt[3]2$.
ratingReason: The external intersection needs a signed coordinate model. The fixed angle then gives a quartic whose useful cubic factor is hidden until the length relation is substituted.

statement: Classify functions $f:\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ satisfying $xf(y)+yf(x)=(x+y)f(x^2+y^2)$ for all nonnegative integers $x,y$.
solution:
Putting $y=0$ and $x>0$ gives $f(x^2)=f(0)$, in particular $f(1)=f(0)$. If $f$ is nonconstant, choose positive integers $u,v$ for which $0<f(v)-f(u)$ is as small as possible. Such positive indices exist because the value at 0 also occurs at 1. Then
$$f(u)<\frac{u f(v)+v f(u)}{u+v}=f(u^2+v^2)<f(v).$$
The middle value is an integer, contradicting minimality of the positive difference. Thus f is constant; every nonnegative integer constant indeed satisfies the equation.
ratingReason: The equation makes f(x²+y²) a strict weighted mean when f(x) and f(y) differ. Choose a pair with minimum positive value difference to contradict integrality; first handle the zero input so both weights are positive.
notes: The original exposition supplies the zero-input check omitted from the shortest official minimal-difference proof.

statement:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle in which $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be the mid-point of $BC$ and $P$ be a point on $AD$. Suppose $E$ is the foot of perpendicular from $P$ on $AC$. If $\frac{AP}{PD} = \frac{BP}{PE} = \lambda$, $\frac{BD}{AD} = m$ and $z = m^2(1+\lambda)$, prove that
$$
z^2 - (\lambda^3 - \lambda^2 - 2)z + 1 = 0
$$
Hence show that $\lambda \geq 2$ and $\lambda = 2$ if and only if $ABC$ is equilateral.
solution:
Let $AD = h$, $PD = y$ and $BD = DC = a$. We
![A triangle ABC with AB equal to AC, D as the midpoint of BC, P on AD, and E as the foot of the perpendicular from P to AC. Sides and segments are labeled with variables a, b, h-y, y, and angle A/2 is marked.](assets/diagrams/bd1e0466aa9c8136a022.jpg)
observe that $BP^2 = a^2 + y^2$. Moreover,
$PE = PA \sin \angle DAC = (h - y) \frac{DC}{AC} = \frac{a(h - y)}{b}$,
where $b = AC = AB$. Using $AP / PD = (h - y) / y$, we obtain $y = h / (1 + \lambda)$. Thus
$$
\lambda^2 = \frac{BP^2}{PE^2} = \frac{(a^2 + y^2) b^2}{(h - y)^2 a^2}
$$
But $(h - y) = \lambda y = \lambda h / (1 + \lambda)$ and $b^2 = a^2 + h^2$. Thus we obtain
$$
\lambda^4 = \frac{(a^2(1 + \lambda)^2 + h^2)(a^2 + h^2)}{a^2 h^2}
$$
Using $m = a / h$ and $z = m^2(1 + \lambda)$, this simplifies to
$$
z^2 - z(\lambda^3 - \lambda^2 - 2) + 1 = 0
$$
Dividing by $z$, this gives
$$
z + \frac{1}{z} = \lambda^3 - \lambda^2 - 2
$$
However $z + (1 / z) \geq 2$ for any positive real number $z$. Thus $\lambda^3 - \lambda^2 - 4 \geq 0$. This may be written in the form $(\lambda - 2)(\lambda^2 + \lambda + 2) \geq 0$. But $\lambda^2 + \lambda + 2 > 0$. (For example, one may check that its discriminant is negative.) Hence $\lambda \geq 2$. If $\lambda = 2$, then $z + (1 / z) = 2$ and hence $z = 1$. This gives $m^2 = 1 / 3$ or $\tan (A / 2) = m = 1 / \sqrt{3}$. Thus $A = 60^\circ$ and hence $ABC$ is equilateral.

Conversely, if triangle $ABC$ is equilateral, then $m = \tan (A / 2) = 1 / \sqrt{3}$ and hence $z = (1 + \lambda) / 3$. Substituting this in the equation satisfied by $z$, we obtain
$$
(1 + \lambda)^2 - 3(1 + \lambda)(\lambda^3 - \lambda^2 - 2) + 9 = 0
$$
This may be written in the form $(\lambda - 2)(3\lambda^3 + 6\lambda^2 + 8\lambda + 8) = 0$. Here the second factor is positive because $\lambda > 0$. We conclude that $\lambda = 2$.
ratingReason: Express all lengths using the altitude and half-base, derive the displayed quadratic, then apply z+1/z at least 2.

statement: Prove that triangle $ABC$ has a point $D$ on $AB$ with $CD^2=AD\cdot DB$ if and only if $\sin A\sin B\leq\sin^2(C/2)$.
solution:
Write $BC=a$, $CA=b$, $AB=c$, and $AD=x$, $DB=y$, so $x+y=c$. Stewart's theorem gives
$$a^2x+b^2y=c(CD^2+xy).$$
Thus $CD^2=xy$ is equivalent to
$$\frac{a^2}{y}+\frac{b^2}{x}=2c.$$
For positive $x,y$ summing to $c$, Cauchy–Schwarz says the left side has minimum $(a+b)^2/c$, attained when $y:x=a:b$. It is continuous and tends to infinity at either endpoint. Therefore the required $D$ exists exactly when $a+b\leq\sqrt2c$.

By the sine rule and sum-to-product identity,
$$\frac{a+b}{c}=\frac{\cos((A-B)/2)}{\sin(C/2)}.$$
Also
$$\sin A\sin B=\cos^2((A-B)/2)-\sin^2(C/2).$$
Consequently $a+b\leq\sqrt2c$ is equivalent to $\sin A\sin B\leq\sin^2(C/2)$, as asserted. A solution cannot be an endpoint because $CD>0$, so the positive $x,y$ analysis covers every possible solution.
ratingReason: Stewart’s theorem converts the distance condition into a reciprocal sum with a fixed total. Its minimum is given by Cauchy–Schwarz, and half-angle identities connect the resulting side condition to the stated one.
notes: Official released statement checked; worked exposition independently written and mathematically assessed.

statement: Let n≥3 and positive integers a₁,…,aₙ satisfy $n(a_k+1)-(n-1)a_{k-1}=1$ for 2≤k≤n. Prove $(n-1)^2$ does not divide aₙ.
solution: Put b_k=a_k+n−1. The recurrence becomes nb_k=(n−1)bₖ₋₁, so $n^{n-1}b_n=(n-1)^{n-1}b_1$. Since n and n−1 are coprime, (n−1)^(n−1) divides bₙ. As n≥3, bₙ is divisible by (n−1)². Therefore aₙ=bₙ−(n−1) is congruent to −(n−1) modulo (n−1)², which is nonzero.
ratingReason: An additive shift turns the affine recurrence into a geometric one; coprimality over all n−1 steps supplies much stronger divisibility than a single step.

statement: There are $n$ ($n \ge 2$) coins in a row. If one of the coins is head, select an odd number of consecutive coins (or even 1 coin) with the one in head on the leftmost, and then flip all the selected coins upside down simultaneously. This is a *move*. No move is allowed if all $n$ coins are tails. Suppose $n$ coins are heads at the initial stage, determine if there is a way to carry out $\lfloor \frac{2^{n+1}}{3} \rfloor$ moves. (posed by Gu Bin)
solution:
Yes. Encode heads by $1$ and tails by $0$, with the leftmost coin the most significant binary digit. In each move choose the rightmost head and flip the longest odd-length block starting there.

If the current binary integer is $V$ and there are $k$ zeroes after its rightmost $1$, then the move decreases $V$ by $1$ when $k$ is even and by $2$ when $k$ is odd. Consequently the process ends at $0$. A skipped integer is always odd, so every positive even integer below $2^n$ is visited. The number of skipped integers is therefore exactly the number of $V$ with $1\le V<2^n$ and odd $2$-adic valuation:
$$\sum_{\substack{1\le j<n\\j\text{ odd}}}2^{n-j-1}=\left\lfloor\frac{2^n}{3}\right\rfloor.$$
Starting at $2^n-1$, the total decrease equals the number of moves plus the number of skipped integers. Thus the number of moves is
$$2^n-1-\left\lfloor\frac{2^n}{3}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor\frac{2^{n+1}}3\right\rfloor,$$
as required.
ratingReason: Encodes positions in binary, constructs a legal descending strategy and counts its skipped states by 2-adic valuation.

statement:
If $x, y, z$ are positive real numbers, prove that
$$
(x+y+z)^{2}(y z+z x+x y)^{2} \leq 3\left(y^{2}+y z+z^{2}\right)\left(z^{2}+z x+x^{2}\right)\left(x^{2}+x y+y^{2}\right)
$$
solution:
We begin with the observation that
$$
x^{2}+x y+y^{2}=\frac{3}{4}(x+y)^{2}+\frac{1}{4}(x-y)^{2} \geq \frac{3}{4}(x+y)^{2}
$$
and similar bounds for $y^{2}+y z+z^{2}, z^{2}+z x+x^{2}$. Thus
$$
3\left(x^{2}+x y+y^{2}\right)\left(y^{2}+y z+z^{2}\right)\left(z^{2}+z x+x^{2}\right) \geq \frac{81}{64}(x+y)^{2}(y+z)^{2}(z+x)^{2}
$$
Thus it is sufficient to prove that
$$
(x+y+z)(x y+y z+z x) \leq \frac{9}{8}(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)
$$
Equivalently, we need to prove that
$$
8(x+y+z)(x y+y z+z x) \leq 9(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)
$$
However, we note that
$$
(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)=(x+y+z)(y z+z x+x y)-x y z
$$
Thus the required inequality takes the form
$$
(x+y)(y+z)(z+x) \geq 8 x y z
$$
This follows from AM-GM inequalities;
$$
x+y \geq 2 \sqrt{x y}, \quad y+z \geq 2 \sqrt{y z}, \quad z+x \geq 2 \sqrt{z x}
$$

statement: Prove that $\displaystyle S_n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom{2n+1}{2k+1}2^{3k}$ is not divisible by five for any integer $n\geq0$.
solution:
The binomial theorem gives
$$S_n=\frac{(1+\sqrt8)^{2n+1}-(1-\sqrt8)^{2n+1}}{2\sqrt8}.$$
The two squared bases have sum $18$ and product $49$, so
$$S_{n+2}=18S_{n+1}-49S_n,$$
with $S_0=1$, $S_1=11$. Reducing modulo five, the recurrence is
$$S_{n+2}\equiv3S_{n+1}+S_n\pmod5.$$
Starting from $(1,1)$, its first fourteen residues are
$$1,1,4,3,3,2,4,4,1,2,2,3,1,1.$$
The last pair repeats the first. Since each pair determines all subsequent terms, the first twelve residues repeat periodically. None is zero, proving that five never divides $S_n$.
ratingReason: Extract odd binomial terms with conjugate radicals, derive an integer recurrence, and establish a short nonzero residue cycle modulo five.
notes: Official released statement checked; worked exposition independently written and mathematically assessed.

title: Parallel stages for cutting a rectangular grid
statement: An $m\times n$ grid must be cut into unit squares. In each stage, any collection of current rectangular pieces may each be cut once along a grid line. What is the minimum number of stages?
solution: The minimum is $\lceil\log_2m\rceil+\lceil\log_2n\rceil$. A cut in an $a\times b$ rectangle leaves one child whose cut dimension is at least half the previous one. Therefore the quantity $\lceil\log_2a\rceil+\lceil\log_2b\rceil$ decreases by at most 1 along a suitable chain of descendants. A unit square has value 0, proving the lower bound. For attainment, bisect the row dimension as evenly as possible in every current piece at each stage, until all heights are 1; this takes $\lceil\log_2m\rceil$ stages. Repeat in the column dimension for $\lceil\log_2n\rceil$ stages.
ratingReason: A logarithmic potential gives a lower bound by following the larger piece at each cut; parallel bisections attain it.

statement: A non-empty set $A \subseteq \{1, 2, 3, \dots, n\}$ is called a *good set* of degree $n$ if $|A| \le \min_{x \in A} x$. Denote by $a_n$ the number of good sets of degree $n$. Prove that $a_{n+2} = a_{n+1} + a_n + 1$ for any positive integer $n$. (posed by Li Weigu)
solution:
Partition the good subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n+2\}$ into three classes. Those not containing $n+2$ are counted by $a_{n+1}$. The singleton $\{n+2\}$ contributes one.

For every remaining set, delete $n+2$ and subtract $1$ from each other element. If the original set has $k+1$ elements, its smallest element is at least $k+1$, so the new nonempty set has $k$ elements, minimum at least $k$, and maximum at most $n$. It is therefore a good set of degree $n$. Conversely, add $1$ to each element of any good set of degree $n$ and then adjoin $n+2$; this reverses the construction. This third class has $a_n$ members, proving $a_{n+2}=a_{n+1}+a_n+1$.
ratingReason: Finds a shift-and-delete bijection for good sets containing the largest element.

statement: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Suppose the incircle $\gamma$ of $ABC$ moves (slides) on $BC$ in the direction of $B$. Prove that when $\gamma$ touches $\Gamma$ internally, it also touches the altitude through $A$.
solution:
Let $\gamma'$ be the position of $\gamma$, when it touches $\Gamma$ internally, and let $K$ be its centre. Let $O$ be the circumcentre and $I$ be the in-centre of $ABC$. Since $AB = AC$, both of these lie on the altitude $AD$. If $T$ is the point of contact of $\Gamma$ and $\gamma'$, then $T, K, O$ are collinear. Hence $OK = OT - KT = R - r$, where $R$ and $r$ are respectively the circumradius and inradius of $ABC$. Note that $K$ and $I$ are at same distance $r$ from $BC$. Thus $KI$ is perpendicular to $AD$ at $I$. Using the right-angled triangle $OKI$, we have $OK^2 = OI^2 + IK^2$. But $OI^2 = R^2 - 2Rr$. Hence we obtain

![](assets/diagrams/3d49a27f99f78735db54.png)

$$
IK^2 = OK^2 - OI^2 = (R-r)^2 - (R^2 - 2Rr) = r^2.
$$

Thus $IK = r$ showing that $\gamma'$ touches $AD$ at $I$.

statement: Partition an $8\times8$ chessboard into nonoverlapping grid rectangles, each with equal numbers of black and white squares. Let their white-square counts be distinct, ordered $a_1<\cdots<a_p$. Determine the largest $p$ and all possible sequences at that value.
solution:
The maximum is $p=7$, and the possible white-square counts are
$$(1,2,3,4,5,7,10),\quad(1,2,3,4,5,8,9),$$
$$(1,2,3,4,6,7,9),\quad(1,2,3,5,6,7,8).$$

A grid rectangle contains equal numbers of the two colours exactly when its area is even. Hence the positive distinct integers $a_i$ sum to 32. Since $1+\cdots+8=36>32$, there can be at most seven pieces.

For seven pieces, put $d_i=a_i-i$. These are nonnegative nondecreasing integers with sum four. The five partitions of four yield the four sequences above and $(1,2,3,4,5,6,11)$. The latter would need a rectangle of area 22, whose only integer side lengths are $1,22$ or $2,11$, so it cannot fit on an eight-by-eight board.

Here are explicit tilings for the other four possibilities. Number columns and rows from 1 to 8. Each tuple below means (white-square count, first column, first row, width, height). In each list the rectangles are disjoint and fill the board; every area is twice its first entry, so its colours balance.

1. $(10,1,1,4,5)$; $(7,5,1,2,7)$; $(5,7,1,2,5)$; $(4,1,6,4,2)$; $(3,7,6,2,3)$; $(2,1,8,4,1)$; $(1,5,8,2,1)$.

2. $(9,1,1,3,6)$; $(8,4,1,2,8)$; $(5,6,1,2,5)$; $(4,8,1,1,8)$; $(3,6,6,2,3)$; $(2,1,7,2,2)$; $(1,3,7,1,2)$.

3. $(9,1,1,3,6)$; $(7,4,1,2,7)$; $(6,6,1,2,6)$; $(4,8,1,1,8)$; $(3,1,7,3,2)$; $(2,6,7,2,2)$; $(1,4,8,2,1)$.

4. $(8,1,1,2,8)$; $(7,3,1,2,7)$; $(6,5,1,2,6)$; $(5,7,1,2,5)$; $(3,7,6,2,3)$; $(2,5,7,2,2)$; $(1,3,8,2,1)$.
ratingReason: The distinct even areas give a sharp partition bound, but one formal size list is geometrically impossible. Four explicit tilings are needed to prove all remaining lists attainable.

statement: Find all positive integers $a$ such that $(2^n - n^2) \mid (a^n - n^a)$ for all positive integers $n \ge 5$. (posed by Yang Mingliang)
solution:
Taking $n=6$ shows that $a$ is even. Suppose an odd prime $p$ divides $a$, and take $n=p^2-1\ge8$. Fermat gives $2^n\equiv1\pmod p$, while $n^2\equiv1\pmod p$. Thus $p\mid2^n-n^2$, but $a^n-n^a\equiv-(-1)^a=-1\pmod p$, a contradiction. Therefore $a=2^t$ for an integer $t\ge1$.

Modulo $2^n-n^2$, we have $a^n=(2^n)^t\equiv n^{2t}$. The required divisibility therefore implies
$$2^n-n^2\mid n^{2t}-n^{2^t}.$$
For fixed $t$, the absolute value of the right side is smaller than $2^n-n^2$ for all sufficiently large $n$, because an exponential eventually exceeds every fixed power. It must consequently be zero, giving $2t=2^t$. The only positive solutions are $t=1,2$; for $t\ge3$, $2^t>2t$ by induction.

Finally $a=2$ gives the divisor itself, and $a=4$ gives $(2^n-n^2)(2^n+n^2)$. Thus $\boxed{a=2,4}$.
ratingReason: Universal divisibility first excludes odd prime factors of a, then exponential growth forces an equality between two polynomial exponents.

statement: Find the complete range, for positive $a,b,c,d$, of $\dfrac a{a+b+d}+\dfrac b{a+b+c}+\dfrac c{b+c+d}+\dfrac d{a+c+d}$.
solution:
The range is the open interval $(1,2)$.

Writing $T=a+b+c+d$, each denominator is less than $T$, so the sum $S$ is greater than $(a+b+c+d)/T=1$. On the other hand,
$$\frac a{a+b+d}+\frac b{a+b+c}<\frac a{a+b}+\frac b{a+b}=1,$$
and similarly the last two terms sum to less than one. Hence $S<2$.

For $a=1$, $b=t$, $c=d=t^2$, letting $t\downarrow0$ gives $S\to1$. For $a=c=1$, $b=d=t$, the same limit gives $S\to2$. Every intermediate value is attained: given $s\in(1,2)$, choose a positive tuple from the first family with $S<s$ and one from the second with $S>s$. The line segment between these tuples stays in the positive orthant, and $S$ is continuous on it. The intermediate value theorem supplies a tuple with $S=s$.
ratingReason: Simple denominator comparisons give strict bounds, but determining the entire range also requires two different limiting families and continuity.

statement: A $3\times3$ array of distinct positive integers has the same product $P$ in each row, column and diagonal. Show that exactly one $P$ lies between 5000 and 6500, and construct an array attaining it.

statement: Consider the quadratic polynomial $p(x) = x^2 + ax + b$, where $a, b$ are in the interval $[-2, 2]$. Find the range of the real roots of $p(x) = 0$, as $a$ and $b$ vary over $[-2, 2]$.
solution:
Suppose $a, b \in [-2, 2]$ and $\alpha$ is a real root of $x^2 + ax + b = 0$. Then
$$
\alpha = \frac{-a \pm \sqrt{a^2 - 4b}}{2},
$$
which shows that
$$
\alpha \leq \frac{2 + \sqrt{4 + 8}}{2} = 1 + \sqrt{3}.
$$
(Take $a = -2$, $b = -2$.) Similarly, we see that $\alpha \ge -1 - \sqrt{3}$, by taking $a = 2$ and $b = -2$. Take any real number $\lambda$ such that $|\lambda| \le 1$. We have
$$
(\lambda\alpha)^2 + (\lambda a)(\lambda\alpha) + \lambda^2 b = \lambda^2 (\alpha^2 + a\alpha + b) = 0.
$$
Thus $\lambda\alpha$ is also a root of the equation $x^2 + cx + d$, where
$c = \lambda a, \ d = \lambda^2 b.$
Note that $|c| \le |a|$ and $|d| \le |b|$. Thus for each real root $\alpha$ of $x^2 + ax + b = 0$ and each real $\lambda$ with $|\lambda| \le 1$, we see that $\lambda\alpha$ is also a root of $x^2 + cx + d$, where $c, d \in [-2, 2]$. Since $1 + \sqrt{3}$ is a root of $x^2 - 2x - 2 = 0$, it follows that $\lambda(1 + \sqrt{3})$ is in the range for any $\lambda$ with $|\lambda| \le 1$. Thus the range is $[-1 - \sqrt{3}, 1 + \sqrt{3}]$.
ratingReason: The quadratic formula gives the extreme root and scaling realizes every intermediate value.

statement: For a nonconstant polynomial $P$ with integer coefficients, let $N$ count the integers $k$ such that $P(k)^2=1$. Prove $N\leq\deg P+2$.
solution:
Let $d=\deg P$. If there are no such integers the claim is immediate. Otherwise choose the smallest one, $r$, and put $\varepsilon=P(r)\in\{1,-1\}$.

The polynomial $P(x)-\varepsilon$ has degree $d$, so at most $d$ distinct integer zeros. If instead $P(s)=-\varepsilon$, then $s>r$ and integer-coefficient polynomial divisibility gives
$$s-r\mid P(s)-P(r)=-2\varepsilon.$$
Thus $s-r$ is either one or two. The opposite-sign equation contributes at most the two integers $r+1,r+2$. Together there are at most $d+2$ occurrences, as required.
ratingReason: Choose the least integer at which the polynomial is plus or minus one. The polynomial difference divisibility restricts every opposite-sign occurrence to the next two integers.

statement: Find all the pairs $(a, b)$ of integers satisfying the following condition: there exists an integer $d \ge 2$ such that $a^n + b^n + 1$ is divisible by $d$ for all positive integers $n$.
solution:
The pairs are exactly those for which $a,b$ have opposite parity, or $a\equiv b\equiv1\pmod3$.

Indeed, let $p$ be a prime factor of a permissible $d$. If both $a,b$ vanish modulo $p$, the condition fails. If exactly one vanishes, use $n=p-1$: Fermat gives $2\equiv0\pmod p$, so $p=2$ and $a,b$ have opposite parity. If neither vanishes, the same exponent gives $3\equiv0\pmod p$, so $p=3$. The case $n=1$ then gives $a+b\equiv2\pmod3$; since both are nonzero residues, each must be $1$.

Conversely, opposite parity makes $a^n+b^n+1$ even for every positive $n$, and $a\equiv b\equiv1\pmod3$ makes it divisible by $3$ for every $n$.
ratingReason: Reduces the universal divisibility to a prime modulus and applies Fermat to classify whether neither or one variable vanishes.

statement:
Let $w_a, w_b, w_c$ be the lengths of the internal angle bisectors of a triangle $ABC$ with sides $a, b, c$.
Let $R$ be its circum-radius. Prove that
$$
\frac{b^2 + c^2}{w_a} + \frac{c^2 + a^2}{w_b} + \frac{a^2 + b^2}{w_c} > 4R.
$$
solution:
We use the standard
$$
w_a = \frac{2bc \cos(A/2)}{(b+c)}, \text{ etc.}
$$

The inequality takes the form
$$
\sum_{\text{cyclic}} \frac{(b^2 + c^2)(b+c)}{4Rbc \cos(A/2)} > 2.
$$
This may be put in the form
$$
\sum_{\text{cyclic}} \frac{(b^2 + c^2)(b+c) \sin(A/2)}{2abc} > 1.
$$
But note that $b^2+c^2 \ge 2bc$ and $b+c > a$. Hence it is sufficient to prove that $\sum_{\text{cyclic}} \sin(A/2) > 1$. We start with the identity
$$
\sum_{\text{cyclic}} \cos A = 1 + 4 \prod_{\text{cyclic}} \sin(A/2),
$$
which shows that $\sum_{\text{cyclic}} \cos A > 1$, in any triangle $ABC$. But, whenever $A, B, C$ are the angles of a triangle, we know that $(\pi - A)/2, (\pi - B)/2, (\pi - C)/2$ are also the angles of some other triangle. For this triangle, we get
$$
\sum_{\text{cyclic}} \cos \left( \frac{\pi - A}{2} \right) > 1.
$$
It follows that
$$
\sum_{\text{cyclic}} \sin \frac{A}{2} > 1,
$$
which is to be proved.

statement: An odd number of unit vectors lie in one closed half-plane bounded by a line through their common origin. Prove that their vector sum has length at least one.
solution:
Write their directions in order as $\theta_1\leq\cdots\leq\theta_{2m+1}$ in an interval of length $\pi$. Project every vector onto the unit direction $\theta_{m+1}$.

The median vector contributes one. Pair the vectors with indices $i$ and $2m+2-i$ for $1\leq i\leq m$. Their deviations from the median direction are $-u$ and $v$, with $u,v\geq0$ and $u+v\leq\pi$. Their total projection is
$$\cos u+\cos v=2\cos\frac{u+v}{2}\cos\frac{u-v}{2}\geq0.$$
Thus the whole sum has projection at least one onto a unit vector. Its length is at least the magnitude of that projection, proving the claim.
ratingReason: Project onto the median unit-vector direction. Pair the directions on opposite sides of the median; the semicircle condition ensures each pair has a nonnegative projection.

statement: There is a stone at each vertex of a given regular $13$-gon, and the color of each stone is black or white. Prove that we may exchange the position of two stones such that the coloring of these stones are symmetric with respect to some symmetric axis of the $13$-gon.
solution:
Let $b\le6$ be the number of stones of the less frequent color, called black. For each of the $13$ reflection axes, let $t$ count reflected pairs of opposite colors. Every black-white pair is paired by exactly one reflection, so the sum of these thirteen values is $b(13-b)$.

If the fixed vertex of an axis is black, then $t\equiv b-1\pmod2$; otherwise $t\equiv b\pmod2$. Suppose every $t$ were at least $3$. If $b$ is odd, the $b$ axes through black vertices have $t\ge4$, so the sum is at least $39+b>b(13-b)$ for $b=1,3,5$. If $b$ is even, the other $13-b$ axes have $t\ge4$, giving sum at least $52-b>b(13-b)$ for $b=0,2,4,6$. Both are impossible. Thus some axis has $t\le2$.

If $t=2$, exchange a black stone in one mismatched pair with a white stone in the other; both pairs become matched. If $t=1$, exchange the fixed-vertex stone with the opposite-colored stone in the mismatched pair. If $t=0$, exchange two stones of the same color. In every case one exchange produces symmetry about this axis.
ratingReason: Double-counts asymmetric pairs across all reflection axes, refines the average using parity, and shows how one swap repairs the resulting axis.

statement:
Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be an arbitrary arrangement of numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$ on a circle. Find
$$
\min \sum_{j=1}^{n} |a_j - a_{j+1}| \quad \text{and} \quad \max \sum_{j=1}^{n} |a_j - a_{j+1}|,
$$
where $a_{n+1} = a_1$ and the extrema are taken over all possible arrangements of $1, 2, \dots, n$.
solution:
**Minimum:** Consider $1$ and $n$ on the circle. They divide the circle into two arcs. The sum of the numbers on either of the arc is at least $n-1$. Suppose for example the numbers $1 = b_1, b_2, \dots, b_k = n$ appear on one of the arcs between $1$ and $n$, in that order. Then the sum of absolute differences of adjacent numbers on this arc is
$$
|1 - b_2| + |b_2 - b_3| + \dots + |b_{k-1} - n| \geq |1 - n| = n - 1.
$$
Similarly, the least sum of absolute differences on the other arc is also $n-1$. Hence we see that
$$
\sum_{j=1}^{n} |a_{j+1} - a_{j}| \geq 2(n-1).
$$
This is achieved by the permutation $(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n)$, where $a_j = j$ for $1 \le j \le n$.

**Maximum:** We have
$$
\sum_{j=1}^{n} |a_{j+1} - a_{j}| = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \pm (a_{j+1} - a_{j}).
$$
Each of the numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$ appear in the right side sum twice. Hence to get a maximum sum we should have positive sign to larger numbers in both occurrences and smaller number should go with negative sign. Thus $n, (n-1), (n-2), \dots, [n/2]$ should get positive signs and $1, 2, 3, \dots, [n/2] - 1$ should get negative signs. This happens when:
for even $n$, the arrangement is $1, n, 2, (n-1), 3, (n-2), \dots, n/2, (n/2) + 1$;
for odd $n$, the arrangement is $1, n, 2, (n-1), 3, (n-2), \dots, [n/2] + 2, [n/2] + 1$.
The corresponding sums are:
$$
\frac{n^2}{2} \text{ when } n \text{ is even, } \quad \frac{n^2-1}{2} \text{ when } n \text{ is odd.}
$$
ratingReason: The minimum uses the two arcs from 1 to n; the maximum counts positive and negative contributions and constructs an alternating arrangement.

statement: Does there exist a finite noncoplanar set of points in space such that for every pair $A,B$, two other points $C,D$ can be chosen with $AB$ and $CD$ parallel and distinct?
solution:
Yes. Take two regular hexagons of the same size, centred at $O$, in perpendicular planes, sharing one pair of opposite vertices. Their union has ten points and is not coplanar.

First, a regular hexagon itself has the required property. For a pair which is not opposite, central reflection gives two other endpoints and a parallel distinct chord. For opposite vertices, their long diagonal is parallel to a side not using either endpoint.

Now consider a pair from the union. If both points lie in one hexagon, use the preceding planar property. Otherwise one point belongs exclusively to each hexagon. Their central reflections $A'=-A$, $B'=-B$ are also in the union and distinct from $A,B$. The lines $AB$ and $A'B'$ are parallel. If they coincided, their common line would pass through $O$, forcing $A,B$ to be antipodal points on the common circumradius sphere. But antipodes lie in the same hexagon, contradicting the chosen cross-plane pair. Hence these lines are distinct, proving the construction works.
ratingReason: Combine two centrally symmetric planar examples along a common diameter. Central reflection supplies parallel partners for cross-plane pairs while the hexagon handles diameters.

statement: Two bags contain positive numbers $m,n$ of balls. You may remove the same number from both bags, or double the number in one bag. Can both bags always be emptied? What changes if doubling is replaced by tripling?
solution: For doubling, repeatedly double the smaller positive count until the counts can be named $a,b$ with $a\le b<2a$. If $a=b$, remove everything. Otherwise subtract $b-a$ from both bags to obtain $(2a-b,a)$. Both counts are positive and the new maximum $a$ is strictly smaller than the old maximum $b$ (doubling the smaller count up to this point never increased that maximum). Induction on the maximum count eventually reaches equal counts. For tripling, the answer is no: starting with opposite parities gives an odd total, and both allowed operations change the total by an even number, so zero total is unreachable.
ratingReason: A descent algorithm proves the positive result, while an invariant distinguishes the altered operation.

title: The least value of an increasing multiplicative function
statement: A function $f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ is strictly increasing and satisfies $f(ab)=f(a)f(b)$ and $f(3)\ge7$. What is the smallest possible $f(3)$?
solution: The choice $f(n)=n^2$ attains 9. Since $f(1)=1$, we have $f(2)\ge2$. If $f(2)=2$, then $f(3)<f(4)=4$, impossible. If $f(2)=3$, monotonicity and multiplicativity give $f(27)=f(3)^3\ge343>243=f(32)$, again impossible. Thus $f(2)\ge4$, so $f(3)^2=f(9)>f(8)=f(2)^3\ge64$. As $f(3)$ is integral, it is at least 9.
ratingReason: Multiplicativity turns strategically chosen comparisons 27<32 and 8<9 into bounds ruling out f(3)=7,8.

statement: The incircle of triangle $ABC$, centered at $I$, touches $AB,AC$ at $D,E$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of $BCI$. Prove $\angle ODB=\angle OEC$.
solution: Let $L$ be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ not containing $A$ in the circumcircle of $ABC$. The line $AL$ is the internal angle bisector, so $A,I,L$ are collinear. The usual angle-bisector arc lemma gives $LB=LC=LI$: for instance, $\angle LBI=(A+B)/2=\angle BIL$, and similarly for $C$. Thus $L$ is the circumcentre of $BCI$, namely $O$. Reflection in $AI$ fixes $O$, exchanges the incircle contact points $D,E$, and carries the ray $DB$ to the ray $EC$. It therefore carries $\angle ODB$ to $\angle OEC$, proving equality.
ratingReason: The circumcentre of BCI is the midpoint of arc BC opposite A; recognising that standard incenter lemma makes reflection across AI finish the problem.

solution:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be the vertices, $I$ the in-center, $H$ the ortho-centre, $O$ the circum-center and $N$ the nine-point center of the triangle.

**Claim 1:** (b) $\Leftrightarrow IH = IO$ (for a non-equilateral triangle).

The line $NI$ joins the centre of nine-point circle and the centre of in-circle, so $NI$ is perpendicular to the common tangent to in-circle and nine-point circle (we use $N \neq I$, as triangle is not equilateral). Thus (b) is equivalent to the statement that $NI$ is perpendicular to the Euler-line.

Since $O$, $H$, $N$ are on the Euler-line and $N$ is the midpoint of $OH$, we have:
(b) $\Leftrightarrow NI$ is the perpendicular bisector of $OH$.

But the perpendicular bisector of $O$, $H$ is simply the locus of all points $P$ such that $OP = HP$. Thus (b) $\Leftrightarrow IH = IO$.

**Claim 2:** $IH = IO \Leftrightarrow AH = AO$ or $A$, $H$, $O$, $I$ are conicyclic.

Because $H$ and $O$ are isogonal conjugates $\angle HAI = \angle OAH$. Also $AI$ is common. Thus the condition $AH = AO$ gives that $\triangle AHI$ and $\triangle OHI$ are congruent. This gives $IH = IO$.

If on the other hand $A$, $H$, $O$, $I$ are con-cyclic, then $IH$ and $IO$ subtend the same angle at $A$. This implies that $IH = IO$.

Thus $AH = AO$ or $A$, $H$, $O$, $I$ con-cyclic implies that $IH = IO$.

Conversely, suppose $IH = IO$. Then $\frac{IH}{AI} = \frac{IO}{AI}$. This implies that
$$
\frac{\sin \angle HAI}{\sin \angle AHI} = \frac{\sin \angle OAI}{\sin \angle AOI}
$$
It follows that $\sin \angle AHI = \sin \angle AOI$ since $AI$ bisects $\angle HAO$. This tells that $\angle AHI + \angle AOI = \pi$ or $\angle AHI = \angle AOI$. In the first case $A$, $H$, $O$, $I$ are conicyclic. In the second case $AH = AO$.

Thus we have shown that $IH = IO$ if and only if $A$, $H$, $O$, $I$ are con-cyclic or $AH = AO$.

**Claim 3:** $IH = IO$ if and only if $AH = AO$, or $BH = BO$, or $CH = CO$

Suppose $IH = IO$. Clearly the circum-circle of $\triangle HOI$ does not pass through all of $A$, $B$, $C$, because then $O$ would lie on the circum-circle of $\triangle A$, $B$, $C$. Without loss of generality, assume that it does not pass through $A$. Then $AH = AO$, because $IH = IO$ and $A$, $H$, $O$, $I$ are not conicyclic. (In the other two cases, we have $BH = BO$ or $CH = CO$ depending on whether the circum-circle does not pass through $B$ or $C$ respectively.) The other part follows directly from claim 2.

**Claim 4:** $AH = AO$, $BH = BO$ or $CH = CO$ if and only if angles of $ABC$ are in arithmetic progression.

Let $R$ be the circum-radius so that $AO = BO = CO = R$. Then $AH = 2R\cos A$, $BH = 2R\cos B$, and $CH = 2R\cos C$. Thus $AH = AO \Leftrightarrow A = \frac{\pi}{3}$; $BH = BO \Leftrightarrow B = \frac{\pi}{3}$; $CH = CO \Leftrightarrow C = \frac{\pi}{3}$.

Now $AH = AO$, $BH = BO$ or $CH = CO$ implies that one of the angles of triangle $ABC$ is $\pi/3$. But clearly, one angle is $\pi/3$ if and only if angles are in arithmetic progression.

Thus (b) $\Leftrightarrow IH = IO$ (by claim 1) $\Leftrightarrow AH = AO$, $BH = BO$, or $CH = CO$ (by claim 3) $\Leftrightarrow$ angles are in arithmetic progression which is (a).

statement: Among real $a,b$ for which $x^4+ax^3+bx^2+ax+1=0$ has a real root, find the least possible value of $a^2+b^2$.
solution:
A root is nonzero. Divide by $x^2$ and put $t=x+1/x$, so $|t|\geq2$. The equation becomes
$$t^2+at+b-2=0.$$
Cauchy–Schwarz gives
$$a^2+b^2\geq\frac{(at+b)^2}{t^2+1}=\frac{(t^2-2)^2}{t^2+1}.$$
For $u=t^2\geq4$,
$$\frac{(u-2)^2}{u+1}-\frac45=\frac{(u-4)(5u-4)}{5(u+1)}\geq0.$$
Thus $a^2+b^2\geq4/5$.

Equality is attained at $(a,b)=(-4/5,-2/5)$, where $x=1$ is a root, and at $(a,b)=(4/5,-2/5)$, where $x=-1$ is a root. Therefore the required minimum is $4/5$.
ratingReason: The reciprocal polynomial reduces to a quadratic in $x+1/x$. Cauchy–Schwarz then minimises the coefficient norm over the feasible parameter range.

statement: Prove that a product of four consecutive positive integers cannot equal a product of two consecutive positive integers.
solution: Write $A=n^2+3n+1$. Then $n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)=A^2-1$. If this equals $m(m+1)$, then $(2m+1)^2=4A^2-3$. Since $n\ge1$, $A\ge5$, and $(2A-1)^2<4A^2-3<(2A)^2$, impossible for a square.
ratingReason: A near-square identity for four consecutive factors turns the problem into a strict gap between consecutive squares.

title: A rotation that exchanges the two edge colours
statement: Join every pair of $n$ labelled points on a circle. Colour each segment red or blue so that rotating both endpoints one position changes its colour. (a) For which $n$ can this be done? (b) Prove any two points can be connected using at most three red segments.
solution: (a) Every edge orbit under rotation must have even length. Non-antipodal edges have orbit length $n$, and antipodal edges (when $n$ is even) have orbit length $n/2$. Hence $4\mid n$, which is also sufficient: alternate colours on each orbit. (For $n=1$ the edge-free case is vacuous.) (b) Rotation is an isomorphism between the red graph and its complement. If two vertices $x,y$ have no blue path of length at most two, then $xy$ is red and every other vertex has a red edge to at least one of $x,y$. Consequently every pair of vertices has a red path of length at most three, through $x,y$ if necessary. If no such pair $x,y$ exists, the blue graph has diameter at most two, and its isomorphic red graph does too.
ratingReason: The antipodal edge orbit determines the parity obstruction; the diameter claim then uses the relation between a graph and its complement.

statement: There are $n$ cities ($n \ge 3$) and two airline companies in a country. Between any two cities, there is exactly one 2-way flight connecting them which is operated by one of the two companies. A female mathematician plans a travel route, so that it starts and ends at the same city, passes through at least two other cities, and each city in the route is visited once. She finds out that wherever she starts and whatever route she chooses, she must take flights of both companies. Find the maximum value of $n$.
solution:
Color each edge of the complete graph by its airline. The hypothesis says that neither color contains a cycle, so each color forms a forest and has at most $n-1$ edges. Therefore
$$\binom n2\le2(n-1),$$
which gives $n\le4$.

For four cities numbered $1,2,3,4$, give one airline the edges $12,23,34$ and the other the edges $13,14,24$. Each color is a path and has no cycle. Thus every round trip using at least three distinct cities uses both colors. The maximum is $\boxed4$.
ratingReason: Interprets each company’s network as a forest, obtains a global edge bound, and constructs a sharp two-path example.

statement:
Let $X$ be the set of all bijective functions from the set $S = \{1, 2, 3, ..., n\}$ to itself. For each $f \in X$, define
$$
T_f(j) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } f^{(12)}(j) = j, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}
$$

Determine
$$ \sum_{f \in X} \sum_{j=1}^{n} T_f(j). $$
(Here $f^{(k)}(x) = f(f^{(k-1)}(x))$ for $k \ge 2$.)
solution: An element $j$ satisfies $f^{(12)}(j)=j$ exactly when its cycle length $d$ divides 12. For fixed $j$ and $d\le n$, choose the other $d-1$ labels in the cycle, order that cycle from $j$, and permute the remaining labels. This gives $\binom{n-1}{d-1}(d-1)!(n-d)!=(n-1)!$ permutations. Summing over $j$ and the eligible divisors gives $\boxed{n!\,\#\{d:d\mid12,\ d\le n\}}$.
ratingReason: Reverse the summation order and count permutations where a fixed element belongs to a cycle whose length divides 12.

statement: A detector senses every point within distance half the altitude of an equilateral triangle. Starting at one vertex, a person must follow a path whose detector covers the entire triangle. Determine a path of minimum length.
solution:
Scale the triangle to side one and label the starting vertex $A$, the others $B,C$. Set $r=\sqrt3/4$, the detector radius. Let $E$ be the midpoint of $AC$, and $X$ the midpoint of $BE$. Thus $BX=EX=r$. On $XC$, choose $Y$ with $CY=r$. The optimal route is $A\to X\to Y$, or its reflection exchanging $B,C$, with length
$$AX+XY=\frac{2\sqrt7-\sqrt3}{4}.$$
For side length $s$, multiply this length by $s$.

To prove the lower bound, any valid route must enter the radius-$r$ disks centred at $B$ and $C$. Suppose it reaches the $B$ disk first, at $U$. The travel up to $U$ and then to the $C$ disk is at least
$$AU+UC-r.$$
Use coordinates with $AC$ horizontal and $E$ its midpoint. Every point $U$ of the $B$ disk has height at least $r$ above $AC$. If that height is $h$, the sum $AU+UC$ is minimised at horizontal coordinate $E$, by reflection and the triangle inequality, and is at least $2\sqrt{1/4+h^2}$. Therefore it is at least $2\sqrt{1/4+r^2}=\sqrt7/2$. Equality occurs at $U=X$, giving the stated bound and route.

Finally verify coverage, not just the two vertices. The set within distance $r$ of a segment is convex. The neighbourhood of $AX$ contains $A,B,E$, because $B,E$ are both distance $r$ from $X$; hence it contains triangle $ABE$. The neighbourhood of $XY$ contains $B,E,C$, using $CY=r$; hence it contains triangle $BCE$. Those triangles fill $ABC$. Thus the proposed path detects the whole region and attains the lower bound.
ratingReason: The two far vertices impose a shortest route through two disks. Symmetry identifies the first contact, and convexity of segment neighbourhoods verifies that the optimal route actually covers the entire triangle.
notes: Official statement checked. The shortest-route argument was checked against Scholes; full-region coverage is explicitly proved using convex segment neighbourhoods.

statement: In acute triangle $ABC$, let $D,E,F$ be the feet of the altitudes from $A,B,C$. Prove $DE+DF\le BC$, and determine equality.
solution: Write $a=BC,b=CA,c=AB$ and let $R$ be the circumradius. The right-angle cyclic quadrilaterals give $DE=c\cos C$ and $DF=b\cos B$. Thus $DE+DF=2R(\sin C\cos C+\sin B\cos B)=2R\sin(B+C)\cos(B-C)=a\cos(B-C)\le a$. Equality holds exactly when $B=C$, equivalently $AB=AC$.
ratingReason: The orthic sides must be expressed in the original angles; the resulting sum reduces to a single cosine bound.

statement: Let $a_1 \le a_2 \le \dots$ be a sequence of positive integers such that $\frac{r}{a_r} = k+1$ for some positive integers $k$ and $r$. Prove that there exists a positive integer $s$ such that $\frac{s}{a_s} = k$.
solution:
Because $r=(k+1)a_r$, there is an index with $s\ge k a_s$. Let $s$ be the least such positive index. If $s=1$, then $1\ge k a_1\ge1$, giving equality. If $s>1$, minimality and integrality imply
$$s-1<k a_{s-1}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad s\le k a_{s-1}\le k a_s\le s,$$
where the middle inequality uses monotonicity. Every inequality is therefore an equality, so $s/a_s=k$.
ratingReason: A first-crossing argument combines integrality with the nondecreasing denominators.

statement:
Let $a, b, c$ be non-negative real numbers such that $a+b \le c+1$, $b+c \le a+1$ and $c+a \le b+1$. Prove that
$$
a^2 + b^2 + c^2 \le 2abc + 1.
$$
solution:
Adding the first two, we get $2b \le 2$ so that $b \le 1$. Similarly, we get $c \le 1$ and $a \le 1$. Put $\alpha = 1 - a$, $\beta = 1 - b$ and $\gamma = 1 - c$. Then $0 \le \alpha, \beta, \gamma \le 1$ and
$$
\alpha + \beta\gamma, \quad \beta + \gamma \ge \alpha, \quad \gamma + \alpha \ge \alpha.
$$
The inequality to be proved reduces to
$$
\alpha^2 + \beta^2 + \gamma^2 \le 2(\alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha) - 2\alpha\beta\gamma.
$$
We may assume that $\gamma$ is the largest among the three, so that $\alpha \le \gamma$ and $\beta \le \gamma$. Using $\gamma \le \alpha + \beta$, we get $\gamma^2 \le \gamma(\alpha + \beta)$. Also $\alpha^2 \le \alpha\gamma$ and $\beta^2 \le \beta\gamma$. Thus $\alpha^2 + \beta^2 + \gamma^2 \le 2(\alpha\gamma + \beta\gamma)$. Hence it suffices to prove that $2\alpha\beta\gamma \le 2\alpha\beta$. This follows from $\gamma \le 1$.
ratingReason: Complement the variables to turn the hypotheses into triangle inequalities; order the new variables and bound each square by a product.

statement: A set $G$ of nonconstant real affine functions $f(x)=ax+b$ is closed under composition and taking inverses. Every member has a real fixed point. Prove that all members share one fixed point.
solution:
If $G$ is empty or consists only of the identity, any real number works. Otherwise choose a nonidentity $f\in G$.

For any $u,v\in G$, their commutator $u\circ v\circ u^{-1}\circ v^{-1}$ belongs to $G$. Its slope is one, so it is a translation $x\mapsto x+c$. The fixed-point hypothesis forces $c=0$. Thus every commutator is the identity and all functions in $G$ commute.

The chosen nonidentity $f$ cannot have slope one, because a nonidentity translation has no fixed point. It therefore has a unique fixed point $k$. For any $g\in G$, commutativity gives
$$f(g(k))=g(f(k))=g(k).$$
So $g(k)$ is also a fixed point of $f$, and uniqueness implies $g(k)=k$. Hence this $k$ is fixed by every member of $G$.
ratingReason: A commutator has slope one and must have a fixed point, so it is the identity. Commutativity then transports one unique fixed point to itself under every group element.

statement: Find the number of integers $k$ in the set $\{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 2012\}$ such that the combination number $\binom{2012}{k} = \frac{2012!}{k!(2012-k)!}$ is a multiple of $2012$.
solution:
Since $2012=4\cdot503$ and $503$ is prime, first count indices for which $4$ divides the binomial coefficient. The binary expansion of $2012$ is $11111011100$, with eight $1$ bits. The standard factorial valuation formula gives
$$v_2\binom Nk=s_2(k)+s_2(N-k)-s_2(N),$$
equivalently the number of carries when adding $k$ and $N-k$ in base two.

There are $2^8=256$ indices with no carry. For exactly one carry, it must start at a zero bit followed immediately by a one bit. In this expansion the only possibilities are positions $1$ and $5$ (positions start at zero). The initiating bit of $k$ is $1$, the next bit is $0$, and the other seven one-bit positions are free. Each position gives $2^7=128$ choices. Thus exactly $512$ coefficients fail divisibility by $4$, leaving $2013-512=1501$ divisible by $4$.

Modulo $503$, the identity $(1+X)^{2012}\equiv(1+X^{503})^4$ shows that only the five indices $0,503,1006,1509,2012$ fail divisibility by $503$. The endpoints are already excluded by the factor $4$ condition. For the other three indices, the binary valuation formula gives respectively $7,8,7$, so all three must be removed from the count $1501$. Therefore the answer is $\boxed{1498}$.
ratingReason: Combines prime-modulus binomial coefficients with a precise count of binary carries for divisibility by four.

statement:
Define $f, g, h$ on $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}$ as follows:
$$
f(x, y, z) = (3x + 2y + 2z, 2x + 2y + z, 2x + y + 2z),
$$
$$
g(x, y, z) = (3x + 2y - 2z, 2x + 2y - z, 2x + y - 2z),
$$
$$
h(x, y, z) = (3x - 2y + 2z, 2x - y + 2z, 2x - 2y + z).
$$
Given a primitive Pythagorean triplet $(x, y, z)$, with $x > y > z$, prove that starting from $(5, 4, 3)$, the triplet $(x, y, z)$ can be obtained, in a unique way, by repeated application of $f, g, h$ in some order. (Example: $(697, 528, 455) = f \circ h \circ g \circ h(5, 4, 3)$.)
solution:
Let
$$
u = u(x, y, z) = 3x - 2y - 2z,$$
$$v = v(x, y, z) = -2x + 2y + z,$$
$$w = w(x, y, z) = -2x + y + 2z.$$
First of all, if $(x, y, z) \neq (5, 4, 3)$ is a primitive Pythagorean triplet with $x > y > z > 0$, then, it is easy to check that $u^2 = v^2 + w^2$. Further, $x^2 + (2y - 2z)^2 > 0 \Rightarrow 9x^2 > 4y^2 + 4z^2 + 8yz \Rightarrow 3x > 2y + 2z \Rightarrow u(x, y, z) > 0$.
Similarly, we have $4y > 3z \Rightarrow 4yz - 3z^2 > 0 \Rightarrow 4y^2 + z^2 + 4yz > 4x^2 \Rightarrow 2y + z > 2x \Rightarrow v(x, y, z) > 0$.
Next, $(3y - 4z)^2 > 0 \Rightarrow 25x^2 + (3y - 4z)^2 > 25x^2 \Rightarrow 25x^2 > 16y^2 + 9z^2 + 24yz \Rightarrow 25x^2 > (4y + 3x)^2 \Rightarrow 5x > 4y + 3z \Rightarrow u(x, y, z) > v(x, y, z)$.

Similarly, we have $u(x, y, z) > w(x, y, z)$. Also, since $x > y$, it follows that $u(x, y, z) > -w(x, y, z)$. And, $y > z$ implies $v(x, y, z) > w(x, y, z)$. Finally, we notice that if $y + z > x$ then it follows that $u(x, y, z) < x$. Now, let
$$
f_1(x, y, z) = (u, v, w),
$$
$$
g_1(x, y, z) = (u, v, -w),
$$
$$
h_1(x, y, z) = (u, -w, v).
$$
Then, it is easy to see that $f_1(f(x, y, z)) = g_1(g(x, y, z)) = h_1(h(x, y, z)) = (x, y, z)$. Further, it is easy to check that $\text{gcd}(u, v, w) = \text{gcd}(x, y, z)$.

Now, we shall prove the result by contradiction. If there are primitive Pythagorean triplets that are not obtained from $(5, 4, 3)$ by repeated application of $f, g$ and $h$ in some order, then let $(a, b, c)$ be the triplet that cannot be obtained from $(5, 4, 3)$ with $a > b > c > 0$ and with least possible value for $a$. So, all the primitive Pythagorean triplets $(x, y, z)$ with $a > x > y > z > 0$ are obtained from $(5, 4, 3)$ (uniquely). Clearly, we have $a > 5$.
Now, let $f_1(a, b, c) = (k, l, m)$. Then, $g_1(a, b, c) = (k, l, -m)$ and $h_1(a, b, c) = (k, -m, l)$. As noted before, $k$ and $l$ are positive, and $k > l, k > m$ and $k > -m$. Thus, there is a unique $\Delta \in \{f_1, g_1, h_1\}$ such that $\Delta(a, b, c) = (r, s, t)$ with $r > s > t > 0$. Also, from the previous calculations, we have

that $a > r$. Thus, by the minimality of $a$, it follows that $(r, s, t)$ is obtained from $(5, 4, 3)$, in a unique way, by repeated applications of $f, g, h$ in some order. But, now $\Delta(a, b, c) = (r, s, t)$ implies that by applying one of $f, g$ and $h$ to $(r, s, t)$ we would get $(a, b, c)$. Therefore, we can obtain $(a, b, c)$ from $(5, 4, 3)$ by repeated applications of $f, g, h$ in some order. This is a contradiction. Uniqueness follows from the uniqueness of $\Delta$. This completes the solution.
ratingReason: Invert the three transformations and prove a unique descending branch with substantial sign and ordering analysis.

statement:
Given positive $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ and $0<q<1$, construct positive $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ such that $b_k>a_k$, $q<b_{k+1}/b_k<1/q$, and
$$\sum_{k=1}^nb_k<\frac{1+q}{1-q}\sum_{k=1}^na_k.$$
solution:
Set $c_i=\sum_{j=1}^na_jq^{|i-j|}$. For every $i<n$,
$$c_{i+1}-qc_i=(1-q^2)\sum_{j=i+1}^na_jq^{j-i-1}>0,$$
and
$$c_i-qc_{i+1}=(1-q^2)\sum_{j=1}^ia_jq^{i-j}>0.$$
Thus $q<c_{i+1}/c_i<1/q$.

Also $c_i\geq a_i$, and reversing the finite sums gives
$$\sum_i c_i=\sum_j a_j\sum_{i=1}^nq^{|i-j|}<\sum_j a_j\left(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}q^k\right)=\frac{1+q}{1-q}\sum_j a_j.$$
The inequality is strict because each finite inner sum omits some positive terms from the infinite two-sided series.

Choose $\varepsilon>0$ sufficiently small that multiplying the left side by $1+\varepsilon$ still preserves this strict total bound, and put $b_i=(1+\varepsilon)c_i$. Then $b_i>a_i$, the adjacent ratios are unchanged, and the total has the desired bound. This also handles $n=1$, when there are no ratio conditions.
ratingReason: Smooth the data with a two-sided geometric kernel. Separate the contributions on either side of each index to control adjacent ratios, then use the geometric-series sum for the total bound.

statement: For a finite sequence of nonnegative integers, replace each term by the number of smaller terms to its right. Repeat this operation. Prove that eventually the sequence stops changing.
solution: The last entry becomes 0 after one operation and stays so. Work backward by induction. Suppose all entries to the right of position $i$ have stabilised at $c_{i+1},\ldots,c_n$. Thereafter position $i$ iterates the map $h(t)=\#\{j>i:c_j<t\}$. This map is nondecreasing and takes values in $\{0,\ldots,n-i\}$. If an iterate is at least its predecessor, monotonicity makes all later iterates nondecreasing; if it is at most its predecessor, all later iterates are nonincreasing. A bounded monotone integer sequence stabilises. Thus position $i$ eventually stabilises too. Induction reaches the first entry.
ratingReason: Stabilisation propagates from the last coordinate to the first; once the tail is fixed, a coordinate iterates a bounded nondecreasing integer map.

One suitable triple is $\boxed{(l,m,n)=(3,11,36)}$. Indeed,
$$\sum_{k=1}^3k=6,\qquad\sum_{k=4}^{11}k=66-6=60,\qquad\sum_{k=12}^{36}k=666-66=600.$$

statement:
1. In a non-equilateral triangle $A B C$, the sides $a, b, c$ form an arithmetic progression. Let $I$ and $O$ denote the incentre and circumcentre of the triangle respectively.

a. Prove that $I O$ is perpendicular to $B I$.

b. Suppose $B I$ extended meets $A C$ in $K$, and $D, E$ are the midpoints of $B C, B A$ respectively. Prove that $I$ is the circumcentre of triangle $D K E$.
solution:
a.
Extend $B I$ to meet the circumcircle in $F$. Then we know that $F A = F I = F C$. (See Figure)

![A geometric diagram of triangle ABC with its circumcircle, incentre I, circumcentre O, and several points and lines: B I extended to meet the circumcircle at F, midpoints D and E, perpendicular IL, and point K on AC. Several auxiliary lines and points are labeled.](assets/diagrams/7e6f06f2c843ed4e6b58.jpg)

Let $B I : I F = \lambda : \mu$. Applying Stewart's theorem to triangle $B A F$, we get
$$
\lambda A F^{2} + \mu A B^{2} = (\lambda + \mu)\left(A I^{2} + B I \cdot I F\right)
$$
Similarly, Stewart's theorem to triangle $B C F$ gives
$$
\lambda C F^{2} + \mu B C^{2} = (\lambda + \mu)\left(C I^{2} + B I \cdot I F\right)
$$
Since $C F = A F$, subtraction gives
$$
\mu\left(A B^{2} - B C^{2}\right) = (\lambda + \mu)\left(A I^{2} - C I^{2}\right)
$$
Using the standard notations $A B = c$, $B C = a$, $C A = b$ and $s = (a + b + c) / 2$, we get $A I^{2} = r^{2} + (s - a)^{2}$ and $C I^{2} = r^{2} + (s - c)^{2}$ where $r$ is the in-radius of $A B C$. Thus
$$
\mu\left(c^{2} - a^{2}\right) = (\lambda + \mu)\left((s - a)^{2} - (s - c)^{2}\right) = (\lambda + \mu)(c - a) b
$$
It follows that either $c = a$ or $\mu(c + a) = (\lambda + \mu) b$. But $c = a$ implies that $a = b = c$ since $a, b, c$ are in arithmetic progression. However, we have taken a non-equilateral triangle $A B C$. Thus $c \neq a$ and we have $\mu(c + a) = (\lambda + \mu) b$. But $c + a = 2 b$ and we obtain
$$
2 b \mu = (\lambda + \mu) b.
$$
We conclude that $\lambda = \mu$. This in turn tells that $I$ is the mid-point of $B F$. Since $O F = O B$, we conclude that $O I$ is perpendicular to $B F$.


Alternatively

Applying Ptolemy's theorem to the cyclic quadrilateral $A B C F$, we get
$$
A B \cdot C F + A F \cdot B C = B F \cdot C A
$$
Since $C F = A F$, we get $C F(c + a) = B F \cdot b = B F(c + a) / 2$. This gives $B F = 2 C F = 2 I F$. Hence $I$ is the mid-point of $B F$ and as earlier we conclude that $O I$ is perpendicular to $B F$.


Alternatively

Join $B O$. We have to prove that $\angle B I O = 90^{\circ}$, which is equivalent to $B I^{2} + I O^{2} = B O^{2}$. Draw $I L$ perpendicular to $A B$. Let $R$ denote the circumradius of $A B C$ and let $\triangle$ denote its area. Observe that $B O = R$, $I O^{2} = R^{2} - 2 R r$,
$$
B I = \frac{B L}{\cos (B / 2)} = (s - b) \sqrt{\frac{c a}{s(s - b)}}
$$
Thus we obtain
$$
B I^{2} = a c (s - b) / s = \frac{a c}{3}
$$
since $a, b, c$ are in arithmetic progression. Thus we need to prove that
$$
\frac{a c}{3} + R^{2} - 2 R r = R^{2}
$$
This reduces to proving $2 R r = a c / 3$. But
$$
2 R r = 2 \cdot \frac{a b c}{4 \Delta} \cdot \frac{\Delta}{s} = \frac{a b c}{2 s} = \frac{a b c}{a + b + c} = \frac{a c}{3}
$$
using $a + c = 2 b$. This proves the claim.


b.
Join $I D$. Note that $\angle B I O = \angle B D O = 90^{\circ}$. Hence $B, D, I, O$ are concyclic and hence $\angle B I D = \angle B O D = A$. Since $\angle D B I = \angle K B A = B / 2$, it follows that triangles $B A K$ and $B I D$ are similar. This gives
$$
\frac{B A}{B I} = \frac{B K}{B D} = \frac{A K}{I D}
$$
However, we have seen earlier that $B I = a c / 3$. Moreover $A K = b c / (a + c)$. Thus we obtain
$$
B K = \frac{B A \cdot B D}{B I} = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{3 a c}, \quad I D = \frac{A K \cdot B I}{B A} = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{a c}{3}}.
$$
By symmetry, we must have $I E = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{a c}{3}}$. Finally
$$
I K = \frac{b}{a + b + c} \cdot B K = \frac{1}{3} B K = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{a c}{3}}
$$
Thus $I D = I E = I K$ and $I$ is the circumcentre of $D K E$.


Alternatively

Observe that $A K = b c / (a + c) = c / 2 = A E$. Since $A I$ bisects angle $A$, we see that $A I E$ is congruent to $A I K$. This gives $I E = I K$. Similarly $C I D$ is congruent to $C I K$ giving $I D = I K$. We conclude that $I D = I K = I E$.

title: Guessing an integer using prime sums
statement: Alice chooses an integer $a$ with $1\le a\le2006$. On each turn Bob names a positive integer $b$ and learns whether $a+b$ is prime. Prove he can always determine $a$ in fewer than 2006 turns.
solution: It suffices to separate any two remaining candidates $u<v$. Put $d=v-u$ and choose a prime $q>v$. The progression $q,q+d,q+2d,\ldots$ starts with a prime, but its term $q+qd=q(1+d)$ is composite. Let $k\ge1$ be the first index with $q+kd$ composite. Then $b=q+(k-1)d-u>0$ makes $u+b$ prime and $v+b$ composite. This query eliminates at least one of the candidates. Repeat while more than one remains. Starting from 2006 candidates requires at most 2005 queries.
ratingReason: Any two candidates can be separated by a prime/composite translate; the separating query comes from the first composite term in a finite prime-started arithmetic progression.

statement: The incircle of $ABC$, with center $I$, touches $AB,BC,CA$ at $D,E,F$. The line $EF$ meets $AI,BI,DI$ at $M,N,K$, respectively. Show that $DM\cdot KE=DN\cdot KF$.
solution:
Tangency gives $I,D,E,B$ concyclic. Since $DF\perp AI$ and the tangent-chord theorem gives $\angle MED=\angle FDA$, the points $I,D,E,M$ are also concyclic. Hence $BM\perp AI$. Similarly $AN\perp BI$. Let $G=BM\cap AN$. Then $I$ is the orthocentre of $GAB$, so $G,I,D$ are collinear. The right angles imply $G,N,D,B$ and $G,M,D,A$ are cyclic. Their angle relations show that $DI$ bisects one of the angles between $DM$ and $DN$. The internal or external angle-bisector theorem, in ordinary positive lengths, gives $DM/DN=KM/KN$.

Finally, the two circles $IDEM$ and $IDFN$ give, by secant power from $K$, $KM\cdot KE=KI\cdot KD=KN\cdot KF$ (or the corresponding directed products). Therefore $DM/DN=KF/KE$, and the required product identity follows.

statement:
Prove that for every positive integer $n$ there exists a unique ordered pair $(a, b)$ of positive integers such that
$$
n = \frac{1}{2}(a + b - 1)(a + b - 2) + a
$$
solution:
We have to prove that $f: \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ defined by
$$
f(a, b) = \frac{1}{2}(a + b - 1)(a + b - 2) + a, \quad \forall a, b \in \mathbb{N}
$$
is a bijection. (Note that the right side is a natural number.) To this end define
$$
T(n) = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}, \quad n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{0\}
$$
An idea of the proof can be obtained by looking at the following table of values of $f(a, b)$ for some small values of $a, b$.
![A table with rows and columns labeled by a and b, showing values of the function f(a, b) for small positive integers a and b. The table illustrates how the function fills the natural numbers along diagonals.](assets/diagrams/bdcbac7a4cc4e0fee0ba.jpg)
We observe that the $n$-th diagonal runs from $(1, n)$-th position to $(n, 1)$-th position and the entries are $n$ consecutive integers; the first entry in the $n$-th diagonal is one more than the last entry of the $(n-1)$-th diagonal. For example the first entry in 5-th diagonal is 11 which is one more than the last entry of 4-th diagonal which is 10. Observe that 5-th diagonal starts from 11 and ends with 15 which accounts for 5 consecutive natural numbers. Thus we see that $f(n-1, 1) + 1 = f(1, n)$. We also observe that the first $n$ diagonals exhaust all the natural numbers from 1 to $T(n)$. (Thus a kind of visual bijection is already there. We formally prove the property.)

We first observe that
$$
f(a, b) - T(a + b - 2) = a > 0
$$
and
$$
T(a + b - 1) - f(a, b) = \frac{(a + b - 1)(a + b)}{2} - \frac{(a + b - 1)(a + b - 2)}{2} - a = b - 1 \geq 0
$$
Thus we have
$$
T(a + b - 2) < f(a, b) = \frac{(a + b - 1)(a + b - 2)}{2} + a \leq T(a + b - 1)
$$
Suppose $f(a_1, b_1) = f(a_2, b_2)$. Then the previous observation shows that
$$
\begin{aligned}
& T(a_1 + b_1 - 2) < f(a_1, b_1) \leq T(a_1 + b_1 - 1) \\
& T(a_2 + b_2 - 2) < f(a_2, b_2) \leq T(a_2 + b_2 - 1)
\end{aligned}
$$
Since the sequence $\langle T(n) \rangle_{n=0}^{\infty}$ is strictly increasing, it follows that $a_1 + b_1 = a_2 + b_2$. But then the relation $f(a_1, b_1) = f(a_2, b_2)$ implies that $a_1 = a_2$ and $b_1 = b_2$. Hence $f$ is one-one.

Let $n$ be any natural number. Since the sequence $\langle T(n) \rangle_{n=0}^{\infty}$ is strictly increasing, we can find a natural number $k$ such that
$$
T(k-1) < n \leq T(k)
$$
Equivalently,
$$
\frac{(k-1)k}{2} < n \leq \frac{k(k+1)}{2}
$$
Now set $a = n - \frac{k(k-1)}{2}$ and $b = k - a + 1$. Observe that $a > 0$. Now (1) shows that
$$
a = n - \frac{k(k-1)}{2} \leq \frac{k(k+1)}{2} - \frac{k(k-1)}{2} = k
$$
Hence $b = k - a + 1 \geq 1$. Thus $a$ and $b$ are both positive integers and
$$
f(a, b) = \frac{1}{2}(a + b - 1)(a + b - 2) + a = \frac{k(k-1)}{2} + a = n
$$
This shows that every natural number is in the range of $f$. Thus $f$ is also onto. We conclude that $f$ is a bijection.

statement: For every integer $n\geq4$, prove that any convex cyclic quadrilateral can be dissected into $n$ convex cyclic quadrilaterals.
solution:
We first dissect the quadrilateral into four cyclic quadrilaterals, one an isosceles trapezoid. Subdividing that trapezoid by lines parallel to its bases into $n-3$ smaller isosceles trapezoids then gives exactly $n$ pieces.

Write the consecutive angles of $ABCD$ as $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$, so $\alpha+\gamma=\beta+\delta=180^\circ$. Use coordinates with $D$ at the origin, ray $DC$ horizontal, and ray $DA$ making angle $\delta$ above it. Choose an angle
$$\max(0,\delta-\alpha)<\theta<\min(\delta,180^\circ-\alpha).$$
This interval is nonempty because $0<\alpha,\delta<180^\circ$. Choose $P$ on the ray from $D$ at angle $\theta$, sufficiently close to $D$.

From $P$, draw rays in the directions
$$\delta,\quad0,\quad-\alpha,\quad\delta-\alpha-180^\circ,$$
meeting $AB,BC,CD,DA$ at $K,L,M,N$, respectively. For small enough $DP$, the first two intersections lie inside $AB,BC$ near $A,C$. To check the latter two explicitly, write $DP=t$. Elementary line intersection gives
$$DM=\frac{t\sin(\alpha+\theta)}{\sin\alpha},\qquad DN=\frac{t\sin(\alpha+\theta-\delta)}{\sin\alpha}.$$
Our choice of $\theta$ makes both positive; by shrinking $t$ they are smaller than $DC,DA$. Thus all four intersections are on the intended side interiors and the rays partition the quadrilateral into four convex pieces.

The consecutive clockwise angles at $P$ are
$$\angle KPL=\delta,\quad\angle LPM=\alpha,\quad\angle MPN=\beta,\quad\angle NPK=\gamma.$$
Each is supplementary to the opposite original corner angle. Hence $BKPL$, $CLPM$, $DMPN$, and $AKPN$ are cyclic.

Moreover $KP\parallel AD$, so $AKPN$ is a cyclic trapezoid, and therefore isosceles. Parallel cuts through this piece produce as many isosceles trapezoids as desired; each is cyclic. This completes the construction for every $n\geq4$.
ratingReason: Construct a four-piece cyclic dissection with one isosceles trapezoid, then subdivide that piece arbitrarily. The delicate step is proving the four rays meet the intended sides rather than their extensions.
notes: Official statement checked. Four-piece/trapezoid idea checked against Scholes; the ray-angle interval and exact intersection formulas were independently supplied to justify admissibility.

statement: Prove that there is a positive integer $k$ such that, for all integers $a,b,c,d,e,f,m$, if $m$ divides $a^n+b^n+c^n-d^n-e^n-f^n$ for $1\le n\le k$, it divides the same expression for every positive integer $n$.
solution: Take $k=6$. Let $P(t)=(t-a)(t-b)(t-c)(t-d)(t-e)(t-f)=t^6+c_5t^5+\cdots+c_0$. Each base $r$ satisfies $r^{n+6}+c_5r^{n+5}+\cdots+c_0r^n=0$ for $n\ge1$. Adding with the prescribed signs shows the sequence $s_n=a^n+b^n+c^n-d^n-e^n-f^n$ satisfies the same recurrence with integer coefficients. If its first six terms are divisible by $m$, induction proves all later terms are too.

statement:
Let $X$ denote the set of all triples $(a, b, c)$ of integers. Define a function $f: X \rightarrow X$ by
$$
f(a, b, c) = (a + b + c, ab + bc + ca, abc)
$$
Find all triples $(a, b, c)$ in $X$ such that $f(f(a, b, c)) = (a, b, c)$.
solution:
We show that the solution set consists of $\{(t, 0, 0) ; t \in \mathbb{Z}\} \cup \{(-1, -1, 1)\}$. Let us put $a + b + c = d$, $ab + bc + ca = e$ and $abc = f$. The given condition $f(f(a, b, c)) = (a, b, c)$ implies that
$$
d + e + f = a, \quad de + ef + fd = b, \quad def = c
$$
Thus $abcdef = fc$ and hence either $cf = 0$ or $abde = 1$.

Case I: Suppose $cf = 0$. Then either $c = 0$ or $f = 0$. However $c = 0$ implies $f = 0$ and vice-versa. Thus we obtain $a + b = d$, $d + e = a$, $ab = e$ and $de = b$. The first two relations give $b = -e$. Thus $e = ab = -ae$ and $de = b = -e$. We get either $e = 0$ or $a = d = -1$.
If $e = 0$, then $b = 0$ and $a = d = t$, say. We get the triple $(a, b, c) = (t, 0, 0)$, where $t \in \mathbb{Z}$. If $e \neq 0$, then $a = d = -1$. But then $d + e + f = a$ implies that $-1 + e + 0 = -1$ forcing $e = 0$. Thus we get the solution family $(a, b, c) = (t, 0, 0)$, where $t \in \mathbb{Z}$.

Case II: Suppose $cf \neq 0$. In this case $abde = 1$. Hence either all are equal to $1$; or two equal to $1$ and the other two equal to $-1$; or all equal to $-1$.
Suppose $a = b = d = e = 1$. Then $a + b + c = d$ shows that $c = -1$. Similarly $f = -1$. Hence $e = ab + bc + ca = 1 - 1 - 1 = -1$ contradicting $e = 1$.
Suppose $a = b = 1$ and $d = e = -1$. Then $a + b + c = d$ gives $c = -3$ and $d + e + f = a$ gives $f = 3$. But then $f = abc = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot (-3) = -3$, a contradiction. Similarly $a = b = -1$ and $d = e = 1$ is not possible.
If $a = 1, b = -1, d = 1, e = -1$, then $a + b + c = d$ gives $c = 1$. Similarly $f = 1$. But then $f = abc = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot (-1) = -1$ a contradiction. If $a = 1, b = -1, d = -1, e = 1$, then $c = -1$ and $e = ab + bc + ca = -1 + 1 - 1 = -1$ and a contradiction to $e = 1$. The symmetry between $(a, b, c)$ and $(d, e, f)$ shows that $a = -1, b = 1, d = 1, e = -1$ is not possible. Finally if $a = -1, b = 1, d = -1$ and $e = 1$, then $c = -1$ and $f = -1$. But then $f = abc$ is not satisfied.
The only case left is that of $a, b, d, e$ being all equal to $-1$. Then $c = 1$ and $f = 1$. It is easy to check that $(-1, -1, 1)$ is indeed a solution.

Alternatively
$cf \neq 0$ implies that $|c| \geq 1$ and $|f| \geq 1$. Observe that
$$
d^{2} - 2e = a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2}, \quad a^{2} - 2b = d^{2} + e^{2} + f^{2}
$$
Adding these two, we get $-2(b + e) = b^{2} + c^{2} + e^{2} + f^{2}$. This may be written in the form
$$
(b + 1)^{2} + (e + 1)^{2} + c^{2} + f^{2} - 2 = 0
$$
We conclude that $c^{2} + f^{2} \leq 2$. Using $|c| \geq 1$ and $|f| \geq 1$, we obtain $|c| = 1$ and $|f| = 1$, $b + 1 = 0$ and $e + 1 = 0$. Thus $b = e = -1$. Now $a + d = d + e + f + a + b + c$ and this gives $b + c + e + f = 0$. It follows that $c = f = 1$ and finally $a = d = -1$.
ratingReason: Iterating the symmetric-polynomial map and adding two square identities bounds the last coordinates by one; handle zero coordinates separately.

statement: For all nonnegative integers $m,n$, prove that $\dfrac{(2m)!(2n)!}{m!\,n!\,(m+n)!}$ is an integer.
solution:
Fix a prime $p$. By Legendre's formula, its exponent in the displayed rational number is
$$\sum_{j\geq1}\left(\left\lfloor\frac{2m}{p^j}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{2n}{p^j}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac m{p^j}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac n{p^j}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{m+n}{p^j}\right\rfloor\right).$$
Every summand is nonnegative. To see this for a positive divisor parameter $d=p^j$, write $m/d=a+x$, $n/d=b+y$, with integers $a,b$ and $0\leq x,y<1$. The expression reduces to
$$\lfloor2x\rfloor+\lfloor2y\rfloor-\lfloor x+y\rfloor.$$
If $x+y<1$, the last floor is zero. If $x+y\geq1$, at least one of $x,y$ is at least $1/2$, so the first two floors sum to at least one, matching the last floor. Thus every prime has nonnegative exponent in the ratio, proving it is an integer. The argument includes $m=0$ or $n=0$.
ratingReason: Legendre’s factorial formula reduces every prime valuation to a floor inequality. The two fractional parts must cross one half whenever their sum crosses one.

statement:
Let real numbers $a, b, c$ and $d$ satisfy
$$
f(x) = a \cos x + b \cos 2x + c \cos 3x + d \cos 4x \le 1
$$
for any real number $x$. Find the values of $a, b, c$ and $d$ such that $a + b - c + d$ takes the maximum number. (posed by Li Shenghong)
solution:
Evaluate at $0,\pi,\pi/3$. Their weighted combination gives
$$a+b-c+d=f(0)+\tfrac23f(\pi)+\tfrac43f(\pi/3)\le3.$$
Equality requires all three evaluations to equal $1$. Solving these linear equations yields $a=1$, $c=-1$ and $b+d=1$.

Write $t=\cos x$. For these values,
$$f(x)-1=-2(1-t^2)\big(4dt^2-2t+1-d\big).$$
Thus the quadratic in parentheses must be nonnegative on $(-1,1)$. At $t=1/2$ it is zero, so its derivative there must vanish: $4d-2=0$. Hence $d=b=1/2$. Conversely with these values the quadratic is $2(t-1/2)^2$, which is nonnegative. Therefore the unique maximizing quadruple is
$$\boxed{(a,b,c,d)=(1,1/2,-1,1/2)},$$
and the maximum objective value is $3$.
ratingReason: A cleverly weighted combination of three evaluations bounds the objective, and global nonpositivity determines the unique remaining coefficient.

solution:
Applying cosine rule to triangle $ABC$, we get
$$
AC^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab \cos 120^\circ = a^2 + b^2 + ab
$$
Observe that $\angle DAC = \angle DBC = 120^\circ - 30^\circ = 90^\circ$. Thus we get
$$
c^2 = \frac{AC^2}{\cos^2 30^\circ} = \frac{4}{3}(a^2 + b^2 + ab)
$$
So
$$
c^2 - (a+b)^2 = \frac{4}{3}(a^2 + b^2 + ab) - (a^2 + b^2 + 2ab) = \frac{(a-b)^2}{3} \geq 0
$$
This proves $c \geq a + b$ and thus (i) is true.

![A cyclic quadrilateral ABCD inscribed in a circle, with sides labeled a, b, c, and angles at B and D marked as 30 and 90 degrees. The triangle ABC and relevant angles and side lengths are shown.](assets/diagrams/b3bee2cb7c5183353779.jpg)

For proving (ii), consider the product
$$
Q = (\alpha + \beta + \gamma)(\alpha - \beta - \gamma)(\alpha + \beta - \gamma)(\alpha - \beta + \gamma)
$$
where $\alpha = \sqrt{c+a}$, $\beta = \sqrt{c+b}$ and $\gamma = \sqrt{c-a-b}$. Expanding the product, we get
$$
\begin{aligned}
Q &= (c+a)^2 + (c+b)^2 + (c-a-b)^2 - 2(c+a)(c+b) - 2(c+a)(c-a-b) - 2(c+b)(c-a-b) \\
&= -3c^2 + 4a^2 + 4b^2 + 4ab \\
&= 0
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus at least one of the factors must be equal to $0$. Since $\alpha + \beta + \gamma > 0$ and $\alpha + \beta - \gamma > 0$, it follows that the product of the remaining two factors is $0$. This gives
$$
\sqrt{c+a} - \sqrt{c+b} = \sqrt{c-a-b} \quad \text{or} \quad \sqrt{c+a} - \sqrt{c+b} = -\sqrt{c-a-b}
$$
We conclude that
$$
|\sqrt{c+a} - \sqrt{c+b}| = \sqrt{c-a-b}
$$
ratingReason: The angle conditions yield a cosine-rule identity; a four-factor radical identity then proves the exact equality.

statement:
Find all positive real five-tuples satisfying, with indices read modulo five,
$$(x_i^2-x_{i+2}x_{i+4})(x_{i+1}^2-x_{i+2}x_{i+4})\leq0\qquad(i=1,2,3,4,5).$$
solution:
Exactly the constant positive tuples $(t,t,t,t,t)$ work.

Let $S$ be the sum of the five left-hand sides, so $S\leq0$. Expanding and regrouping gives the identity
$$2S=\sum_{i=1}^5x_i^2\left((x_{i+1}-x_{i+3})^2+(x_{i+2}-x_{i+4})^2\right),$$
with subscripts modulo five. One can verify it by comparing the squared-product terms and the terms of the form $x_i^2x_jx_k$; each appears with the same coefficient on both sides.

The right side is nonnegative. Therefore it is zero, and since every $x_i>0$, all its squared differences vanish. In particular $x_{i+1}=x_{i+3}$ for every $i$. Stepping by two runs through all five indices, so every variable equals the same positive number. Conversely a constant positive tuple makes all five original products zero.
ratingReason: Summing the five constraints reveals a hidden sum-of-squares identity. Positivity of the variables then propagates equality around the cyclic indices.
notes: Official system checked. The sum-of-squares identity was independently verified by exact polynomial coefficient comparison; the factor 2 omitted in some informal descriptions is included.

statement: Find all integers x for which $x(x+1)(x+7)(x+8)$ is a perfect square.
solution: Put t=x²+8x=(x+4)²−16. The product is t(t+7). If t>9, then $(t+3)^2<t(t+7)<(t+4)^2$, so it is not a square. Thus (x+4)²≤25 and −9≤x≤1. The possible t values in this range are −16,−15,−12,−7,0,9, giving products 144,120,60,0,0,144 respectively. The square cases therefore give x=−9,−8,−7,−4,−1,0,1. Each listed value works.

title: Permutations with equal displacement at every position
statement: How many permutations $a_1,\ldots,a_{2004}$ of $1,\ldots,2004$ satisfy $|a_i-i|=d>0$ for every position $i$?
solution: For fixed $d$, view each residue class modulo $d$ as an increasing path of available values. The smallest vertex can only map to the next one. Conversely that next vertex must map back, since the smallest value has no other possible preimage. Removing the pair and repeating shows every path must have even length, with its adjacent vertices swapped uniquely. Writing $2004=qd+r$ with $0\le r<d$, the paths have lengths $q$ or $q+1$. Both cannot occur, so $r=0$ and $q$ is even. Thus exactly the positive divisors $d$ of 1002 work. Since $1002=2\cdot3\cdot167$, there are 8.
ratingReason: Each residue chain modulo the fixed displacement must be paired by adjacent swaps, so the displacement is a divisor of 1002 and each choice is unique.

statement:
a. Prove that if $n$ is a positive integer such that $n \geq 4011^{2}$, then there exists an integer $l$ such that $n < l^{2} < \left(1 + \frac{1}{2005}\right) n$.

b. Find the smallest positive integer $M$ for which whenever an integer $n$ is such that $n \geq M$, there exists an integer $l$, such that $n < l^{2} < \left(1 + \frac{1}{2005}\right) n$.
solution:
a. Let $n \geq 4011^{2}$ and $m \in \mathbb{N}$ be such that $m^{2} \leq n < (m+1)^{2}$. Then
$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(1+\frac{1}{2005}\right) n - (m+1)^{2} & \geq \left(1+\frac{1}{2005}\right) m^{2} - (m+1)^{2} \\
& = \frac{m^{2}}{2005} - 2m - 1 \\
& = \frac{1}{2005}\left(m^{2} - 4010m - 2005\right) \\
& = \frac{1}{2005}\left((m-2005)^{2} - 2005^{2} - 2005\right) \\
& \geq \frac{1}{2005}\left((4011-2005)^{2} - 2005^{2} - 2005\right) \\
& = \frac{1}{2005}\left(2006^{2} - 2005^{2} - 2005\right) \\
& = \frac{1}{2005}(4011 - 2005) = \frac{2006}{2005} > 0
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus we get
$$
n < (m+1)^{2} < \left(1 + \frac{1}{2005}\right) n
$$
and $l^{2} = (m+1)^{2}$ is the desired square.

b. We show that $M = 4010^{2} + 1$ is the required least number. Suppose $n \geq M$. Write $n = 4010^{2} + k$, where $k$ is a positive integer. Note that we may assume $n < 4011^{2}$ by part (a). Now
$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(1 + \frac{1}{2005}\right) n - 4011^{2} & = \left(1 + \frac{1}{2005}\right)\left(4010^{2} + k\right) - 4011^{2} \\
& = 4010^{2} + 2 \cdot 4010 + k + \frac{k}{2005} - 4011^{2} \\
& = (4010 + 1)^{2} + (k - 1) + \frac{k}{2005} - 4011^{2} \\
& = (k - 1) + \frac{k}{2005} > 0
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus we obtain
$$
4010^{2} < n < 4011^{2} < \left(1 + \frac{1}{2005}\right) n
$$
We check that $M = 4010^{2}$ will not work. For suppose $n = 4010^{2}$. Then
$$
\left(1 + \frac{1}{2005}\right) 4010^{2} = 4010^{2} + 2 \cdot 4010 = 4011^{2} - 1 < 4011^{2}
$$
Thus there is no square integer between $n$ and $\left(1 + \frac{1}{2005}\right) n$.
This proves (b).
ratingReason: Locate n between consecutive squares, then identify the last failing perfect square to prove the exact threshold.

statement: Real-valued functions $f,g$ on $\mathbb R$ satisfy $f(x+y)+f(x-y)=2f(x)g(y)$ for all real $x,y$. Suppose $f$ is not identically zero and $|f(x)|\leq1$ everywhere. Prove $|g(y)|\leq1$ everywhere.
solution:
Let $M=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}|f(x)|$. The hypotheses give $0<M\leq1$. Fix any real $y$. The functional equation and triangle inequality imply
$$2|f(x)||g(y)|\leq|f(x+y)|+|f(x-y)|\leq2M$$
for every $x$.

Choose a sequence of inputs $x_j$ with $|f(x_j)|\to M$, as permitted by the definition of supremum. Passing to the limit in $|f(x_j)||g(y)|\leq M$ gives $M|g(y)|\leq M$. Since $M>0$, we obtain $|g(y)|\leq1$. The choice of $y$ was arbitrary, proving the assertion.
ratingReason: Use the actual supremum of the bounded nonzero function. Inputs approaching that supremum turn the functional equation into a sharp bound on the multiplier, without any regularity assumption.
