statement: Let $n$ be a positive integer divisible by $4$. Find the number of permutations $\sigma$ of $(1, 2, 3, \ldots, n)$ which satisfy the condition $\sigma(j) + \sigma^{-1}(j) = n + 1$, for all $j \in \{1, 2, 3, \ldots, n\}$.
solution: Write $n=4k$. From the given equation, if $\sigma(a)=b$ then $\sigma(b)=n+1-a$, $\sigma(n+1-a)=n+1-b$, and $\sigma(n+1-b)=a$. These four labels are distinct, since a fixed point or a complementary two-cycle would give an even number equal to $n+1$. Hence every cycle pairs two of the $2k$ complementary pairs $\{j,n+1-j\}$. Partition those $2k$ pairs into $k$ unordered pairs in $(2k)!/(2^k k!)$ ways, and choose one of the two cycle orientations independently for each. The answer is $\boxed{(2k)!/k!}$.

statement: Given four distinct parallel planes in space, prove that a regular tetrahedron exists with one vertex on each plane.
solution:
Take the common normal direction as vertical, and let the four plane heights be $h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4$. Subtract their mean $\bar h$ and write $z_i=h_i-\bar h$, so $\sum z_i=0$.

Use the four vertex vectors of a regular tetrahedron
$$v_1=(1,1,1),\ v_2=(1,-1,-1),\ v_3=(-1,1,-1),\ v_4=(-1,-1,1).$$
They satisfy $v_i\cdot v_i=3$ and $v_i\cdot v_j=-1$ for $i\ne j$. Define
$$w=\frac14\sum_{i=1}^4z_iv_i.$$
Then
$$w\cdot v_j=\frac14\left(3z_j-\sum_{i\ne j}z_i\right)=z_j.$$
The vector $w$ is nonzero, since otherwise all the distinct heights would equal their mean.

Scale this regular tetrahedron by $|w|$ and rotate it so that the direction $w/|w|$ becomes vertical. The height of its $j$th vertex after this operation is $|w|v_j\cdot(w/|w|)=z_j$. Translate vertically by $\bar h$. Its four heights are now exactly $h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4$, as required. Scaling, rotation and translation preserve regularity.
ratingReason: Encode a regular tetrahedron by four symmetric vectors. Every four prescribed heights with zero sum arise as their projections onto a suitable vector; scaling and rotation realise the planes.

statement: In triangle ABC, angle B is obtuse. The perpendicular to AB at B meets AC at D, and CD=AB. Prove $AD^2=AB\cdot BC$ exactly when angle CBD=30°.
solution: Write B=(0,0), A=(c,0), D=(0,d), with c,d>0, and l=AD. Since CD=c and C lies beyond D, $C=(-c^2/l,d(1+c/l))$. Put u=c/l, so 0<u<1, and a=BC. Squaring the coordinates gives $a^2/l^2=1+2u-2u^3$. Also, for θ=∠CBD, $\sin\theta=c^2/(la)=u^2l/a$. If l²=ca then a/l=1/u, and the squared-length identity becomes $(2u^3-1)(u^2-1)=0$. Thus u³=1/2 and sinθ=u³=1/2, giving θ=30°. Conversely, if θ=30°, then a/l=2u². Substitution gives $(2u+1)(2u^3-1)=0$, so u³=1/2 and a/l=1/u. Hence l²=ca.
ratingReason: A coordinate description handles the external intersection, but the equivalence requires two different factorisations and careful use of the acute angle CBD.

statement: Find all triples $(a, b, c)$ integers such that $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, $\text{gcd}(a, b, c) = 1$ and $2000 \le a, b, c \le 3000$.
solution:
We use the known characterisation of primitive Pythagorean triples $(a, b, c)$: $a = 2pq$, $b = p^2 - q^2$, $c = p^2 + q^2$, where $p$ and $q$ are relatively prime integers, one even and $q < p$. The given condition entails $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 > 2 \times 2000^2$. Hence $2000\sqrt{2} < c = p^2 + q^2 < 3000$. Using the approximation $\sqrt{2} = 1.4142$, we get $2828 < p^2 + q^2 < 3000$. We also have $2000 < b = p^2 - q^2$. Adding these two, we obtain $4828 < 2p^2$, whence $50 \le p$. Again, we have $2000 < a = 2pq$. Subtracting this from $p^2+q^2 < 3000$, we get $(p-q)^2 < 1000$ giving $p-q \le 31$. Using $50 \le p$ and $p-q \le 31$, we obtain $19 \le q$ and hence $3000 > p^2+q^2 \ge p^2+19^2$. It follows that $p^2 < 2639$ and thus $p \le 51$. We obtain $2000/51 < 2pq/p = 2q$.

We thus obtain a better bound for $q$: $20 \le q$ and hence a better bound for $p$: $p^2 < 2639$ and hence $p \le 50$. We have seen earlier that $p \ge 50$, thus getting $p = 50$. Using $p^2 + q^2 < 3000$, we now get $q^2 < 500$. This implies that $q \le 22$. Thus $20 \le q \le 22$. However $q$ has to be odd since $p$ is even. We conclude that $q = 21$. We see that $a = 2100$, $b = 2059$ and $c = 2941$ give only one triple in the given range.
tags: Techniques: modulo, size analysis, order analysis, inequalities
ratingReason: Primitive Pythagorean parametrisation and successive numerical bounds restrict the parameters to 50 and 21.

statement: For $n>2$, let $E_n=\sum_{i=1}^n\prod_{j\ne i}(a_i-a_j)$. Prove that $E_n\geq0$ for every real tuple $(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$ exactly when $n=3$ or $5$.
solution:
For $n=3$ or $5$, reorder so $a_1\geq a_2\geq\cdots\geq a_n$. Denote the summands by $T_i$.

The first two satisfy
$$T_1+T_2=(a_1-a_2)\left(\prod_{j=3}^n(a_1-a_j)-\prod_{j=3}^n(a_2-a_j)\right)\geq0,$$
since corresponding factors are nonnegative and those in the first product are larger. For $n=3$, the remaining summand is also nonnegative.

For $n=5$, the middle term $T_3$ has two nonpositive and two nonnegative factors, hence is nonnegative. At the lower end,
$$T_4+T_5=(a_4-a_5)\left(\prod_{j=1}^3(a_j-a_5)-\prod_{j=1}^3(a_j-a_4)\right)\geq0.$$
Thus both asserted sizes work, including repeated-variable cases.

For even $n$, take $a_1=-1$ and all other entries zero. Only $T_1$ survives, and it equals $-1$. For odd $n\geq7$, take one entry zero, three entries $-1$, and the remaining $n-4$ entries $1$. Every repeated-entry term vanishes. The zero entry contributes $1^3(-1)^{n-4}=-1$. These counterexamples exclude every other $n>2$.
ratingReason: Order the variables and pair the alternating-sign terms for the two valid sizes. Repeated variables then isolate a single negative term to build counterexamples for all other sizes.

statement: Find all integer-sided right triangles whose area equals their perimeter.
solution: Write the two legs as a,b and the hypotenuse as c. The condition ab/2=a+b+c and c²=a²+b² imply $ab=2(a+b+c)$. Divide the original equality by a+b+c to see the inradius is 2. Hence a+b−c=4. Squaring c=a+b−4 gives $2ab-8a-8b+16=0$, or $(a-4)(b-4)=8$. Since c>max(a,b), both a,b exceed four. The positive factor pairs of eight yield legs (5,12) or (6,8), up to order. Their hypotenuses are 13 and 10, and both triangles satisfy the condition.
ratingReason: The area-perimeter condition fixes the inradius. Combining this with Pythagoras converts the classification into a small factor-pair problem.

statement: Let $m$ be a positive integer, $n = 2^m - 1$, and $P_n = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ be the set of $n$ points on the number axis. A grasshopper jumps between adjacent points on $P_n$. Find the maximal number of $m$ such that for any $x, y \in P_n$, the number of ways that a grasshopper jumping from $x$ to $y$ by 2012 steps is even (passing $x$ or $y$ on the way is permitted). (posed by Zhang Sihui)
solution:
The answer is $\boxed{10}$. If $m\ge11$, the path contains vertices $1$ and $2013$, and exactly one $2012$-step walk joins them: every step moves right. Thus larger $m$ fail.

We prove by induction that on a path with $2^m-1$ vertices every walk count of length $k\ge2^m-1$ is even. The case $m=1$ is immediate. In the induction step let $c=2^{m-1}$ be the central vertex and $L=c-1$ the number of vertices on either side.

Walks that never visit $c$ are counted evenly by induction. For walks that visit $c$ exactly once, fix the visit time and the adjacent vertices. The segments before and after the visit have total length $k-2\ge2L-1$, so at least one has length at least $L$ and is counted evenly by induction. If the sole visit is an endpoint, the remaining segment has length $k-1\ge L$.

Finally pair every walk visiting $c$ at least twice with the walk obtained by reflecting the segment between its first two visits across $c$. This is an involution without fixed walks. Hence these are counted evenly too.

For $m=10$, $2012\ge1023=2^{10}-1$, so the claim applies and completes the proof.
ratingReason: A recursive parity argument separates paths according to visits to the central vertex and pairs repeated visits by reflection.

statement:
Let $(u_{jk})$, $1 \le j \le 3$, $1 \le k \le 2$ be real numbers and let $N$ be an integer such that
$$
\max_{1 \le k \le 2} \sum_{j=1}^{3} |u_{jk}| \le N.
$$
Suppose $M$ and $l$ are positive integers such that $l^2 < (M+1)^3$. Prove that there exist integers $\xi_1, \xi_2, \xi_3$, not all zero, such that
$$
\max_{1 \le j \le 3} |\xi_j| \le M \quad \text{and} \quad \left| \sum_{j=1}^{3} u_{jk} \xi_j \right| \le \frac{MN}{l}, \quad \text{for } k = 1, 2.
$$
solution: For $0\le a_j\le M$, the signed linear form $L_k(a)=\sum_j u_{jk}a_j$ lies in the interval $[M\sum_{u_{jk}<0}u_{jk},M\sum_{u_{jk}>0}u_{jk}]$, of length at most $MN$. Divide each interval into $l$ pieces of length at most $MN/l$, assigning endpoints consistently. The $(M+1)^3$ vectors $a$ fall into $l^2$ rectangles. Since $(M+1)^3>l^2$, two distinct vectors $a,b$ share a rectangle. Set $\xi_j=a_j-b_j$. Then $|\xi_j|\le M$ and $|L_k(\xi)|\le MN/l$ for both $k$. If $N=0$, all coefficients vanish and any unit vector works.
ratingReason: Map all integer triples in a cube to two real linear forms and partition a rectangle into l squared boxes; a difference of two vectors yields the bound.

statement: A convex polyhedron $P$ has nine vertices $A_1,\ldots,A_9$. For each $i$, translate $P$ by the vector $\overrightarrow{A_1A_i}$ to obtain $P_i$ (so $P_1=P$). Prove that two of these polyhedra have a common interior point.
solution:
Take $A_1$ as the origin. A point of $P_i$ has the form $x+A_i$ with $x\in P$. By convexity, $(x+A_i)/2\in P$. Hence every $P_i$ lies in the dilation $2P$.

Let $V>0$ be the volume of $P$. The nine translates each have volume $V$, whereas $2P$ has volume $8V$. If their interiors were pairwise disjoint, their union would have volume $9V$: boundaries of polyhedra have zero volume. But that union is contained in $2P$, a contradiction. Thus some pair has an interior point in common.
ratingReason: All nine translates fit inside one doubled copy by convexity. Their total volume exceeds that container’s volume, forcing interior overlap.

statement: Choose signs $a_3,a_4,\ldots,a_{2008}\in\{-1,1\}$ so that $\sum_{i=3}^{2008}a_i2^i=2008$, and prove the choice is unique.
solution: If every sign were positive, the sum would be 2²⁰⁰⁹−8. Changing to a negative sign at an index i subtracts 2^(i+1). Thus the powers 2^i with negative signs must sum to 2²⁰⁰⁸−1008. Its binary expansion is $2^{2008}-2^{10}+16=2^{10}+2^{11}+\cdots+2^{2007}+2^4$. Therefore the negative signs occur exactly at i=4 and at i=10,…,2007; all other signs are positive. Uniqueness follows from uniqueness of binary expansion.
ratingReason: Comparing with the all-positive sum converts a signed representation into an ordinary binary subset sum; the long block of negative signs then follows without trial and error.

title: Red beads in an indivisible balanced necklace
statement: A necklace has an even number $n\ge4$ of red, blue and green beads, with equally many blue and green. It cannot be split into two strings of positive even lengths, each containing equally many blue and green beads. Determine the possible number of red beads.
solution: There must be exactly two red beads. Give blue weight 1, green weight −1 and red weight 0. Take partial sums after every two beads. No proper even-length zero-sum interval is allowed, so these partial sums are distinct except for the final return to zero. Consecutive values differ by 1 or 2 in absolute value; a zero difference would already be forbidden. For a cycle with at least three vertices, exactly two edges have odd length. To prove this, its smallest vertex has neighbours exactly one and two units larger; remove it and replace its two incident edges by the edge between these neighbours. The number of odd edges is unchanged, and induction reduces to a triangle. In the two-edge case there are either two odd edges or none; the latter would give no red beads, impossible because some adjacent blue and green pair would form a forbidden balanced string. A two-bead block has odd weight exactly when it contains one red bead; it cannot contain two reds. Hence the red count is two. This is attainable with equal positive runs of blue and green separated by the two reds: every even balanced proper interval would need both separating reds and then either no or all of each run, which is impossible.
ratingReason: Even-position partial sums form a simple cycle on the integer line with jumps at most two; such a cycle has exactly two odd jumps, accounting for the red beads.

statement: Prove that, among any $n$ vertexes of a regular $2n-1$ polygon ($n \ge 3$), there are three points, which are the vertexes of an isosceles triangle.
solution:
Scale the circumcircle to unit radius and represent its vertices by vectors. Put $N=2n-1$. From any vertex of the regular $N$-gon there are exactly $n-1$ possible positive distances, each represented by two vertices.

Suppose the selected set $S$ of $n$ vertices contains no isosceles triangle. From each selected vertex $P$, the other $n-1$ selected vertices must then realize all these distances exactly once. The sum of squared distances from $P$ to all $N$ polygon vertices is $2N$, because their vector sum is zero. Therefore
$$\sum_{Q\in S}|P-Q|^2=N.$$
Let $Z=\sum_{Q\in S}Q$. Since all selected vectors have length $1$, the left side is $2n-2P\cdot Z$. As $N=2n-1$, this gives $P\cdot Z=1/2$ for every selected vertex. Thus $Z\ne0$ and all selected vertices lie on one line. A line meets the unit circle in at most two points, contradicting $n\ge3$.
ratingReason: Assuming distinct distances from each selected vertex gives a rigid squared-distance sum; a vector identity would place three circle points on a line.

solution:
We use induction on $n$. The case $n = 1$ is immediate. Assume the result for $n$ and consider the case of $n+1$. Thus $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_{n+1}$ are subsets of $S$ with $|A_j| = 8$.
Now if we consider the sets $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_{j-1}, A_{j+1}, \dots, A_{n+1}$, these satisfy induction hypothesis for each $j = 1, 2, 3, \dots, n+1$. Hence there exists
$$
x_j \in A_1 \cap A_2 \cap \dots \cap A_{j-1} \cap A_{j+1} \cap \dots \cap A_{n+1},
$$
for each $j = 1, 2, \dots, n+1$. If $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{n+1}$ are not all distinct, then we are through. Suppose they are all distinct. Consider $B = A_1 \cup A_2 \cup \dots \cup A_{n+1}$. We show that $|B| \le 25$. Note that each $x_j$ is over counted $n-1$ times in the union. Thus
$$
|B| \le |A_1| + |A_2| + \dots + |A_{n+1}| - (n-1)(n+1) = 8(n+1) - (n^2-1) \le 25,
$$
since $n^2 - 8n + 16 = (n-4)^2 \ge 0$. Thus the condition (i) fails. Clearly, the condition (2) also fails. Hence (iii) must hold.
ratingReason: A minimal subfamily with empty intersection supplies distinct witnesses; counting their repeated membership bounds its union by 25 via a quadratic.

statement: Prove that the numbers $2^k-3$, for integers $k\geq2$, contain an infinite subset whose distinct members are pairwise coprime.
solution:
Start with $2^3-3=5$. Suppose distinct pairwise coprime terms $b_1,\ldots,b_s$ have been chosen, and let $M=b_1\cdots b_s$. All these numbers are odd, so $\gcd(2,M)=1$. Euler's theorem gives $2^{\varphi(M)}\equiv1\pmod M$.

Choose an integer $t$ sufficiently large that $k=1+t\varphi(M)$ exceeds every previously used exponent. Then
$$2^k-3\equiv2-3\equiv-1\pmod M.$$
Thus the new term is coprime to $M$, and therefore to every previous term. It is also larger than all of them. Repeating this finite extension indefinitely constructs the desired infinite subset.
ratingReason: Use induction on a selected finite set and choose the next exponent so the new term is minus one modulo the product of all previous terms.
notes: Official released statement checked; worked exposition independently written and mathematically assessed.

statement: For k∈{0,1,2,3}, let f_k(n) count length-n sequences with entries in {−1,0,1} whose sum is k modulo 4. Prove f₁(n)=f₃(n) and $f_0(n)=(3^n+2+(-1)^n)/4$.
solution: Negating every entry gives a bijection between residue-one and residue-three sequences. Let E=f₀+f₂ and O=f₁+f₃. Appending a digit gives Eₙ₊₁=Eₙ+2Oₙ and Oₙ₊₁=2Eₙ+Oₙ, so Eₙ−Oₙ=(−1)ⁿ, while Eₙ+Oₙ=3ⁿ. Also f₀(n+1)=f₀(n)+f₁(n)+f₃(n) and f₂(n+1)=f₂(n)+f₁(n)+f₃(n), so f₀−f₂ stays equal to its empty-sequence value one. Combining these identities gives the formula.
ratingReason: Symmetry reduces four residue counts to two, and two conserved or alternating differences then determine the desired closed form.

statement: Let $E$ be a given set with $n$ elements. Suppose that $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_k$ are $k$ distinct nonempty subsets of $E$, with either $A_i \cap A_j = \emptyset$, $A_i \subset A_j$, or $A_j \subset A_i$ for any $1 \le i < j \le k$. Find the maximum value of $k$.
solution:
We may enlarge the family by adding $E$ and every singleton, preserving its property. Arrange the sets as a rooted inclusion tree with root $E$, each set joined to its smallest strict superset in the family. Its leaves are exactly the $n$ singletons. Every nonleaf has at least two children: maximal proper submembers are disjoint and cover the parent, since all singleton subsets are present.

If there are $I$ internal nodes and $n$ leaves, the tree has $I+n-1$ edges but at least $2I$ edges, so $I\le n-1$. Hence $k\le2n-1$.

Equality is attained by all $n$ singletons together with the $n-1$ sets $\{1,2\},\{1,2,3\},\ldots,\{1,\ldots,n\}$ after labeling $E$. Thus the maximum is $\boxed{2n-1}$.
ratingReason: Represents a laminar family as a rooted inclusion tree and bounds its internal nodes by its singleton leaves.

statement: Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram. A variable line $l$ through the point $A$ intersects the rays $BC$ and $DC$ at $X$ and $Y$ respectively. Let $K$ and $L$ be the centres of the excircles of triangles $ABX$ and $ADY$, touching the sides $BX$ and $DY$ respectively. Prove that the size of $\angle KCL$ does not depend on the choice of the line $l$. (Short-list, IMO-2005)
solution:
Let $\angle DAX = 2\gamma$ and $\angle YAP = 2\alpha$. Now $K$ being the ex-centre of triangle $ABX$, it lies on the bisectors of $\angle XAB$ and $\angle XBP$. Note that $\angle ABX = 180^\circ - 2\alpha - 2\gamma$ and hence $\angle XBK = (2\alpha + 2\gamma)/2 = \alpha + \gamma$. Thus the angles of triangle $ABK$ are $\alpha$, $\gamma$, $180^\circ - \alpha - \gamma$.

Similarly, the angles of $ADL$ are also $x$, $y$, $180^\circ - x - y$. Thus $ABK$ is similar to $LDA$ and hence $AB/LD = BK/AD$. However $AB = DC$ and $AD = BC$. Thus we obtain $DC/LD = BK/BC$. Note also that $\angle CBK = \angle LDC$. We hence get the similarity of triangles $CBK$ and $LDC$. If we take $\angle ALC = \theta$, then $\angle DCL = 180^\circ - 2x - \theta$. But by similarity of $CBK$ and $LDC$, we have $\angle DCL = \angle BKC$, giving $\angle BKC = 180^\circ - 2x - \theta$. This gives $\angle KCX = x + \theta$.

![](assets/diagrams/fcf1c2d00b5628704c02.png)

This gives
$$
\angle KCL = 360^\circ - (x + \theta) - (2x + 2y) - (180^\circ - 2x - y - \theta) \\
= 180^\circ + x + y = 180^\circ + (\angle A)/2
$$
which depends only on the parallelogram but not on the line $l$.

statement: Let $H$ and $O$ be the orthocenter and circumcenter of an acute triangle $ABC$ ($A$, $H$, $O$ are non-collinear). Suppose that $D$ is the projection of $A$ onto the line $BC$, and the perpendicular bisector of the segment $AO$ meets the line $BC$ at $E$. Prove that the midpoint of $OH$ is on the circumcircle of triangle $ADE$.
solution:
Choose $D=(0,0)$, $A=(0,a)$ and let $BC$ be the horizontal axis. Write $O=(u,v)$ and $H=(0,h)$. The standard orthocenter relation in these coordinates is $h=a-2v$; it also follows by equating circumcenter distances and writing the altitude from $B$.

Let $E=(e,0)$. Since $EA=EO$, we have
$$2eu=u^2+v^2-a^2.$$
The circle through $A,D,E$ has equation $x^2+y^2-ex-ay=0$. The midpoint $N$ of $OH$ is $(u/2,(a-v)/2)$. Substituting its coordinates into the circle equation gives
$$\frac14\big(u^2+v^2-a^2-2eu\big)=0.$$
Hence $N$ lies on the required circle. The noncollinearity assumption ensures $u\ne0$, so the construction is nondegenerate.

statement: There are $n$ markers, each with one side white and the other side black, aligned in a row so that their white sides are all up in the beginning. In each step, if possible, we choose a marker with the white side up (but not the one of outermost markers), remove it, and reverse the closest marker to the left and the closest marker to the right of it. Prove that one can achieve the state with only two markers remaining if and only if $(n-1)$ is not divisible by $3$. (Short-list, IMO-2005)
solution:
It is easy to handle the cases $n = 3, 5, 6$:

a. $n=3$: $WWW \rightarrow BB$, by removing middle $W$ and reversing the other two;

b. $n=5$: $(WWW)WW \rightarrow (BB)WW = B(BWW) \rightarrow BWB \rightarrow WW$;

c. $n = 6$: $(WWW)WWW \rightarrow BB(WWW) = B(BWW)W \rightarrow B(WB)W = (BWB)W \rightarrow WWW$.

The last reduction shows that for $n > 6$, we can pick any six $W$'s and reduce it three $W$'s there by reducing the case to that of $n - 3$. Since we have ended with 2 markers for $n = 3$ and $5$, it follows by induction that the 'two marker state' is achievable for $n = 3k$ or $3k + 2$.

We have to show that this is not possible for $n = 3k + 1$. Observe that the number of $B$'s is invariant modulo $2$ in each move: $WWW \rightarrow BB$; $WWB \rightarrow BW$; $BWW \rightarrow WB$; $BWB \rightarrow WW$. Since all are $W$ in the beginning, the final two markers must be either $BB$ or $WW$. We assign weights to $W$ and $B$.

Take the group of symmetries of an equilateral triangle with centre at origin and $y$-axis passing through a vertex; let $\phi$ denote rotation by $120^\circ$ about the centre in clock-wise direction; and let $\psi$ denote the reflection in $y$ axis. Then it is easy to see that
$$
\phi^3 = \psi^2 = 1, \phi^2\psi = \psi\phi, \psi\phi^2 = \phi\psi, \psi\phi\psi = \phi^2.
$$
Thus we may assign $\omega(W) = \phi$, $\omega(B) = \psi$. The properties of $\phi$ and $\psi$ show that they obey the reductions $WWW \rightarrow BB$, $WWB \rightarrow BW$; $BWW \rightarrow WB$; $BWB \rightarrow WW$ and the total weights remain unchanged after each move. Hence if the 'two marker state is achievable, then the end weights must be either $\phi^2$ or $\psi^2$ (corresponding to $WW$ and $BB$ respectively). If $n = 3k + 1$, the total weight at the beginning is $\phi^{(3k+1)} = \phi$. But $\phi \neq \phi^2$ or $\psi^2$ as is evident from the definitions of these functions. Hence 'two marker state' is not achievable for $n = 3k + 1$.
ratingReason: A noncommutative invariant using triangle symmetries is the difficult obstruction; constructive three-marker reductions finish the other direction.

statement: For every positive integer $m$, prove that there is a finite set of points in the plane such that each point has exactly $m$ other points at distance one.
solution:
We induct on $m$, beginning with a one-point set for $m=0$. Suppose a finite set $S$ has exactly $m$ unit-distance neighbours at each point.

Choose a unit vector $v$ and consider $S\cup(S+v)$. Each $a\in S$ acquires the intended neighbour $a+v$. We choose $v$ to prevent any coincidence or additional unit distance between the two copies.

There are only finitely many forbidden choices. A coincidence $a=b+v$ fixes $v=a-b$. For distinct $a,b\in S$, an unwanted cross distance requires $|a-b-v|=1$ with $|v|=1$. Squaring gives the line equation
$$2(a-b)\cdot v=|a-b|^2.$$
That line meets the unit circle in at most two points. Thus all such restrictions exclude only finitely many unit vectors, while infinitely many remain available.

For an allowed choice, the copies are disjoint, all original unit distances are retained within them, and the only cross unit distances are the matched pairs $a,a+v$. Every point therefore has exactly $m+1$ unit-distance neighbours. Induction proves the assertion for all $m$.
ratingReason: Build the desired unit-distance graph inductively by adjoining a translated copy. The key is proving that a generic unit translation creates only the intended new neighbour for each point.

statement: In triangle $ABC$, $\angle ACB=2\angle ABC$. A point $D$ inside the triangle satisfies $AD=AC$ and $DB=DC$. Prove $\angle BAC=3\angle BAD$.
solution: Write $\angle ABC=\beta$ and $\angle DBC=\angle BCD=t$. Then $\angle ACD=2\beta-t$, and $AD=AC$ gives $DC=2AC\cos(2\beta-t)$. Also $DB=DC$ gives $BC=2DC\cos t$. The sine rule in $ABC$ therefore yields $\sin3\beta/\sin\beta=4\cos t\cos(2\beta-t)$. Expanding both sides cancels $2\cos2\beta$ and leaves $2\cos(2\beta-2t)=1$. Because $0<\beta-t<60^\circ$, this gives $\beta-t=30^\circ$. Finally $\angle BAD=\beta-2t=60^\circ-\beta$, whereas $\angle BAC=180^\circ-3\beta$.
ratingReason: Angle variables alone leave a parameter; the sine rule plus the isosceles condition then force a 30-degree relation.

Sequence $\{a_n\}$ is defined by:
$$
a_0 = \frac{1}{2},\ a_{n+1} = a_n + \frac{a_n^2}{2012},\ n = 0, 1, \dots
$$

Find the integer $k$ such that $a_k < 1 < a_{k+1}$.
solution:
Set $b_n=2012/a_n$. The recurrence becomes
$$b_{n+1}=b_n-1+\frac1{b_n+1},\qquad b_0=4024.$$
Thus $b_n$ strictly decreases and each decrease is less than $1$. In particular $b_{2012}>4024-2012=2012$, so $a_{2012}<1$.

Suppose $b_{2013}\ge2012$. Then $b_i\ge2012$ for $0\le i\le2012$, with strict inequality for earlier indices. Summing the recurrence gives
$$b_{2013}=4024-2013+\sum_{i=0}^{2012}\frac1{b_i+1}<2011+\frac{2013}{2013}=2012,$$
a contradiction. Hence $a_{2013}>1$. Monotonicity now gives the unique answer $\boxed{k=2012}$.
ratingReason: A reciprocal substitution turns the nonlinear growth into a nearly unit descent, allowing two sharp crossing bounds.

statement: An $n\times n$ matrix has nonnegative integer entries. Whenever an entry is zero, the sum of its row and the sum of its column together are at least $n$. Prove the total of all entries is at least $n^2/2$.
solution:
Let $x$ be the smallest of all row and column sums. If $x\geq n/2$, summing the rows proves the result. Otherwise, transpose if necessary so that a row has sum $x<n/2$.

Let $y$ be the number of nonzero entries in that row. Since each is an integer at least one, $y\leq x<n/2$. The $y$ columns through those entries have sums at least $x$ by minimality. The other $n-y$ columns pass through zero entries, so their sums are at least $n-x$ by the hypothesis.

The total $T$ therefore satisfies
$$T\geq xy+(n-y)(n-x)=\frac{n^2}{2}+\frac{(n-2x)(n-2y)}2>\frac{n^2}{2}.$$
This completes both cases.
ratingReason: Choose the smallest row or column sum. Its zero positions force large sums in the perpendicular direction, while integrality bounds how many nonzero positions it can have.
notes: Official released statement checked; worked exposition independently written and mathematically assessed.

statement: Two airlines divide all direct routes between six cities, with exactly one airline serving each unordered pair. Prove one airline operates a four-city round trip.
solution: One airline operates at least eight of the fifteen routes. We prove every graph on six vertices with eight edges contains a four-cycle. Suppose not. Choose a vertex v of maximum degree d. If d≥4, no other vertex can have two neighbours among the neighbours of v, or it would complete a four-cycle with v. Thus the edges inside that neighbour set form a matching. If d=5, there are at most5+2=7 edges. If d=4, the one remaining vertex has at most one edge into that neighbour set, giving at most4+2+1=7. Otherwise d≤3. Eight edges force d=3. Its three neighbours have at most one internal edge, and each of the other two vertices has at most one edge to those neighbours. Including their possible mutual edge gives at most3+1+2+1=7, again a contradiction. A four-cycle is exactly the required round trip.
ratingReason: Reducing to the denser airline is only the first step. A sharp six-vertex extremal bound requires separate maximum-degree cases and common-neighbour restrictions.

statement: Let $p(x)$ be a monic integer polynomial of degree 2003. Prove that $p(x)^2-25$ has at most 2003 distinct integer roots.
solution: If there were at least 2004, one of $p-5,p+5$ would have at least 1002 distinct integer roots $r_i$. Suppose it is $p-5$. Divide out their linear factors to get $p(x)-5=s(x)\prod_{i=1}^{1002}(x-r_i)$ with $s\in\mathbb Z[x]$. At any integer $m$ with $p(m)=-5$, the nonzero distinct integers $m-r_i$ would have product dividing $-10$. Their absolute product is at least $(501!)^2>10$, impossible. Thus every integer root belongs to $p-5$, which has degree 2003. The other sign is identical.

statement: Find all prime numbers $p$, for which there are infinitely many positive integers $n$, such that: $p \mid n^{n+1} + (n+1)^n$.
solution:
The answer is every odd prime. For $p=2$, if $n$ is even the second summand is odd and the first even; if $n$ is odd the reverse holds. Thus the sum is never divisible by $2$.

For an odd prime $p$, take
$$n=p-2+t\,p(p-1),\qquad t=0,1,2,\ldots.$$
Then $n\equiv-2\pmod p$, $n+1\equiv-1\pmod p$, $p-1\mid n+1$, and $n$ is odd. Fermat therefore gives
$$n^{n+1}+(n+1)^n\equiv(-2)^{n+1}+(-1)^n\equiv1-1=0\pmod p.$$
These are infinitely many positive integers $n$.
ratingReason: Chooses a residue and exponent simultaneously so Fermat turns the two terms into 1 and −1.

statement: Let $p$ be a prime and $X$ be a finite set containing at least $p$ elements. A collection of mutually disjoint $p$-element subsets of $X$ is called a $p$-family. The empty collection itself is regarded as a $p$-family. Let $A$ (respectively, $B$) denote the number of $p$-families having an even (respectively, odd) number of $p$-element subsets of $X$. Prove that $A$ and $B$ differ by a multiple of $p$.
solution: Choose a fixed $p$-element subset $P\subset X$ and cyclically permute its elements, fixing $X\setminus P$. This acts on the families in orbits of size $1$ or $p$, preserving the parity of their number of blocks. Thus only fixed families matter modulo $p$. In a fixed family, a block meeting both $P$ and its complement would have to be invariant: otherwise its $p$ translates would share an outside element, contradicting disjointness. But an invariant block contains either all of $P$ or none, so a mixed block is impossible. Likewise a nonempty proper subset of $P$ cannot be a block: its translates would have to be disjoint, requiring $p$ times its size to be at most $p$, hence singleton blocks, which have size different from $p$. Therefore a fixed family either contains $P$ as a block or avoids $P$ completely. Toggle the block $P$ to pair these fixed families with opposite parity. Their signed contributions cancel, proving $A-B\equiv0\pmod p$.
ratingReason: A cyclic action on p distinguished elements reduces the signed count modulo p to fixed families, which cancel by adding or deleting the distinguished block.

statement:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with sides $a$, $b$, $c$, circumradius $R$ and inradius $r$.
Prove that
$$
\frac{R}{2r} \ge \left( \frac{64a^2 b^2 c^2}{(4a^2 - (b-c)^2)(4b^2 - (c-a)^2)(4c^2 - (a-b)^2)} \right)^2
$$
solution:
Put $x=s-a$, $y=s-b$, $z=s-c$, all positive. Then $a=y+z$, $b=z+x$, $c=x+y$, and $R/(2r)=(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)/(8xyz)$. Also $4a^2-(b-c)^2=(3y+z)(3z+y)$, with cyclic analogues. AM-GM gives
$$ (3x+y)(3y+x)=3(x+y)^2+4xy\ge4\bigl(4xy(x+y)^6\bigr)^{1/4}, $$
so $(3x+y)^2(3y+x)^2\ge32\sqrt{xy}(x+y)^3$. Multiply its three cyclic forms to obtain exactly the desired inequality after substituting the displayed expressions. Equality holds for $x=y=z$, equivalently an equilateral triangle.

statement: Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$. Let the median $AM$ intersect the incircle of $ABC$ at $K$ and $L$, $K$ being nearer to $A$ than $L$. If $AK = KL = LM$, prove that the sides of triangle $ABC$ are in the ratio $5 : 10 : 13$ in some order.
solution:
Let $I$ be the incentre of triangle $ABC$ and $D$ be its projection on $BC$. Observe that $AB \neq AC$ as $AB = AC$ implies that $D = L = M$. So assume that $AC > AB$. Let $N$ be the projection of $I$ on $KL$. Then the perpendicular $IN$ from $I$ to $KL$ is a bisector of $KL$ and as $AK = LM$, it is a bisector of $AM$ also. Hence $AI = IM$.

![A triangle ABC with incircle centered at I, tangent to BC at D. The median AM is drawn, intersecting the incircle at points K and L. M is the midpoint of BC, and N is the foot of the perpendicular from I to KL. The segments AK, KL, and LM are marked as equal.](assets/diagrams/6b4041e45a177c676079.jpg)

Fig. 1.

But $AI = \frac{r}{\sin(A/2)} = r \operatorname{cosec}(A/2)$ and
$$
\begin{aligned}
IM^2 & = ID^2 + DM^2 = r^2 + (BM - BD)^2 \\
& = r^2 + \left(\frac{a}{2} - (s-b)\right)^2
\end{aligned}
$$
Hence $r^2 \operatorname{cosec}^2(A/2) = r^2 + \left((a/2) - (s-b)\right)^2$ giving $r^2 \cot^2(A/2) = ((b-c)/2)^2$. Since $b > c$, we obtain $r \cot(A/2) = ((b-c)/2)$. So $s-a = ((b-c)/2)$. This gives $a = 2c$.

As $KN = NL$ and $AK = KL = LM$, we have $NL = AM/6$. We also have $AN = NM$. Now
$$
\begin{aligned}
r^2 = IL^2 = IN^2 + NL^2 & = AI^2 - AN^2 + NL^2 \\
& = AI^2 - \frac{1}{4} m_a^2 + \frac{1}{36} m_a^2 \\
& = r^2 \operatorname{cosec}^2(A/2) - \frac{2}{9} m_a^2
\end{aligned}
$$
Hence $r^2 \cot^2(A/2) = \frac{2}{9} m_a^2$. From the above, we get
$$
\left(\frac{b-c}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{2}{9} \cdot \frac{1}{4} (2b^2 + 2c^2 - a^2)
$$
Simplification gives $5b^2 + 13c^2 - 18bc = 0$. This can be written as $(b-c)(5b-13c) = 0$. As $b \neq c$, we get $5b - 13c = 0$. To conclude, $a = 2c$, $5b = 13c$ yield
$$
\frac{a}{10} = \frac{b}{13} = \frac{c}{5}
$$

statement:
Let $1=a_0\leq a_1\leq a_2\leq\cdots$ and define
$$b_n=\sum_{k=1}^n\left(1-\frac{a_{k-1}}{a_k}\right)\frac1{\sqrt{a_k}}.$$
Prove $0\leq b_n<2$. Also prove that for every $0\leq c<2$ a sequence of this kind exists with $b_n>c$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
solution:
Put $y=1/\sqrt{a_{k-1}}$, $x=1/\sqrt{a_k}$, so $0<x\leq y$. With $t=x/y\leq1$,
$$\left(1-\frac{a_{k-1}}{a_k}\right)\frac1{\sqrt{a_k}}=y\,t(1-t^2)\leq2y(1-t)=2(y-x),$$
since $t(1+t)\leq2$. Summing telescopically gives
$$0\leq b_n\leq2\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt{a_n}}\right)<2.$$

To approach the bound, choose $t>1$ and set $a_k=t^{2k}$. Then
$$b_n=(1-t^{-2})\sum_{k=1}^nt^{-k}=\frac{t+1}{t^2}(1-t^{-n}).$$
As $t$ decreases to one, $(t+1)/t^2$ tends to two. Given $c<2$, choose $t>1$ so that this quantity exceeds $c$, then choose $n$ sufficiently large that $b_n>c$. Since this expression increases with $n$, it remains above $c$ thereafter.
ratingReason: Bound each summand by a telescoping difference of reciprocal square roots. The sharpness part needs a geometric sequence with ratio approaching one, not just equality analysis.

statement:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be positive integers such that
$$
\frac{43}{197}<\frac{\alpha}{\beta}<\frac{17}{77}
$$

Find the minimum possible value of $\beta$.
solution:
We have
$$
\frac{77}{17}<\frac{\beta}{\alpha}<\frac{197}{43}
$$
That is,
$$
4+\frac{9}{17}<\frac{\beta}{\alpha}<4+\frac{25}{43}
$$
Thus $4<\frac{\beta}{\alpha}<5$. Since $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are positive integers, we may write $\beta=4 \alpha+x$, where $0<x<\alpha$. Now we get
$$
4+\frac{9}{17}<4+\frac{x}{\alpha}<4+\frac{25}{43}
$$
So $\frac{9}{17}<\frac{x}{\alpha}<\frac{25}{43}$; that is, $\frac{43 x}{25}<\alpha<\frac{17 x}{9}$.
We find the smallest value of $x$ for which $\alpha$ becomes a well-defined integer. For $x=1,2,3$ the bounds of $\alpha$ are respectively $\left(1 \frac{18}{25}, 1 \frac{8}{9}\right),\left(3 \frac{11}{25}, 3 \frac{7}{9}\right),\left(5 \frac{4}{9}, 5 \frac{2}{3}\right)$. None of these pairs contain an integer between them.
For $x=4$, we have $\frac{43 x}{25}=6 \frac{12}{25}$ and $\frac{17 x}{9}=7 \frac{5}{9}$. Hence, in this case $\alpha=7$, and $\beta=4 \alpha+x=28+4=32$.
This is also the least possible value, because, if $x \geq 5$, then $\alpha>\frac{43 x}{25} \geq \frac{43}{5}>8$, and so $\beta>37$.
Hence the minimum possible value of $\beta$ is 32.
ratingReason: Invert the interval, write the numerator as four times the denominator plus a small remainder, and check the first four possible remainders.

statement: Find all positive integers $n$ for which $\{n,n+1,\ldots,n+5\}$ can be split into two subsets with equal products.
solution:
There are no such integers.

If a prime $p\geq7$ divided one of the six consecutive integers, it could divide none of the others. Whichever subset contained that integer would have product divisible by $p$, while the other would not. Hence every prime divisor of all six integers must belong to $\{2,3,5\}$.

Exactly three of the six integers are odd. Among those three, at most one is divisible by three and at most one by five. Therefore at least one of them has no prime divisor at all and must equal one. This forces $n=1$.

But $\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ contains exactly one number divisible by five, again making equal subset products impossible. Thus no $n$ works.
ratingReason: A prime at least seven can occur in only one of the six terms. Restricting the remaining prime factors and examining the three odd terms then forces an impossible small case.

statement:
Let $p, q, r$ be positive real numbers, not all equal, such that some two of the equations
$$
p x^{2}+2 q x+r=0, \quad q x^{2}+2 r x+p=0, \quad r x^{2}+2 p x+q=0
$$
have a common root, say $\alpha$. Prove that
(a) $\alpha$ is real and negative; and
(b) the third equation has non-real roots.
solution:
Consider the discriminants of the three equations
$$
\begin{array}{r}
p x^{2}+2 q x+r=0 \\
q x^{2}+2 r x+p=0 \\
r x^{2}+2 p x+q=0
\end{array}
$$
Let us denote them by $D_{1}, D_{2}, D_{3}$ respectively. Then we have
$$
D_{1}=4\left(q^{2}-r p\right), \quad D_{2}=4\left(r^{2}-p q\right), \quad D_{3}=4\left(p^{2}-q r\right)
$$
We observe that
$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{1}+D_{2}+D_{3} & =4\left(p^{2}+q^{2}+r^{2}-p q-q r-r p\right) \\
& =2\left\{(p-q)^{2}+(q-r)^{2}+(r-p)^{2}\right\}>0
\end{aligned}
$$
since $p, q, r$ are not all equal. Hence at least one of $D_{1}, D_{2}, D_{3}$ must be positive. We may assume $D_{1}>0$.
Suppose $D_{2}<0$ and $D_{3}<0$. In this case both the equations (2) and (3) have only non-real roots and equation (1) has only real roots. Hence the common root $\alpha$ must be between (2) and (3). But then $\bar{\alpha}$ is the other root of both (2) and (3). Hence it follows that (2) and (3) have same set of roots. This implies that
$$
\frac{q}{r}=\frac{r}{p}=\frac{p}{q}
$$
Thus $p=q=r$ contradicting the given condition. Hence both $D_{2}$ and $D_{3}$ cannot be negative. We may assume $D_{2} \geq 0$. Thus we have
$$
q^{2}-r p>0, \quad r^{2}-p q \geq 0
$$
These two give
$$
q^{2} r^{2}>p^{2} q r
$$
since $p, q, r$ are all positive. Hence we obtain $q r>p^{2}$ or $D_{3}<0$. We conclude that the common root must be between equations (1) and (2).
Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}
& p \alpha^{2}+2 q \alpha+r=0 \\
& q \alpha^{2}+2 r \alpha+p=0
\end{aligned}
$$
Eliminating $\alpha^{2}$, we obtain
$$
2\left(q^{2}-p r\right) \alpha=p^{2}-q r
$$
Since $q^{2}-p r>0$ and $p^{2}-q r<0$, we conclude that $\alpha<0$.
The condition $p^{2}-q r<0$ implies that the equation (3) has only non-real roots.

Alternately one can argue as follows. Suppose $\alpha$ is a common root of two equations, say, (1) and (2). If $\alpha$ is non-real, then $\bar{\alpha}$ is also a root of both (1) and (2). Hence the coefficients of (1) and (2) are proportional. This forces $p=q=r$, a contradiction. Hence the common root between any two equations cannot be non-real. Looking at the coefficients, we conclude that the common root $\alpha$ must be negative. If (1) and (2) have common root $\alpha$, then $q^{2} \geq r p$ and $r^{2} \geq p q$. Here at least one inequality is strict for $q^{2}=p r$ and $r^{2}=p q$ forces $p=q=r$. Hence $q^{2} r^{2}>p^{2} q r$. This gives $p^{2}<q r$ and hence (3) has non-real roots.
ratingReason: Separate a nonreal common root, which forces proportional real quadratics, from the real case; multiplying two discriminant inequalities rules out roots of the third quadratic.

statement:
In tetrahedron $ABCD$, $\angle BDC=90^\circ$. The perpendicular projection of $D$ onto plane $ABC$ is the orthocentre of $ABC$. Prove
$$(AB+BC+CA)^2\leq6(AD^2+BD^2+CD^2),$$
and determine equality.
solution:
Let $H$ be the given projection. Since $AH\perp BC$ and $DH$ is perpendicular to the whole base plane, $AD\perp BC$. Similarly $BD\perp AC$ and $CD\perp AB$.

Put $D$ at the origin and denote the other vertex vectors by $a,b,c$. The given right angle says $b\cdot c=0$. Since $BD\perp AC$, we have $b\cdot(c-a)=0$, hence $a\cdot b=0$. Likewise $CD\perp AB$ gives $a\cdot c=0$. Thus the three edges from $D$ are mutually perpendicular.

Writing $x=AD^2$, $y=BD^2$, $z=CD^2$, Pythagoras gives
$$AB=\sqrt{x+y},\quad BC=\sqrt{y+z},\quad CA=\sqrt{z+x}.$$
Cauchy–Schwarz yields
$$(AB+BC+CA)^2\leq3((x+y)+(y+z)+(z+x))=6(x+y+z).$$
Equality holds exactly when the three square roots are equal, or $x=y=z$. Thus equality occurs precisely when the three mutually perpendicular edges $DA,DB,DC$ also have equal lengths.
ratingReason: The projection hypothesis turns the right angle into three pairwise perpendicular edges. Pythagoras and Cauchy–Schwarz then give the inequality and equality case.

statement: Find the number of trailing zeros of2007!, and its last nonzero decimal digit.
solution: The number of factors of five is401+80+16+3=500, while there are more factors of two, so there are500 trailing zeros. Let U=2007!/5⁵⁰⁰. Modulo five, remove multiples of five repeatedly. For each quotient q=2007,401,80,16,3, the product of its nonmultiples of five is $(-1)^{\lfloor q/5\rfloor}(q\bmod5)!$ by Wilson’s theorem. Thus $U\equiv(-1)^{500}2!1!0!1!3!\equiv2\pmod5$. Dividing out the corresponding500 factors of two changes nothing modulo five because2⁵⁰⁰≡1. The remaining integer2007!/10⁵⁰⁰ is even and congruent to2 modulo five, so its last digit is2.
ratingReason: Counting zeros is routine, but the final nonzero digit requires recursively stripping factors of five and then accounting for the removed twos modulo five.

statement: Find all functions $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $f(x)f(y)=f(x+y)+xy$ for all real $x,y$.
solution: Putting $x=y=0$ gives $f(0)\in\{0,1\}$; the value $0$ would force $f$ identically zero and contradict the equation, so $f(0)=1$. Expand $f(x)f(y)f(z)$ first grouping $x,y$, then grouping $y,z$. Subtraction yields $y[x f(z)-z f(x)+z-x]=0$. Taking $y=1,z=1$ gives $f(x)=1+cx$ for a constant $c$. Substitution into the original equation forces $c^2=1$. Thus exactly $f(x)=1+x$ and $f(x)=1-x$ work.
ratingReason: The decisive step is evaluating a triple product in two ways; pointwise substitutions alone leave too much freedom.

statement: All possible 6-digit numbers, in each of which the digits occur in non-increasing order (from left to right, e.g., $877550$) are written as a sequence in increasing order. Find the $2005$-th number in this sequence.
solution:
Consider a 6-digit number whose digits from left to right are in non-increasing order. If $1$ is the first digit of such a number, then the subsequent digits cannot exceed $1$. The set of all such numbers with initial digit equal to $1$ is
$$
\{100000, 110000, 111000, 111100, 111110, 111111\}.
$$
There are $6$ elements in this set.

Let us consider 6-digit numbers with initial digit $2$. Starting from $200000$, we can go up to $222222$. We count these numbers as follows:

| $200000$ | - | $211111$ | $:$ | $6$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $220000$ | - | $221111$ | $:$ | $5$ |
| $222000$ | - | $222111$ | $:$ | $4$ |
| $222200$ | - | $222211$ | $:$ | $3$ |
| $222220$ | - | $222221$ | $:$ | $2$ |
| $222222$ | - | $222222$ | $:$ | $1$ |

The number of such numbers is $21$.

Similarly we count numbers with initial digit $3$; the sequence starts from $300000$ and ends with $333333$. We have

| $300000$ | - | $322222$ | $:$ | $21$ |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| $330000$ | - | $332222$ | $:$ | $15$ |
| $333000$ | - | $333222$ | $:$ | $10$ |
| $333300$ | - | $333322$ | $:$ | $6$ |
| $333330$ | - | $333332$ | $:$ | $3$ |
| $333333$ | - | $333333$ | $:$ | $1$ |

We obtain the total number of numbers starting from $3$ equal to $56$.

Similarly,

| $400000$ | $433333$ | $56$ |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| $440000$ | $443333$ | $35$ |
| $444000$ | $444333$ | $20$ |
| $444400$ | $444433$ | $10$ |
| $444440$ | $444443$ | $4$ |
| $444444$ | $444444$ | $1$ |
|  |  | $126$ |

| $500000$ | $544444$ | $126$ |
| $550000$ | $554444$ | $70$ |
| $555000$ | $555444$ | $35$ |
| $555500$ | $555544$ | $15$ |
| $555550$ | $555554$ | $5$ |
| $555555$ | $555555$ | $1$ |
|  |  | $252$ |

| $600000$ | $655555$ | $252$ |
| $660000$ | $665555$ | $126$ |
| $666000$ | $666555$ | $56$ |
| $666600$ | $666655$ | $21$ |
| $666660$ | $666665$ | $6$ |
| $666666$ | $666666$ | $1$ |
|  |  | $462$ |

| $700000$ | $766666$ | $462$ |
| $770000$ | $776666$ | $210$ |
| $777000$ | $777666$ | $84$ |
| $777700$ | $777766$ | $28$ |
| $777770$ | $777776$ | $7$ |
| $777777$ | $777777$ | $1$ |
|  |  | $792$ |

Thus the number of 6-digit numbers where digits are non-increasing starting from $100000$ and ending with $777777$ is
$$
792 + 462 + 252 + 126 + 56 + 21 + 6 = 1715
$$
Since $2005 - 1715 = 290$, we have to consider only $290$ numbers in the sequence with initial digit $8$. We have
$$
\begin{aligned}
& 800000 - 855555 \quad: \quad 252 \\
& 860000 - 863333: 35 \\
& 864000 - 864110 \quad: \quad 3
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus the required number is $\underline{864110}$.


It is known that the number of ways of choosing $r$ objects from $n$ different types of objects (with repetitions allowed) is $\binom{n+r-1}{r}$. In particular, if we want to write $r$-digit numbers using $n$ digits allowing for repetitions with the additional condition that the digits appear in non-increasing order, we see that this can be done in $\binom{n+r-1}{r}$ ways.

Now we group the given numbers into different classes and write the number of ways in which each class can be obtained. To keep track we also write the cumulative sums of the number of numbers so obtained. Observe that the numbers themselves are written in ascending order. So we exhaust numbers beginning with $1$, then beginning with $2$ and so on.

| Numbers | Digits used other than the fixed part | $n$ | $r$ | $\overline{\binom{n+r-1}{r}}$ | Cumulative sum |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| beginning with $1$ | $1,0$ | $2$ | $5$ | $\binom{6}{5} = 6$ | $6$ |
| $2$ | $2,1,0$ | $3$ | $5$ | $\binom{7}{5} = 21$ | $27$ |
| $3$ | $3,2,1,0$ | $4$ | $5$ | $\binom{8}{5} = 56$ | $83$ |
| $4$ | $4,3,2,1,0$ | $5$ | $5$ | $\binom{9}{5} = 126$ | $209$ |
| $5$ | $5,4,3,2,1,0$ | $6$ | $5$ | $\binom{10}{5} = 252$ | $461$ |
| $6$ | $6,5,4,3,2,1,0$ | $7$ | $5$ | $\binom{11}{5} = 462$ | $923$ |
| $7$ | $7,6,5,4,3,2,1,0$ | $8$ | $5$ | $\binom{12}{5} = 792$ | $1715$ |
| from $800000$ to $855555$ | $5,4,3,2,1,0$ | $6$ | $5$ | $\binom{10}{5} = 252$ | $1967$ |
| from $860000$ to $863333$ | $3,2,1,0$ | $4$ | $4$ | $\binom{7}{4} = 35$ | $2002$ |

The next three 6-digit numbers are $864000, 864100, 864110$.

Hence the $2005$-th number in the sequence is $864110$.

statement: Among all triangles determined by 100 points in the plane, with no three collinear, prove that at most 70% are acute.
solution:
Any four points determine a nonacute triangle. If they form a convex quadrilateral, at least one of its interior angles is at least $90^\circ$, and its two adjacent vertices complete such a triangle. If one point lies inside the triangle of the other three, the three angles about that interior point sum to $360^\circ$; one is at least $120^\circ$, again giving a nonacute triangle.

Now choose any five points. Each of their five four-point subsets has at most three acute triangles. Every triangle belongs to exactly two of those four-point subsets. If $T_5$ is the number of acute triangles, then $2T_5\leq15$. Since $T_5$ is an integer, $T_5\leq7$ out of the ten possible triangles.

Finally let $T$ be the number of acute triangles among all 100 points. Count pairs consisting of an acute triangle and a five-point subset containing it. Each triangle occurs in $\binom{97}{2}$ such subsets, while each five-point subset contributes at most seven. Thus
$$T\binom{97}{2}\leq7\binom{100}{5}=\frac7{10}\binom{100}{3}\binom{97}{2}.$$
Cancel the positive common factor to obtain the required 70% bound.
ratingReason: A four-point geometric obstruction gives a 75% bound. Applying it to five points and using integrality improves it to 70%, which a second double count transfers to the full set.

statement: An unknown integer point $(x,y)$ is specified by the labelled values $A=x^2+y$ and $B=x+y^2$, where $A\ne B$. Prove that the known pair $(A,B)$ determines $(x,y)$ uniquely.
solution: Suppose $(u,v)$ produces the same two values. If $x=u$, the first equation gives $y=v$. Otherwise, subtracting the equations gives $v-y=(x-u)(x+u)$ and $u-x=(y-v)(y+v)$, hence $(x+u)(y+v)=1$. Thus both sums equal some $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$. Substituting $u=\varepsilon-x,v=\varepsilon-y$ into the first difference gives $2y=\varepsilon+1-2\varepsilon x$. If $\varepsilon=1$, then $y=1-x$; if $\varepsilon=-1$, then $y=x$. In either case $x^2+y=x+y^2$, contrary to the given distinctness.
ratingReason: Comparing two candidate points yields a product of two integers equal to one; both sign cases must then contradict the distinct outputs.

solution:
(a) Let us assume that there are no even numbers in the sequence. This means that $x_{n+1}$ is obtained from $x_{n}$, by adding a nonzero even digit of $x_{n}$ to $x_{n}$, for each $n \geq 1$.
Let $E$ be the left most even digit in $x_{1}$ which may be taken in the form
$$
x_{1} = O_{1} O_{2} \cdots O_{k} E D_{1} D_{2} \cdots D_{l}
$$
where $O_{1}, O_{2}, \ldots, O_{k}$ are odd digits $(k \geq 0)$; $D_{1}, D_{2}, \ldots, D_{l-1}$ are even or odd; and $D_{l}$ odd, $l \geq 1$.
Since each time we are adding at least 2 to a term of the sequence to get the next term, at some stage, we will have a term of the form
$$
x_{r} = O_{1} O_{2} \cdots O_{k} E 999 \cdots 9 F
$$
where $F = 3, 5, 7$ or $9$. Now we are forced to add $E$ to $x_{r}$ to get $x_{r+1}$, as it is the only even digit available. After at most four steps of addition, we see that some next term is of the form
$$
x_{s} = O_{1} O_{2} \cdots O_{k} G 000 \cdots M
$$
where $G$ replaces $E$ of $x_{r}$, $G = E+1$, $M = 1, 3, 5$, or $7$. But $x_{s}$ has no nonzero even digit contradicting our assumption. Hence the sequence has some even number as its term.

(b) If there are only finitely many even terms and $x_{t}$ is the last term, then the sequence $\langle x_{n}\rangle_{n=t+1}^{\infty} = \langle x_{t+1}, x_{t+2}, \ldots \rangle$ is obtained in a similar manner and hence must have an even term by (a), a contradiction. Thus $\langle x_{n}\rangle_{n=1}^{\infty}$ has infinitely many even terms.
ratingReason: An eventual all-odd tail must add only nonzero even digits; following the first such digit to the next decimal boundary traps the process in a number with no legal even increment.

statement: Prove that infinitely many positive integers $a$ have the property that $n^4+a$ is composite for every positive integer $n$.
solution:
Choose $a=4m^4$ for any integer $m\geq2$. Sophie Germain's identity gives
$$n^4+4m^4=(n^2-2mn+2m^2)(n^2+2mn+2m^2).$$
The first factor is $(n-m)^2+m^2\geq m^2>1$, and the second is still larger. Thus every $n^4+a$ is composite. The distinct choices $m=2,3,\ldots$ give infinitely many such $a$.
ratingReason: Discover a family matched to Sophie Germain’s factorisation, then check that neither factor can degenerate to one.

statement:
Find all functions $f: \mathbf{R} \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$ such that
$$
f\left(x^{2}+y f(z)\right)=x f(x)+z f(y)
$$
for all $x, y, z$ in $\mathbf{R}$. (Here $\mathbf{R}$ denotes the set of all real numbers.)
solution:
Taking $x=y=0$ in (1), we get $z f(0)=f(0)$ for all $z \in \mathbf{R}$. Hence we obtain $f(0)=0$.

Taking $y=0$ in (1), we get
$$
f\left(x^{2}\right)=x f(x)
$$
Similarly $x=0$ in (1) gives
$$
f(y f(z))=z f(y)
$$
Putting $y=1$ in (3), we get
$$
f(f(z))=z f(1) \quad \forall z \in \mathbf{R}
$$
Now using (2) and (4), we obtain
$$
f(x f(x))=f\left(f\left(x^{2}\right)\right)=x^{2} f(1)
$$
Put $y=z=x$ in (3) also given
$$
f(x f(x))=x f(x)
$$
Comparing (5) and (6), it follows that $x^{2} f(1)=x f(x)$. If $x \neq 0$, then $f(x)=c x$, for some constant $c$. Since $f(0)=0$, we have $f(x)=c x$ for $x=0$ as well. Substituting this in (1), we see that
$$
c\left(x^{2}+c y z\right)=c x^{2}+c y z
$$
or
$$
c^{2} y z=c y z \quad \forall y, z \in \mathbf{R}
$$
This implies that $c^{2}=c$. Hence $c=0$ or $1$. We obtain $f(x)=0$ for all $x$ or $f(x)=x$ for all $x$. It is easy to verify that these two are solutions of the given equation.
ratingReason: Zero substitutions first give the square and product identities; evaluating the same product in two ways forces f(x)=xf(1), leaving only two constants.

statement: For arbitrary real $a_1,\ldots,a_n$, define $f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^n2^{1-j}\cos(a_j+x)$. If $f(x_1)=f(x_2)=0$, prove that $x_2-x_1$ is an integer multiple of $\pi$.
solution:
Write
$$Z=\sum_{j=1}^n2^{1-j}e^{ia_j},\qquad f(x)=\operatorname{Re}(Ze^{ix}).$$
The first summand has modulus one, while the others have total modulus at most
$$\frac12+\cdots+\frac1{2^{n-1}}=1-\frac1{2^{n-1}}<1.$$
The reverse triangle inequality therefore gives $|Z|\geq2^{1-n}>0$.

Write $Z=Re^{i\phi}$ with $R>0$. Then $f(x)=R\cos(x+\phi)$, whose zeros are exactly $x+\phi=\pi/2+k\pi$. Any two zeros differ by an integer multiple of $\pi$. The same argument can be expressed with the real sine and cosine coefficients instead of complex numbers.
ratingReason: Combine the phase-shifted cosines into one sinusoid. The dominant first coefficient is essential to rule out the identically zero function.
notes: Official released statement checked; worked exposition independently written and mathematically assessed.

statement:
Consider a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, in which $K, L, M, N$ are the midpoints of the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$ respectively. Suppose
(a) $BD$ bisects $KM$ at $Q$;
(b) $QA = QB = QC = QD$; and
(c) $LK / LM = CD / CB$.
Prove that $ABCD$ is a square.
solution:
![A convex quadrilateral ABCD with midpoints K, L, M, N marked on sides AB, BC, CD, DA respectively. The diagonals and lines connecting midpoints form a parallelogram KLMN inside, with intersection point Q marked at the center. Several segments are marked as equal with tick marks.](assets/diagrams/1a17e31532fc09426185.jpg)
Fig. 1.
Observe that $KLMN$ is a parallelogram, $Q$ is the midpoint of $MK$ and hence $NL$ also passes through $Q$. Let $T$ be the point of intersection of $AC$ and $BD$; and let $S$ be the point of intersection of $BD$ and $MN$.

Consider the triangle $MNK$. Note that $SQ$ is parallel to $NK$ and $Q$ is the midpoint of $MK$. Hence $S$ is the midpoint of $MN$. Since $MN$ is parallel to $AC$, it follows that $T$ is the midpoint of $AC$. Now $Q$ is the circumcentre of $\triangle ABC$ and the median $BT$ passes through $Q$. Here there are two possibilities:
(i) $ABC$ is a right triangle with $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$ and $T = Q$; and
(ii) $T \neq Q$ in which case $BT$ is perpendicular to $AC$.

Suppose $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$ and $T = Q$. Observe that $Q$ is the circumcentre of the triangle $DCB$ and hence $\angle DCB = 90^\circ$. Similarly $\angle DAB = 90^\circ$. It follows that $\angle ADC = 90^\circ$ and $ABCD$ is a rectangle. This implies that $KLMN$ is a rhombus. Hence $LK / LM = 1$ and this gives $CD = CB$. Thus $ABCD$ is a square.

In the second case, observe that $BD$ is perpendicular to $AC$, $KL$ is parallel to $AC$ and $LM$ is parallel to $BD$. Hence it follows that $ML$ is perpendicular to $LK$. Similar reasoning shows that $KLMN$ is a rectangle.

Using $LK / LM = CD / CB$, we get that $CBD$ is similar to $LMK$. In particular, $\angle LMK = \angle CBD = \alpha$ say. Since $LM$ is parallel to $DB$, we also get $\angle BQK = \alpha$. Since $KLMN$ is a cyclic quadrilateral we also get $\angle LNK = \angle LMK = \alpha$. Using the fact that $BD$ is parallel to $NK$, we get $\angle LQB = \angle LNK = \alpha$. Since $BD$ bisects $\angle CBA$, we also have $\angle KBQ = \alpha$. Thus
$$
QK = KB = BL = LQ
$$
and $BL$ is parallel to $QK$. This gives $QM$ is parallel to $LC$ and
$$
QM = QL = BL = LC
$$
It follows that $QLCM$ is a parallelogram. But $\angle LCM = 90^\circ$. Hence $\angle MQL = 90^\circ$. This implies that $KLMN$ is a square. Also observe that $\angle LQK = 90^\circ$ and hence $\angle CBA = \angle LQK = 90^\circ$. This gives $\angle CDA = 90^\circ$ and hence $ABCD$ is a rectangle. Since $BA = BC$, it follows that $ABCD$ is a square.

statement: For each $k=1,2,3,4,5$, determine exactly which $a>0$ allow a nondegenerate tetrahedron with $k$ edge lengths equal to $a$ and the other $6-k$ equal to $1$.
solution:
The ranges are
$$\begin{array}{c|c}k&\text{admissible }a\\\hline
1&(0,\sqrt3)\\
2&(0,\sqrt{2+\sqrt3})\\
3&(0,\infty)\\
4&(\sqrt{2-\sqrt3},\infty)\\
5&(1/\sqrt3,\infty).
\end{array}$$
For $k=1$, take $AB=a$. The two equilateral triangles $ACD,BCD$ have unit sides. Their vertices $A,B$ lie on the circle perpendicular to $CD$ through its midpoint, of radius $\sqrt3/2$. Their chord length can be any number strictly between $0$ and $\sqrt3$; the endpoints give a degenerate tetrahedron. This proves the first range.

For $k=2$, either the exceptional edges are opposite or adjacent. In the opposite case $AB=CD=a$, place
$$A=(-a/2,0,0),\ B=(a/2,0,0),\ C=(0,-a/2,h),\ D=(0,a/2,h).$$
All cross edges are one exactly when $h^2=1-a^2/2$. Conversely the equal cross edges force the midpoint line perpendicular to both equal opposite edges, and their directions perpendicular to one another, so this condition is necessary. The range is $0<a<\sqrt2$.

For the adjacent case let $AC=AD=a$, with all other edges one. Place
$$C=(-1/2,0,0),\ D=(1/2,0,0),\ B=(0,\sqrt3/2,0),\ A=(0,y,z).$$
The equations $AC=a$ and $AB=1$ give
$$y=\frac{a^2-1/2}{\sqrt3},\qquad z^2=\frac{-a^4+4a^2-1}{3}.$$
A nondegenerate tetrahedron exists exactly when $z^2>0$, or $2-\sqrt3<a^2<2+\sqrt3$. Combining this interval with the opposite-edge interval proves the second row.

For $k=3$ and $a\leq1$, use an equilateral base of side $a$ and three unit edges to its apex; its height squared is $1-a^2/3>0$. For $a\geq1$, use a unit equilateral base and three edges of length $a$; its height squared is $a^2-1/3>0$. Thus every positive $a$ works.

Finally scaling every length by $1/a$ exchanges $k$ with $6-k$ and $a$ with $1/a$. The first two rows therefore give the last two.
ratingReason: Classify the two possible placements of two exceptional edges, obtain exact nondegeneracy intervals, and use reciprocal scaling for four and five edges. The three-edge case needs a separate construction.
notes: Official statement checked; configurations independently derived by coordinates, confirming the published classification. At a=1, the assignment of distinguished edges is formal, and the regular tetrahedron is allowed.

statement: Find all functions $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ with f(1)=1 and $f(xy+f(x))=xf(y)+f(x)$ for all real x,y.
solution: The substitution x=1 gives f(y+1)=f(y)+1, hence f(0)=0 and f(−1)=−1. Taking y=0 yields f(f(x))=f(x); taking y=±1 shows f(x)±x are fixed points. We claim every fixed point a is a translation period in the sense f(z+a)=f(z)+a. For a=0 this is immediate. For nonzero fixed a, the equation gives f(ay+a)=af(y)+a. Replace y by y−1 and use f(y−1)=f(y)−1 to obtain f(ay)=af(y). Subtraction proves the claim for every z=ay. Consequently the difference of two fixed points is fixed: if a,b are fixed, f(a−b)=f(a)−b=a−b. Applying this to f(x)+x and f(x)−x shows 2x is fixed for every real x. Therefore f(t)=t for every real t, and substitution verifies it.
ratingReason: The decisive structure is the set of fixed points. Two substitutions generate enough of them, but a separate translation lemma is needed to show their differences are fixed.

title: A smallest flight network with two-step alternatives
statement: A finite directed graph has no pair of opposite arcs and each vertex has an outgoing arc. Every arc $A\to C$ also admits a two-step path $A\to B\to C$. Find the smallest possible number of vertices.
solution: The answer is 7. Fix a vertex $A$. For every out-neighbour $C$, the two-step condition gives another out-neighbour $B$ with $B\to C$. Hence the graph induced by the out-neighbours has positive indegree at every vertex. It contains a directed cycle, whose length is at least three because loops and opposite arcs are unavailable. Thus every vertex has outdegree at least three. If there are $n$ vertices, $3n\le n(n-1)/2$, so $n\ge7$. For attainment use vertices modulo 7, with arcs from $x$ to $x+1,x+2,x+4$. There are no opposite arcs, and each allowed difference is twice another allowed difference modulo 7: $1=4+4$, $2=1+1$, $4=2+2$. These identities supply all required two-step paths.
ratingReason: Every out-neighbourhood must contain a directed cycle, forcing outdegree at least three; a seven-vertex cyclic tournament attains the bound.

statement: Choose a subset $M\subseteq\{1,\ldots,2011\}$ so that every three distinct members include two for which one divides the other. What is the greatest possible size of $M$?
solution:
List the members increasingly as $a_1<\cdots<a_k$. If $a_{i+2}<2a_i$, no two of $a_i,a_{i+1},a_{i+2}$ divide one another. Hence $a_{i+2}\ge2a_i$. Were $k\ge22$, we would have $a_{22}\ge2^{10}a_2\ge2048$, impossible.

The bound $21$ is attained by
$$\{1,2,2^2,\ldots,2^{10}\}\ \cup\ \{3,6,3\cdot2^2,\ldots,3\cdot2^9\}.$$
Each of these two sets is a divisibility chain; any three chosen members contain two from the same chain.
ratingReason: Ordering the chosen integers reveals aᵢ₊₂≥2aᵢ, giving the sharp logarithmic bound; constructing two interleaved divisibility chains achieves 21.

statement:
Suppose $p$ is a prime greater than $3$. Find all pairs of integers $(a, b)$ satisfying the equation
$$
a^{2} + 3 a b + 2 p(a + b) + p^{2} = 0
$$
solution: Put $d=3a+2p$, which cannot be zero because $p>3$ is prime. Rearranging gives $b=-(a+p)^2/d$. Hence $d\mid 9(a+p)^2=(d+p)^2$, so $d\mid p^2$. Conversely, if $d\in\{\pm1,\pm p,\pm p^2\}$ and $d\equiv2p\pmod3$, then $a=(d-2p)/3$ is an integer. As $3\nmid d$ and $d\mid(d+p)^2$, the integer $b=-(d+p)^2/(9d)$ exists and satisfies the equation. Thus all pairs, without case ambiguities, are $\bigl((d-2p)/3,-(d+p)^2/(9d)\bigr)$ for precisely those six signed divisors satisfying $d\equiv2p\pmod3$.

statement: Let $C$ lie strictly on the semicircle with diameter $AB$, and let $D$ be its perpendicular foot on $AB$. Consider the incircle of $ABC$, and the two circles inside the semicircle tangent to $AB$, $CD$ and the semicircular arc, one on each side of $CD$. Prove the three circles share a tangent other than $AB$.
solution:
Write $BC=a$, $CA=b$, $AB=c$, so $a^2+b^2=c^2$. Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(c,0)$, and $D=(d,0)$, where $d=b^2/c$. Let the left and right auxiliary radii be $u,v$. Their centres are
$$L=(d-u,u),\qquad R=(d+v,v).$$
Internal tangency to the circle of centre $(c/2,0)$ and radius $c/2$ gives
$$(d-u-c/2)^2+u^2=(c/2-u)^2.$$
After simplifying, $u^2+2(c-d)u-d(c-d)=0$. Its positive root is
$$u=\sqrt{c(c-d)}-(c-d)=a-a^2/c.$$
The symmetric calculation gives $v=b-b^2/c$. Hence
$$L=(c-a,a-a^2/c),\qquad R=(b,b-b^2/c).$$
The incircle has radius $r=(a+b-c)/2$ and centre
$$I=((b+c-a)/2,r).$$
Since $a^2+b^2=c^2$, the midpoint of $L,R$ is exactly $I$.

Reflect the line $AB$ in the line $LR$. Each of the three centres is fixed by this reflection, so its circle is preserved. The reflected line is consequently tangent to all three circles. It differs from $AB$: the line $LR$ is not $AB$, since both auxiliary radii are positive, and it is not perpendicular to $AB$, since the difference of its endpoint abscissas is $a+b-c>0$. This supplies the second common tangent.
ratingReason: Compute the two auxiliary radii using the semicircle tangency condition. The unexpected key is that the original incenter is the midpoint of the other two centres, giving a common tangent by reflection.

statement: For $n\ge2$, prove that all subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ can be listed as $A_1,\ldots,A_{2^n}$ so that consecutive cardinalities differ by $1$, including the last and first. For every such cyclic listing, determine all possible values of $\sum_{i=1}^{2^n}(-1)^i\sum_{x\in A_i}x$.
solution:
For existence use the reflected Gray-code construction. Start with the cyclic list $\varnothing,\{1\}$. From a list $B_1,\ldots,B_{2^k}$ beginning with $\varnothing$, form
$$B_1,\ldots,B_{2^k},\ B_{2^k}\cup\{k+1\},\ldots,B_1\cup\{k+1\}.$$
Neighbours differ by one element, including the junctions and the last-to-first junction. Induction gives the required listing.

In any admissible listing, cardinality parity alternates, so the desired sum is, up to an overall sign,
$$\sum_{A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}(-1)^{|A|}\sum_{x\in A}x.$$
Fix an element $x$ and another element $y\ne x$. Among subsets containing $x$, toggling $y$ pairs one even and one odd cardinality subset. Thus the coefficient of $x$ in the sum is zero. Every element cancels, and the only possible value is $0$.
ratingReason: Construct a cyclic Gray-code ordering by reflection, then notice parity fixes every alternating sign and cancel each element contribution by toggling a different element. Construction and invariant are separate insights.

statement: If $\alpha$ is a real root of the equation $x^{5}-x^{3}+x-2=0$, prove that $\left[\alpha^{6}\right]=3$. (For any real number $a$, we denote by $[a]$ the greatest integer not exceeding $a$.)
solution: Write $P(x)=x(x^4-x^2+1)-2$. Since $x^4-x^2+1=(x^2-1/2)^2+3/4>0$, no nonpositive x is a root. For $0<x\le1$, $x^4-x^2+1\le1$, so $P(x)<0$; for $x\ge2$, $P(x)>0$. Thus $1<\alpha<2$. The root equation gives $\alpha^6=\alpha^4-\alpha^2+2\alpha$ and consequently $\alpha^7=2\alpha^2-\alpha+2$. Therefore $\alpha(\alpha^6-3)=2(\alpha-1)^2\ge0$, while $\alpha(\alpha^6-4)=2\alpha^2-5\alpha+2=(2\alpha-1)(\alpha-2)<0$. Hence $3\le\alpha^6<4$, as required.
ratingReason: Rather than estimating the root numerically, multiply the defining relation to turn the two sixth-power bounds into a square and a factored quadratic.

statement: For $n>4$ points in the plane with no three collinear, prove that at least $\binom{n-3}{2}$ of their four-point subsets form convex quadrilaterals.
solution:
Any five such points contain a convex quadrilateral. If their convex hull has at least four vertices, choose four of those. Otherwise the hull is a triangle $ABC$ with two interior points $D,E$. The line $DE$ leaves two of $A,B,C$ on one side and the third on the other. Those two vertices together with $D,E$ form a convex quadrilateral. The original hull vertices remain extreme points. Neither $D$ nor $E$ can lie in the triangle formed by the other three selected points: the supporting line $DE$ meets that triangle only at its other endpoint. Thus all four selected points are extreme.

Let $Q$ count the convex quadrilaterals. Every five-point subset contains one, while each fixed quadrilateral belongs to exactly $n-4$ five-point subsets. Therefore
$$Q(n-4)\geq\binom n5,\qquad Q\geq\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)}{120}.$$
For integer $n\geq5$,
$$n(n-1)(n-2)-60(n-4)=(n-5)(n-6)(n+8)\geq0.$$
The preceding lower bound is consequently at least $(n-3)(n-4)/2=\binom{n-3}{2}$, as required.
ratingReason: First prove the five-point convex-quadrilateral lemma, then double-count its occurrences in five-element subsets. An integer polynomial comparison turns the resulting stronger bound into the requested one.
notes: Official released statement checked; worked exposition independently written and mathematically assessed.

statement: In triangle ABC, points D,E occur in that order on BC; F,G occur in that order on CA; and H,K occur in that order on AB. All six points lie on a circle. Given AH=AG=1, BK=BD=2, CE=CF=4 and angle B=60°, find the inradius of ABC.
solution: Write a=BC,b=CA,c=AB. Equal powers from A give AH·AK=AG·AF, so c−2=b−4. Powers from B give BK·BH=BD·BE, hence c−1=a−4. Thus a=b+1 and c=b−2. The cosine rule at B gives b²=a²+c²−ac; substitution yields b=7, so a=8,c=5. The area is (1/2)ac sin60°=10√3 and the semiperimeter is 10. Therefore the inradius is √3.

statement: Can an odd number $n\ge3$ of distinct primes be arranged cyclically so that the sum of every two neighbours is a perfect square? Prove your answer.
solution:
No. If all primes are odd, neighbouring sums are even squares and hence divisible by $4$. The residues of the primes must therefore alternate between $1$ and $3$ modulo $4$, impossible around an odd cycle.

Otherwise exactly one prime is $2$. Each of its two neighbours is $3\pmod4$, since an odd square is $1\pmod4$. The remaining $n-1$ odd primes form a path whose residues alternate. A path with an even number of vertices has opposite endpoint residues, contradicting the fact that both endpoints are $3\pmod4$.
ratingReason: An odd cycle cannot alternate residues 1 and 3 modulo 4; the possible exceptional prime 2 needs a separate endpoint check, which produces the same parity obstruction.

solution:
We know that $2R = \frac{abc}{2\triangle}$ and $r_{a} = \frac{\triangle}{s-a}$, where $a, b, c$ are the sides of the triangle $ABC$, $s = \frac{a+b+c}{2}$ and $\triangle$ is the area of $ABC$. Thus the given condition $2R \leq r_{a}$ translates to
$$
abc \leq \frac{2\triangle^{2}}{s-a}
$$
Putting $s-a = p$, $s-b = q$, $s-c = r$, we get $a = q + r$, $b = r + p$, $c = p + q$ and the condition now is
$$
p(p+q)(q+r)(r+p) \leq 2\triangle^{2}
$$
But Heron's formula gives, $\triangle^{2} = s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c) = pqr(p+q+r)$. We obtain $(p+q)(q+r)(r+p) \leq 2qr(p+q+r)$. Expanding and effecting some cancellations, we get
$$
p^{2}(q+r) + p(q^{2} + r^{2}) \leq qr(q+r)
$$
Suppose $a \leq b$. This implies that $q + r \leq r + p$ and hence $q \leq p$. This implies that $q^{2} r \leq p^{2} r$ and $q r^{2} \leq p r^{2}$ giving $qr(q+r) \leq p^{2} r + p r^{2} < p^{2} r + p r^{2} + p^{2} q + p q^{2} = p^{2}(q+r) + p(q^{2} + r^{2})$ which contradicts $(\star)$. Similarly, $a \leq c$ is also not possible. This proves (i).

Suppose $2R \leq r_{b}$. As above this takes the form
$$
q^{2}(r+p) + q(r^{2} + p^{2}) \leq pr(p+r)
$$
Since $a > b$ and $a > c$, we have $q > p$, $r > p$. Thus $q^{2} r > p^{2} r$ and $q r^{2} > p r^{2}$. Hence
$$
q^{2}(r+p) + q(r^{2} + p^{2}) > q^{2} r + q r^{2} > p^{2} r + p r^{2} = pr(p+r)
$$
which contradicts $(\star\star)$. Hence $2R > r_{b}$. Similarly, we can prove that $2R > r_{c}$. This proves (ii).

statement:
Suppose $x_1,x_2>0$ and $A_i=x_iy_i-z_i^2>0$ for $i=1,2$. Prove
$$\frac8{(x_1+x_2)(y_1+y_2)-(z_1+z_2)^2}\leq\frac1{A_1}+\frac1{A_2},$$
and determine the equality conditions.
solution:
Write $D=(x_1+x_2)(y_1+y_2)-(z_1+z_2)^2$. Substituting $y_i=(A_i+z_i^2)/x_i$ gives
$$D=A_1+A_2+\frac{x_1A_2}{x_2}+\frac{x_2A_1}{x_1}+\left(\sqrt{\frac{x_1}{x_2}}z_2-\sqrt{\frac{x_2}{x_1}}z_1\right)^2.$$
Consequently
$$D\geq A_1+A_2+2\sqrt{A_1A_2}\geq4\sqrt{A_1A_2}>0.$$
Taking reciprocals and applying AM–GM once more yields
$$\frac8D\leq\frac2{\sqrt{A_1A_2}}\leq\frac1{A_1}+\frac1{A_2}.$$
For equality, the last inequality requires $A_1=A_2$. Equality in the first pair of reciprocal terms then gives $x_1=x_2$, and the square term gives $z_1=z_2$. The definition of $A_i$ now gives $y_1=y_2$. Conversely equal triples clearly give equality. Thus equality holds exactly when $(x_1,y_1,z_1)=(x_2,y_2,z_2)$.
ratingReason: Rewrite the mixed determinant terms as a positive square plus two reciprocal terms, then apply AM–GM twice. Track equality through all three steps.

statement: Real numbers $x_i,y_i$ satisfy $0<x_1y_1<\cdots<x_ny_n$ and $\sum_{j=1}^i x_j\ge\sum_{j=1}^i y_j$ for every $i$. Prove $\sum 1/x_i\le\sum 1/y_i$ and determine equality.
solution: Put $A_i=\sum_{j=1}^i(x_j-y_j)\ge0$ and $w_i=1/(x_iy_i)$, so $w_1>\cdots>w_n>0$. Summation by parts gives $\sum_{i=1}^n(1/y_i-1/x_i)=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-y_i)w_i=A_nw_n+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}A_i(w_i-w_{i+1})\ge0$. Each coefficient is positive, so equality holds exactly when all $A_i=0$, equivalently $x_i=y_i$ for every $i$.

statement: Find every integer pair $(a,b)$ such that $n\mid a^n+b^{n+1}$ for every positive integer $n$.
solution:
If $b=0$, every prime divides $a$ by Fermat, so $a=0$. Now assume $b\ne0$. For every sufficiently large prime $p$, Fermat gives
$$0\equiv a^p+b^{p+1}\equiv a+b^2\pmod p.$$
An integer divisible by arbitrarily large primes is zero, hence $a=-b^2$.

Take $n=2q$, where $q$ is any sufficiently large prime not dividing $b$. Modulo $q$ the condition becomes
$$0\equiv b^{4q}+b^{2q+1}\equiv b^4+b^3=b^3(b+1).$$
Thus arbitrarily large primes divide $b+1$, forcing $b=-1$ and $a=-1$. Both $(0,0)$ and $(-1,-1)$ satisfy the required divisibilities.
ratingReason: Substitute arbitrarily large primes to force a+b²=0, then twice a large prime to force b+1=0. Turning infinitely many divisibilities into exact integer equalities is the central insight.

statement:
Let $S$ denote the set of all 6-tuples $(a, b, c, d, e, f)$ of positive integers such that $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}+e^{2}=f^{2}$. Consider the set
$$
T=\{a b c d e f:(a, b, c, d, e, f) \in S\}
$$
Find the greatest common divisor of all the members of $T$.
solution:
We show that the required gcd is 24. Consider an element $(a, b, c, d, e, f) \in S$. We have
$$
a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}+e^{2}=f^{2}
$$
We first observe that not all $a, b, c, d, e$ can be odd. Otherwise, we have $a^{2} \equiv b^{2} \equiv c^{2} \equiv d^{2} \equiv e^{2} \equiv 1$ $(\bmod 8)$ and hence $f^{2} \equiv 5(\bmod 8)$, which is impossible because no square can be congruent to 5 modulo 8. Thus at least one of $a, b, c, d, e$ is even.

Similarly if none of $a, b, c, d, e$ is divisible by 3, then $a^{2} \equiv b^{2} \equiv c^{2} \equiv d^{2} \equiv e^{2} \equiv 1(\bmod 3)$ and hence $f^{2} \equiv 2(\bmod 3)$ which again is impossible because no square is congruent to 2 modulo 3. Thus 3 divides $a b c d e f$.

There are several possibilities for $a, b, c, d, e$.

Case 1: Suppose one of them is even and the other four are odd; say $a$ is even, $b, c, d, e$ are odd. Then $b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}+e^{2} \equiv 4(\bmod 8)$. If $a^{2} \equiv 4(\bmod 8)$, then $f^{2} \equiv 0(\bmod 8)$ and hence $2|a, 4| f$ giving $8 \mid a f$. If $a^{2} \equiv 0(\bmod 8)$, then $f^{2} \equiv 4(\bmod 8)$ which again gives that $4 \mid a$ and $2 \mid f$ so that $8 \mid a f$. It follows that $8 \mid a b c d e f$ and hence $24 \mid a b c d e f$.

Case 2: Suppose $a, b$ are even and $c, d, e$ are odd. Then $c^{2}+d^{2}+e^{2} \equiv 3(\bmod 8)$. Since $a^{2}+b^{2} \equiv 0$ or $4$ modulo 8, it follows that $f^{2} \equiv 3$ or $7(\bmod 8)$ which is impossible. Hence this case does not arise.

Case 3: If three of $a, b, c, d, e$ are even and two odd, then $8 \mid a b c d e f$ and hence $24|a b c d e f$.

Case 4: If four of $a, b, c, d, e$ are even, then again $8 \mid a b c d e f$ and $24|a b c d e f$.

Here again for any six tuple $(a, b, c, d, e, f)$ in $S$, we observe that $24 \mid a b c d e f$. Since
$$
1^{2}+1^{2}+1^{2}+2^{2}+3^{2}=4^{2}
$$
We see that $(1,1,1,2,3,4) \in S$ and hence $24 \in T$. Thus 24 is the gcd of $T$.
ratingReason: A mod-8 case analysis is needed to force three factors of two, followed by a mod-3 obstruction and a sharp example.

statement: Prove that exactly one triangle has consecutive positive integer side lengths and an angle twice another angle. Determine its side lengths.
solution:
If sides $u,v,w$ are opposite angles $U,V,W$ and $V=2U$, the sine and cosine rules give
$$v=2u\cos U,\qquad 2vw\cos U=v^2+w^2-u^2.$$
Eliminating $\cos U$ and using $w\ne u$ yields
$$v^2=u(u+w).$$
Conversely this identity for a triangle with distinct sides implies $v=2u\cos U$ and then $\sin V=\sin2U$. Since $v>u$, the supplementary alternative $V=180^\circ-2U$ would give $W=U$, hence $w=u$, excluded. Thus it characterises the required doubled angle.

Write the consecutive sides as $x,x+1,x+2$, with $x\geq2$ for a nondegenerate triangle. The doubled angle must be the larger of a pair, leaving three possibilities:

- $u=x,v=x+1,w=x+2$ gives $(x+1)^2=x(2x+2)$, hence $x=1$, inadmissible.
- $u=x,v=x+2,w=x+1$ gives $(x+2)^2=x(2x+1)$, hence $(x-4)(x+1)=0$, so $x=4$.
- $u=x+1,v=x+2,w=x$ gives $x^2-x-3=0$, which has no integer root.

Therefore the unique side lengths are $4,5,6$. Since $6^2=4(4+5)$, the angle opposite $6$ is twice that opposite $4$.
ratingReason: Translate a doubled-angle relation into a side-length identity, then treat all three possible ordered angle pairs. Only one yields a nondegenerate integer triangle.

statement: For positive integer n, determine the greatest common divisor of $\binom{2n}{1},\binom{2n}{3},\ldots,\binom{2n}{2n-1}$.
solution: Let 2ᵗ be the highest power of two dividing 2n. For every odd r, the identity $r\binom{2n}{r}=2n\binom{2n-1}{r-1}$ shows 2ᵗ divides the coefficient. Their sum is 2^(2n−1), so their gcd is a power of two. Since their first member is 2n, that gcd has two-adic valuation at most t. Hence it is exactly 2ᵗ.

title: Four points on a Steiner line
statement: Points $A,B,C,A',B',C'$ lie on a circle with $AA'\perp BC$, $BB'\perp CA$, $CC'\perp AB$. For another point $D$ on the circle, let $A''=DA'\cap BC$, $B''=DB'\cap CA$, and $C''=DC'\cap AB$. Prove that these three points and the orthocentre of $ABC$ are collinear.
solution: Use complex coordinates on the unit circle, denoting vertices by lower-case letters. The orthocentre is $h=a+b+c$. Reflection in $BC$ sends a point $z$ to $b+c-bc\bar z$; thus it sends $H$ to $a'=-bc/a$, the second intersection of the altitude with the circle. Let $D_a,D_b,D_c$ be the reflections of $D$ in the three sides. Then $d_a-h=-(ad+bc)/d$, and cyclically $d_b-h=-(bd+ca)/d$, $d_c-h=-(cd+ab)/d$. Each of $ad+bc,bd+ca,cd+ab$ has conjugate equal to itself divided by $abcd$, so their ratios are real: $H,D_a,D_b,D_c$ are collinear. Reflecting the line $DA'$ in $BC$ gives $D_aH$; its intersection with the mirror line is unchanged. Hence $A''$ lies on that same line, and likewise $B'',C''$.
ratingReason: Reflecting the construction in the triangle sides reduces it to the Steiner line of a circumcircle point; the reflected orthocentre supplies the key identification.
