statement: A function $f:\mathbb Z_{>0}\to\mathbb Z_{>0}$ satisfies $f(ab)=f(a)f(b)$ when gcd(a,b)=1, and $f(p+q)=f(p)+f(q)$ for primes p,q. Prove $f(2)=2$, $f(3)=3$, and $f(1999)=1999$.
solution: From $f(6)=f(2)f(3)=2f(3)$ obtain f(2)=2, hence f(4)=4. Write b=f(3), c=f(5), d=f(7). The identities at 10 and 12 give $2c=b+d$ and $4b=c+d$, so $(b,c,d)=(3t,5t,7t)$ for a positive integer t. Also f(8)=8t and f(17)=f(20)−f(3)=17t. Let h=f(19). From 24, $h=24t^2-5t$. From 22, $2f(11)=3t+h$, so $f(11)=12t^2-t$. The two prime decompositions 16=3+13=5+11 give $f(13)=12t^2+t$. Finally 30=2·3·5=13+17 yields $30t^2=12t^2+18t$, forcing t=1. Thus f(3)=3, f(7)=7, f(11)=11 and f(13)=13. Since 1999 is prime and $1999+3=2002=2\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13$, we get $f(1999)+3=2002$, as required.

statement: Find all positive integers m for which the fourth power of the number of positive divisors of m equals m.
solution: Write m=n⁴ and $n=\prod p^{a_p}$. The condition becomes $n=\prod(4a_p+1)$, so n is odd. For a≥1, $4a+1\le5^a$, with equality only at a=1. Therefore if 3 does not divide n, every factor $(4a_p+1)/p^{a_p}$ is at most one, and equality requires n=1 or 5. If the exponent of 3 is at least two, its factor is one at exponent two and less than one afterwards; all other factors are at most one. This yields n=9 or 45. If the exponent of 3 is one, its factor is 5/3, so the other factors must multiply to 3/5. A prime at least 11 contributes at most 5/11<3/5; exponent at least two for 5 or 7 also contributes less than 3/5. Thus only primes 5 and 7, each to exponent one, could occur; their factors are 1 and 5/7, neither giving the needed product. Hence $n\in\{1,5,9,45\}$ and $m\in\{1,625,6561,4100625\}$.
ratingReason: Passing to a fourth root turns the problem into a multiplicative balance. Sharp bounds for each prime exponent leave a special three-adic case to resolve.

solution: The right side and floor term are integers, so $x$ is a positive integer. Write $x=6q+r$, $0\le r\le5$. Cancelling $7q$ gives $r=\lfloor r/2\rfloor+\lfloor2r/3\rfloor$. statement: Eleven theatre groups attend a festival. On each day some groups perform and the others watch. Every group must watch at least one performance of every other group. What is the minimum number of days?
solution: The answer is six. Assign to each group its set of performing days. For two groups to watch one another, neither set may contain the other; thus the eleven sets form an antichain. On five days, count permutations of the days in which a particular set of size $k$ is an initial segment: there are $k!(5-k)!$. At most one set in an antichain can be an initial segment of the same permutation, so $\sum_S1/\binom5{|S|}\le1$. Since every binomial coefficient here is at most 10, there can be at most 10 groups. Fewer days cannot help, by adding unused days. For six days, choose eleven distinct three-element subsets as performing schedules; any two are incomparable.

statement: A triangle has positive integer sides, $\angle A=2\angle B$, and $\angle C>90^\circ$. Determine its smallest possible perimeter.
solution: Writing opposite sides as a,b,c, the sine and cosine rules imply $a^2=b(b+c)$. Put $a/b=u/v$ in lowest terms. Integrality then gives $(a,b,c)=k(uv,v^2,u^2-v^2)$ for positive integers k,u,v with gcd(u,v)=1. The obtuse condition is c>2b, while the triangle inequality gives a<2b; hence $\sqrt3v<u<2v$. There is no integer u for v=1,2,3. At v=4, u=7 works and gives sides $(28,16,33)$, perimeter 77. For v≥5, the perimeter $ku(u+v)>(3+\sqrt3)v^2>77$. Thus the minimum is 77.

statement: Distinct numbered cards are placed in a rectangular array. Sort each row increasingly from left to right, then sort each column increasingly from top to bottom. Must every row still increase from left to right?
solution: Yes. Consider any two adjacent columns just after the row sorting. Their entries can be paired as $a_i<b_i$. Let $a_{(k)},b_{(k)}$ be their respective $k$th smallest entries. Among the $k$ entries $b_i\le b_{(k)}$, their paired $a_i$ are all strictly smaller than $b_{(k)}$. Hence $a_{(k)}<b_{(k)}$. This holds for every $k$ and every adjacent column pair, so sorting the columns preserves increasing rows.

statement: Prove no four-digit decimal integer of the form $xyxy$ is a cube. Find the smallest integer base $b>1$ in which a four-digit cube of this form exists.
solution: In base b the value is $(xb+y)(b^2+1)$, where $b\le xb+y<b^2$. In decimal, the prime 101 occurs exactly once, so the number cannot be a cube. For bases 2,4,6, the factor $b^2+1$ is respectively the prime 5,17,37, larger than the two-digit factor, again impossible. For base 3, the squarefree factor 10 would require the other factor to be divisible by $2^2 5^2=100$, impossible. For base 5 the squarefree factor 26 similarly requires a factor divisible by $2^2 13^2=676$. In base 7, $2626_7=20\cdot50=1000=10^3$. Hence the least base is 7.
ratingReason: Factoring the repeated block exposes a prime-valuation obstruction; the small-base search needs separate treatment of the composite factors ten and twenty-six.

statement: Among triangles with a fixed angle $A$ and fixed inradius $r$, which has least perimeter?
solution: If the other angles are $B,C$, the semiperimeter is $r(\cot(A/2)+\cot(B/2)+\cot(C/2))$, by the tangent lengths from each vertex. Put $u=B/2$, $v=C/2$; their sum is fixed. Now $\cot u+\cot v=\sin(u+v)/(\sin u\sin v)$, and $\sin u\sin v=[\cos(u-v)-\cos(u+v)]/2$ is largest exactly when $u=v$. Thus the least perimeter occurs uniquely when $B=C$, namely for the isosceles triangle with the specified angle as its vertex angle.
ratingReason: The inradius constraint is best converted to tangent lengths; optimizing the remaining cotangent sum identifies the equality configuration.

statement: Show that seven closed discs of radius one can cover a closed disc of radius two.
solution: Place one small disc at the centre O and the other six at the vertices of a regular hexagon of circumradius $\sqrt3$. A point with distance at most one from O is covered by the central disc. For a remaining point, write its polar radius as $1\le r\le2$ and choose the nearest hexagon direction, at angular distance $\theta\le30^\circ$. Its squared distance to that small-disc centre is $r^2+3-2\sqrt3r\cos\theta\le r^2+3-3r$. This convex quadratic is at most one on [1,2], as both endpoint values are one. Thus every point is covered.

statement: A fair coin gives one point for heads and two points for tails. Toss it repeatedly. Prove that the probability the running total ever equals a given nonnegative integer $n$ is $\frac13(2+(-\frac12)^n)$.

statement: Let $x$ be real. If $x^2-x$ and $x^n-x$ are integers for some integer $n\ge3$, prove x is an integer.
solution: Put $k=x^2-x$. Since $x^2-x\ge-1/4$, the integer k is nonnegative. If k=0, then x=0 or 1. If k>0, successive reduction using $x^2=x+k$ writes $x^j=A_jx+B_j$ with integer coefficients, where $A_1=A_2=1$ and $A_{j+1}=A_j+kA_{j-1}$. Therefore $A_n>1$ for n≥3. Since $(A_n-1)x+B_n=x^n-x$ is an integer, x is rational. A rational root of the monic integer polynomial $t^2-t-k$ is an integer.

statement: Every nondegenerate section of a parallelepiped parallel to a face has the same perimeter as that face. Does any other polyhedron have this property for every face direction?

For $-1<t<1$, the section $x+y+z=t$ is a hexagon whose vertices are the permutations of $((1+t)/2,-(1-t)/2,0)$. Its three alternating side lengths are $(1+t)/\sqrt2$ and its other three are $(1-t)/\sqrt2$, giving total $3\sqrt2$. At $t=\pm1$ the section is the triangular face with the same perimeter. Changing coordinate signs handles every other face direction. The octahedron is not a parallelepiped.

statement: Prove that the sum of the six interior dihedral angles of a tetrahedron is not the same for all tetrahedra.
solution: Consider tetrahedra with a fixed equilateral base and an apex at height $h>0$ above its centre. At the regular tetrahedron height, all six dihedral angles are $\arccos(1/3)$, so their sum is strictly less than $3\pi$. As $h$ tends to zero, each of the three base-edge interior dihedral angles tends to 0, while each of the other three tends to $\pi$. Thus the sum tends to $3\pi$. If the sum were constant throughout this family, its limit would equal its regular-tetrahedron value, a contradiction. All tetrahedra in the family with $h>0$ are nondegenerate.

If $b\ge2a$, the first term is at most $1/b$, and induction bounds the rest by $(1-2^{-(k-1)})/b$; together these are at most $(1-2^{-k})/a$. If $a<b<2a$, use $\gcd(a,b)\le b-a$, so $1/\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\le1/a-1/b$. Adding the inductive bound gives $1/a-1/(2^{k-1}b)<(1-2^{-k})/a$. Take $k=4$ and $a\ge1$. Equality occurs for $1,2,4,8,16$.

statement: A tetromino is a shape formed by four unit squares joined edge-to-edge. Regard rotations in the plane as identical, but do not identify reflections. (a) Prove there are seven distinct tetrominoes. (b) Can all seven be packed, without overlap, into a $4\times7$ rectangle?

Hence all seven together have colour imbalance $2$, while a $4\times7$ rectangle has equal colour counts. The packing is impossible.

statement: A rabbit runs along the wall of a circular arena. A dog starts at its centre and runs at the same speed, always remaining on the radius through the rabbit. Show that it catches the rabbit after the rabbit travels one quarter of the circumference.

In Cartesian coordinates this is the circle $x^2+(y-R/2)^2=(R/2)^2$, starting at the origin. Its arc from the origin to angle $\theta$ has central angle $2\theta$ and length $R\theta$, exactly the rabbit’s travelled distance. It stays on the rabbit’s radius and inside the arena until $\theta=\pi/2$, when $r=R$. Thus this is the prescribed equal-speed pursuit path, and capture occurs after one quarter turn.

statement: For each odd integer $a>1$, define $\delta(a)$ by $2^{\delta(a)}<a<2^{\delta(a)+1}$. On these integers put $a*b=2^{\delta(a)-1}(b-3)+a$. Prove this operation is closed and associative.

statement: Two players alternately fill empty cells of a $3\times3$ board, choosing a black or white counter independently at every move. statement: How many 1000-digit positive integers have only odd digits and have adjacent digits differing by exactly two?
solution: The digits 1,3,5,7,9 form a path. By reflection, let a,b,c be the counts of strings ending at either endpoint, at the middle vertex, and at either of the two remaining vertices, respectively. Appending a digit transforms $(a,b,c)$ to $(c,2c,a+b)$. For length two the triple is $(1,2,2)$, and two further steps multiply this triple by 3. Thus at length 1000 it is $3^{499}(1,2,2)$, and the total is $2a+b+2c=8\cdot3^{499}$.
ratingReason: Reflection reduces five ending-digit counts to three; the two-step recurrence then has a simple multiplicative form.

statement: Find the smallest base $b$ in which the numeral $777$ represents a fourth power of an integer.
solution: The represented value is $7(b^2+b+1)$. If this equals $a^4$, primality of 7 gives $7\mid a$, so $a\ge7$. Thus $b^2+b+1\ge7^3=343$. Since $17^2+17+1=307$ and $18^2+18+1=343$, the smallest possible base is $18$, and it works because $7\cdot343=7^4$.
ratingReason: Divisibility of a fourth power forces its root to be a multiple of 7, giving a sharp size lower bound that is exactly attained.

statement: In how many ways can seven distinct people be partitioned into four nonempty, unordered teams? Answer the same question for eight people.
solution: Let $S(n,k)$ count partitions into $k$ nonempty unordered groups. The final person either joins one of $k$ existing groups or forms a singleton, so $S(n,k)=kS(n-1,k)+S(n-1,k-1)$, with $S(n,1)=S(n,n)=1$. Iterating gives $S(6,3)=90$, $S(6,4)=65$, hence $S(7,4)=4\cdot65+90=350$. Also $S(7,3)=3\cdot90+31=301$, so $S(8,4)=4\cdot350+301=1701$.
ratingReason: Counting by team-size patterns or a Stirling recurrence requires avoiding overcounting equal-sized teams.

statement: Discs occupy distinct cells of a $5\times9$ board. In each complete move every disc moves to an adjacent cell, no two ending in one cell. Each disc must alternate horizontal and vertical moves. Prove 33 initial discs cannot move forever, but 32 can.
solution: Colour a cell by the parity pair of its row and column. The smallest colour class has $2\cdot4=8$ cells. In any four consecutive configurations of a disc following alternating horizontal and vertical moves, it occupies each of the four colour classes exactly once. If 33 discs could make three complete moves, the four resulting configurations, including the initial one, would therefore contain 33 visits to the smallest colour class. They can hold at most $4\cdot8=32$ such visits, a contradiction. For 32 discs, use a $4\times8$ subboard partitioned into eight disjoint $2\times2$ blocks. Fill every cell and rotate the four discs around each block at every move. Each disc alternates horizontal and vertical movement, and no collisions occur, so this continues forever.
ratingReason: Four parity classes are needed rather than ordinary checkerboard colouring; summing occupancy over a full four-step parity cycle gives the sharp obstruction.

statement: Let $S(n)$ be the decimal digit sum. Prove $S(2n)\le2S(n)\le10S(2n)$ for every positive integer $n$. Also construct $n$ satisfying $S(n)=1996S(3n)$.
solution: Carrying never increases digit sum, so $S(u+v)\le S(u)+S(v)$ and consequently $S(kn)\le kS(n)$ for positive integers k. Thus $S(2n)\le2S(n)$, and $S(n)=S(10n)=S(5\cdot2n)\le5S(2n)$ proves the second inequality. For the construction take $n=(10^{5987}+8)/3$, whose decimal expansion has 5986 copies of 3 followed by 6. Then $S(n)=3\cdot5986+6=17964$, while $3n=10^{5987}+8$ has digit sum 9. Hence $S(n)=1996S(3n)$.
ratingReason: The inequalities use carrying in both directions, but the large-ratio construction must deliberately make multiplication by three collapse almost all nonzero digits.

statement: A rectangular grid has $m$ by $n$ unit cells. A pedestrian travels along grid edges from the southwest corner to the northeast corner without visiting any vertex twice. Prove that there are at most $2^{mn}$ possible routes.
solution: Fix one boundary route $B$ between the two corners. For any admissible route $P$, take the symmetric difference $E=P\triangle B$ of their edge sets. Every vertex has even degree in $E$. Such an edge set uniquely determines a subset of the $mn$ cells: colour the exterior white, and change colour whenever a path between adjacent faces crosses an edge of $E$. This is consistent because every vertex has even degree; equivalently, any closed dual walk crosses $E$ an even number of times. The black cells have boundary exactly $E$. Conversely their boundary recovers $E$, then $P=E\triangle B$. An edge set of a simple route determines that route uniquely from its starting corner. Thus the routes inject into the $2^{mn}$ subsets of cells.
ratingReason: The useful encoding is not a sequence of local turns but the mod-two region bounded by the route and a fixed boundary path; consistency and injectivity both require proof.

statement: Two grade-seven students join a round-robin chess tournament with some grade-eight students. A win earns $1$, a draw $1/2$, and a loss $0$. The younger students score $8$ points in total, and every older student has the same score. How many older students can there be?
solution: Let there be $m$ older students, each scoring $s$. The total points equal the number of games, so $ms=(m+2)(m+1)/2-8$, or $2s=m+3-14/m$. Since $2s$ is integral, $m\mid14$. The younger pair can score at most $2m+1$, which excludes $m=1,2$, leaving $m=7,14$. Both occur. With $m=7$, make every game a draw. With $m=14$, let older students draw against one another, beat one younger student, and draw against the other; the younger pair’s mutual game contributes the remaining one point.
ratingReason: The score identity creates a divisor restriction, but the count is not unique; feasibility constructions are needed to distinguish algebraic possibilities from actual tournaments.

statement: Find a positive constant $c$ for which $xy^2-y^2-x+y=c$ has exactly three solutions in positive integers $(x,y)$.
solution: Take $c=11$. Rewrite as $(x-1)(y^2-1)+y=11$. The case $y=1$ is impossible. Since $x\ge1$, we have $2\le y\le11$. If $x=1$, then $y=11$. If $x\ge2$, then $y^2+y-1\le11$, so $y=2$ or $3$. These yield $x=4$ and $2$ respectively. Thus precisely $(4,2),(2,3),(1,11)$ work.

statement: Let $p$ be prime and let $a,n$ be positive integers. Prove $2^p+3^p=a^n$ implies $n=1$.
solution: For $p=2$ the sum is 13. For odd p, expand $3^p=(5-2)^p$ modulo 25. This gives $2^p+3^p\equiv5p\,2^{p-1}\pmod{25}$. If $p\ne5$, the sum is divisible by 5 but not 25, forcing n=1. If $p=5$, the sum is $275=5^2\cdot11$, and the exponent of 11 again forces n=1.

statement: Prove that a positive integer can be written as a sum of at least two consecutive positive integers if and only if it is not a power of two.
solution: If $n=a+(a+1)+\cdots+(a+\ell-1)$ with $a\ge1$, $\ell\ge2$, then $2n=\ell(2a+\ell-1)$. The two factors have opposite parity, and the odd one exceeds 1, so $n$ is not a power of two. Conversely write $n=2^k m$ with odd $m>1$. If $m<2^{k+1}$, use $m$ consecutive terms centred at $2^k$; the first is $2^k-(m-1)/2\ge1$. If $m>2^{k+1}$, use $2^{k+1}$ consecutive terms centred at $m/2$; the first is $(m-2^{k+1}+1)/2\ge1$. Both sums equal $n$.
ratingReason: The factorization of twice the sum gives the obstruction; constructing a positive run requires switching between odd and even lengths according to the size of the odd part.

statement: Four points $A,B,C,D$ in space satisfy $\angle ABC=\angle BCD=\angle CDA=\angle DAB=90^\circ$. Prove they are coplanar.

The last equation gives $|c|^2=|b|^2+|d|^2$. Write $c=b+d+w$, where the first three equations ensure that $w$ is orthogonal to both $b$ and $d$. Then $|c|^2=|b|^2+|d|^2+|w|^2$, so $w=0$. Thus $C=B+D$ in these coordinates, proving coplanarity.

statement: Colour every edge joining nine points red or blue. Suppose no triangle has all three edges blue. Prove that some four points have all six joining edges red.
solution: If a vertex has at least four blue neighbours, all edges between those neighbours are red, giving the result. Otherwise all blue degrees are at most 3. The sum of nine odd degrees cannot be even, so some vertex has even blue degree, at most 2. It therefore has at least six red neighbours. Among any six vertices there is a monochromatic triangle: from one vertex, at least three incident edges have one colour, and either an edge among their endpoints shares that colour or those endpoints form a triangle of the other colour. Since blue triangles are forbidden, the six red neighbours contain a red triangle. Adding the chosen vertex gives the required red four-set.
ratingReason: The sharp nine-vertex bound needs a parity improvement to the degree bound followed by the six-vertex Ramsey argument.

statement: For which integers $a$ does $x^2+axy+y^2=1$ have infinitely many integer solutions $(x,y)$?
solution: The answer is $|a|\ge2$. For $|a|\le1$, the form is at least $(x^2+y^2)/2$, so only finitely many integer pairs can give 1. For $a=\pm2$, the equation is $(x\pm y)^2=1$, which has infinitely many solutions. For $A=|a|>2$, changing the sign of one variable if necessary reduces to $x^2-Axy+y^2=1$. Starting at $(x,y)=(0,1)$, repeatedly replace $(x,y)$ by $(y,Ay-x)$. The form is unchanged. If $0\le x<y$, then $Ay-x>y$, so this gives infinitely many distinct positive pairs after the first step.
ratingReason: The small parameters produce a positive-definite form, while the larger parameters require an explicit integral transformation that preserves the equation and grows without cycling.

statement: For nonnegative $p,q,r$ with $p+q+r=1$, prove $7(pq+qr+rp)\le2+9pqr$.

For completeness, Schur here follows by assuming $p\ge q\ge r$ and writing $\sum p(p-q)(p-r)=(p-q)[p(p-r)-q(q-r)]+r(r-p)(r-q)\ge0$; expansion and $p+q+r=1$ give $1+9t-4s\ge0$.
ratingReason: A sharp symmetric inequality can be assembled from Schur and the quadratic bound, but that decomposition is not obvious.

statement: All roots of $x^3+ax^2+bx+c$ have modulus 1, where $a,b,c$ are complex. Prove all roots of $x^3+|a|x^2+|b|x+|c|$ also have modulus 1.
solution: Let the original roots be $u,v,w$. Then $|c|=|uvw|=1$, and $b=uv+vw+wu=uvw(\overline u+\overline v+\overline w)$, so $|b|=|a|=:t$. Also $0\le t\le3$. The new polynomial factors as $(x+1)(x^2+(t-1)x+1)$. Since $-1\le t-1\le2$, the quadratic has conjugate roots on the unit circle, including the repeated root -1 at the endpoint t=3. Thus every new root has modulus 1.
ratingReason: Conjugating unit-modulus roots relates the two nonconstant coefficients; the absolute-value polynomial then factors into a linear term and a controlled reciprocal quadratic.

statement: Prove there is exactly one sequence of positive integers $(a_n)$ such that $a_1=1$, $a_2=2$, $a_4=12$ and $a_{n+1}a_{n-1}=a_n^2\pm1$ for every $n\ge2$. The sign may vary with $n$.
solution: From $2a_4=a_3^2\pm1$ we get $a_3=5$. Define a sequence by $a_1=1,a_2=2$ and $a_{n+1}=2a_n+a_{n-1}$. It starts $1,2,5,12$ and is positive integral. If $D_n=a_{n+1}a_{n-1}-a_n^2$, substitution gives $D_{n+1}=-D_n$; since $D_2=1$, this sequence satisfies the condition. For uniqueness, once two consecutive terms are known and the earlier one exceeds $2$, the two candidates $(a_n^2\pm1)/a_{n-1}$ differ by $2/a_{n-1}<1$, so at most one can be integral. The initial terms through $a_4$ have already been fixed, completing induction.
ratingReason: The initial constraint fixes a branch, then integrality forces uniqueness; a second-order linear recurrence supplies existence.

statement: For each $0<t<1$, take the part of the unit square lying on or above the line joining $(t,0)$ to $(0,1-t)$. Prove the intersection of all these regions is exactly $\sqrt x+\sqrt y\ge1$ within the square.
solution: The half-plane condition is $x/t+y/(1-t)\ge1$. Cauchy-Schwarz gives $x/t+y/(1-t)\ge(\sqrt x+\sqrt y)^2$, so the proposed region satisfies every condition. If x,y are positive, equality in this bound occurs at $t=\sqrt x/(\sqrt x+\sqrt y)$; hence a point with $\sqrt x+\sqrt y<1$ fails one condition. If x or y is zero, the same conclusion follows by taking t sufficiently close to 0 or 1.
ratingReason: The intersection over all line positions becomes a minimisation in t; equality in Cauchy-Schwarz identifies the boundary curve.

statement: Is the function $f(x)=\sin(x^2)$ periodic on the real line? Prove your answer.
solution: It is not. Suppose $p>0$ were a period. Since $f(0)=0$, we have $p^2=k\pi$ for a positive integer $k$. Also $f(\sqrt\pi+p)=f(\sqrt\pi)=0$, so $k+1+2\sqrt k$ is an integer, making $2\sqrt k$ an integer. Applying the same argument at $\sqrt{2\pi}$ makes $2\sqrt{2k}$ an integer. The ratio of these two nonzero integers would be $\sqrt2$, a contradiction.

statement: A square is partitioned into $n$ convex polygons. What is the largest possible number of edges in the resulting subdivision?
solution: Let $V,E$ denote the subdivision’s vertices and edges, counting each shared edge once and splitting edges at every junction. Euler gives $V-E+n=1$. Every vertex except the four original square corners has degree at least 3, while the corners have degree at least 2; hence $2E\ge3V-4$. Combining yields $V\le2n+2$ and $E\le3n+1$. The bound is attained by repeatedly cutting one convex region with a segment whose endpoints lie in the interiors of two of its edges, avoiding existing vertices. Each cut adds one region, two vertices and three edges, preserving convexity. Starting with four edges gives exactly $3n+1$.
ratingReason: Euler’s formula must be combined with the four exceptional boundary corners, and the edge bound needs a convex subdivision construction to prove sharpness.

statement: Positive integers $x,y,z$ satisfy $1/x-1/y=1/z$. Let $h=\gcd(x,y,z)$. Prove that both $hxyz$ and $h(y-x)$ are perfect squares.
solution: Write $x=ha,y=hb,z=hc$ with $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$. The equation is $c(b-a)=ab$. Put $g=\gcd(a,b)$, $a=gu,b=gv$ with $\gcd(u,v)=1$ and $v>u$. Then $c(v-u)=guv$. As $\gcd(v-u,uv)=1$, write $g=t(v-u)$ and $c=tuv$. Now $a=t u(v-u)$ and $b=t v(v-u)$, so their common gcd with $c$ is exactly $t$; hence $t=1$. Therefore $abc=u^2v^2(v-u)^2$ and $b-a=(v-u)^2$. Multiplying back gives $hxyz=h^4abc$ and $h(y-x)=h^2(b-a)$, both squares.
ratingReason: The equation has a useful coprime parametrisation; keeping track of the common divisor is the main challenge.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the official paper. Difficulty is an individual AI estimate, not an official UKMT rating.

statement: Find all real polynomials satisfying $f(x^2)=f(x)f(x-1)$ for every real $x$.
solution: The zero polynomial works. For a nonzero solution, the leading coefficient comparison gives 1. Any complex root $\alpha$ produces roots $\alpha^2$ and $(\alpha+1)^2$. A root of modulus greater than 1 would have infinitely many distinct successive squares, impossible. A nonzero root of modulus less than 1 also produces infinitely many distinct squares. Zero cannot be a root, since it would force 1 and then 4 to be roots. Consequently every root has modulus 1, as does $(\alpha+1)^2$, so $|\alpha+1|=1$. Hence $\alpha$ is one of the two primitive cube roots of unity. Real coefficients give equal multiplicities to this conjugate pair, so $f=(x^2+x+1)^k$ for an integer $k\ge0$. Finally $(x^2+x+1)(x^2-x+1)=x^4+x^2+1$ verifies every such power.
ratingReason: Two different root-propagation maps force every root onto the intersection of two unit circles; real coefficients then determine the multiplicities.

Every negative coefficient is best paired with 0 and every positive coefficient with 1; the possible central zero coefficient makes no difference. Thus the maximum is $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$, attained by taking $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ zeros and the remaining entries ones.

There are $200-10b$ choices for the number of $10$ coins; the $1$ coins are then forced. This gives $\sum_{b=0}^{19}(200-10b)=2100$. With one $1000$ coin, the same calculation gives $\sum_{b=0}^{9}(100-10b)=550$. The total is $2650$.

statement: Using any number of $8$-cent and $15$-cent stamps, what is the largest integer amount of postage that cannot be formed?
solution: The answer is $97$. If $97=8a+15b$ with nonnegative integers $a,b$, reduction modulo 8 gives $b\equiv7\pmod8$, so $15b\ge105$, impossible. For any $N\ge98$, choose $b\in\{0,1,\ldots,7\}$ with $15b\equiv N\pmod8$. Then $N-15b\ge-7$ and is divisible by 8, hence is nonnegative. This gives the desired representation.

statement: Two nine-digit positive integers $M,N$ have the property that replacing any single digit of $M$ by the corresponding digit of $N$ produces a multiple of $7$. Prove the analogous statement with $M,N$ reversed. Find some $d>9$ for which the same assertion holds for all $d$-digit pairs.

statement: (a) A rectangle of integer side lengths $\ell,m$ is divided into unit squares. Prove its diagonal passes through the interiors of $\ell+m-\gcd(\ell,m)$ squares. (b) A box with positive integer edge lengths $\ell,m,n$ is divided into unit cubes. Determine how many cube interiors its space diagonal passes through.
solution: Each time the diagonal crosses a new grid line, it enters another square, unless two grid lines are crossed simultaneously. There are $(\ell-1)+(m-1)$ crossings counted separately, and $\gcd(\ell,m)-1$ simultaneous pairs. Including the first square gives $\ell+m-\gcd(\ell,m)$. In three dimensions, count crossings of the three families of internal planes. Pairwise coincidences number the three pairwise gcds minus one each, and triple coincidences number $\gcd(\ell,m,n)-1$. Inclusion-exclusion and the initial cube give $\ell+m+n-\gcd(\ell,m)-\gcd(m,n)-\gcd(n,\ell)+\gcd(\ell,m,n)$.
ratingReason: The planar count is a warm-up; in space, pairwise and triple simultaneous crossings must be distinguished with inclusion-exclusion.

statement: Points $A,B$ on a circle are distinct and not on one diameter. As $XY$ runs through diameters, let $P=AX\cap BY$ whenever the defining lines and their intersection exist. Determine the locus of $P$.
solution: Normalize the circle to the complex unit circle and write $a,b,x,p$ for the points, with $Y=-x$. A line joining unit points $u,v$ has equation $z+uv\bar z=u+v$. Thus $p+ax\bar p=a+x$ and $p-bx\bar p=b-x$. Dividing by $a,b$ respectively and adding yields $x=[(a+b)p-2ab]/(b-a)$. Since $|x|=1$, the locus lies on $|p-2ab/(a+b)|=|b-a|/|a+b|$. Its centre is the intersection of the tangents at $A,B$, and it passes through both. Conversely, a point on this circle determines a unit $x$ by the displayed formula; substituting the circle equation verifies both line equations. Omit the two points $p=(3ab-a^2)/(a+b)$ and $p=(3ab-b^2)/(a+b)$, corresponding respectively to $X=A$ and $Y=B$, where a defining chord has coincident endpoints. All other points occur; in particular $A$ and $B$ themselves do occur.
ratingReason: The moving diameter creates a nonstandard circle centred at the intersection of two tangents. A complex line equation establishes both the locus and its converse, including excluded endpoints.
notes: Statement restated in original wording. Official CMS paper checked; original independent proof supplied because no worked solution is linked in the official archive.

statement: Call a positive integer $n$ good if there is exactly one multiset of $k\ge2$ positive integers whose sum and product are both $n$. Characterise the good integers in terms of prime factors.
solution: The good integers are exactly products of two primes, allowing the primes to be equal. A nontrivial factorisation $n=b_1\cdots b_r$ with all $b_i\ge2$ has $b_1+\cdots+b_r\le n$; this follows inductively from $u+v\le uv$ for $u,v\ge2$. Append exactly $n-\sum b_i$ ones to make its sum n. Conversely every admissible multiset gives such a nontrivial multiplicative factorisation after removing its ones. A prime has none. A product of two primes has exactly one. If n has at least three prime factors, counted with multiplicity, the full prime factorisation and a factorisation obtained by merging two of those factors are distinct and both have at least two factors, giving at least two representations.
ratingReason: Removing the ones converts the sum-product condition into a question about unordered multiplicative factorizations; one must show every nontrivial factorisation can be padded with ones.
notes: Mathematical statement paraphrased from Mark Dukes’s UCD-hosted IrMO compendium. The solution below is independently written, not an official marking scheme.

statement: What is the greatest possible length of a geometric progression of integers between $100$ and $1000$, inclusive, whose common ratio exceeds $1$?
solution: The maximum is six, attained by $128,192,288,432,648,972$. Write the common ratio as $p/q>1$ in lowest terms. A progression of length $k$ has first term divisible by $q^{k-1}$ and last term divisible by $p^{k-1}$. If $k\ge7$, then $p^6\le1000$, so $p\le3$. Since $1\le q<p$, this forces $p/q\ge3/2$. Its last-to-first ratio would then be at least $(3/2)^6>10$, contrary to the allowed interval.
ratingReason: Integrality constrains both endpoints through powers of the reduced numerator and denominator; combining this with the interval ratio gives the sharp obstruction.

statement: For positive integers $n$, define $q(n)=\left\lfloor n/\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\right\rfloor$. Find all $n$ for which $q(n)>q(n+1)$.
solution: If $\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor=\lfloor\sqrt{n+1}\rfloor$, increasing the numerator cannot decrease $q$. Hence a decrease can occur only at $n=k^2-1$, with $k\ge2$. At such a point $q(n)=\lfloor(k^2-1)/(k-1)\rfloor=k+1$, while $q(n+1)=k$. Thus precisely the integers $k^2-1$ for $k\ge2$ work.
ratingReason: The useful observation is that the denominator changes only at a square; the discontinuity then needs an exact check.

statement: Distinct real $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ and real $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ satisfy $\prod_{j=1}^n(a_i+b_j)=\alpha$ for every $i$. Prove there is a real $\beta$ such that $\prod_{i=1}^n(a_i+b_j)=\beta$ for every $j$.
solution: The monic polynomial $F(t)=\prod_j(t+b_j)-\alpha$ has the n distinct roots $a_i$, so $F(t)=\prod_i(t-a_i)$. At $t=-b_j$, this gives $-\alpha=(-1)^n\prod_i(a_i+b_j)$. Thus the second product always equals $\beta=(-1)^{n+1}\alpha$.
ratingReason: The equal product values identify an entire monic polynomial from its distinct roots; evaluation at the other family gives the dual statement.

statement: Find all triples of nonnegative integers $(x,y,z)$ satisfying $2^x+3^y=z^2$.
solution: If $x=0$, then $(z-1)(z+1)=3^y$. Both factors are odd and coprime, so $z-1=1,z+1=3$, giving $(x,y,z)=(0,1,2)$. For $x=1$ or $2$, reducing modulo $8$ rules out all $y$. Let $x\ge3$. Modulo $8$ forces $y=2r$ even. Now $(z-3^r)(z+3^r)=2^x$, and the two positive even factors have gcd $2$, so they are $2$ and $2^{x-1}$. Thus $3^r=2^{x-2}-1$. If $r=0$, this gives $x=3,z=3$. If $r\ge1$, reducing modulo $8$ shows $x-2\le2$, hence $x=4,r=1,z=5$. These three triples all work.
ratingReason: Parity and modulus eight split the problem into branches; the surviving exponential factorisation must be exhausted rigorously.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the official paper. Difficulty is an individual AI estimate, not an official UKMT rating.

statement: Prove that $x^3+11^3=y^3$ has no solution in positive integers $x,y$.
solution: Put $d=y-x>0$. Then $1331=d(3x^2+3xd+d^2)$, so $d\mid11^3$ and $d^3<11^3$. Therefore $d<11$, forcing $d=1$. But cubes are congruent to their bases modulo 3, so $y^3-x^3\equiv y-x=1\pmod3$, whereas $1331\equiv2\pmod3$.

statement: (a) Show that both roots of $x=(x^2+1)/198$ lie strictly between $1/198$ and $198-1/198$. (b) Deduce $\sqrt2<1.41\overline{421356}$. (c) Decide whether $\sqrt2<1.41421356$.

In particular, $99-70\sqrt2>1/198$, whence $\sqrt2<19601/13860=1.41\overline{421356}$. The finite decimal in (c) is smaller than $\sqrt2$: indeed $141421356^2=19999999932878736<2\cdot10^{16}$. Thus the asserted finite-decimal inequality is false.

statement: How many ordered real triples $(x,y,z)$ satisfy $x^2+y^2+z^2=9$, $x^4+y^4+z^4=33$, and $xyz=-4$?

Thus the squared magnitudes are a permutation of $(1,4,4)$, giving three positions for the magnitude 1. For each position there are four sign patterns with negative product. Therefore there are $3\cdot4=12$ triples.

statement: A cube of side $2$ has top face $ABCD$ and bottom face $FGHE$, with vertical edges $AF,BG,CH,DE$. Let $M,N$ be the midpoints of $BC,EF$. (a) Find the area of quadrilateral $AMHN$. (b) Let $P,Q$ be the midpoints of $AB,HE$, and put $X=AM\cap CP$, $Y=HN\cap FQ$. Find $XY$.
solution: Use coordinates $A=(0,0,2),B=(2,0,2),C=(2,2,2),D=(0,2,2)$ and $F=(0,0,0),G=(2,0,0),H=(2,2,0),E=(0,2,0)$. Then $M=(2,1,2)$ and $N=(0,1,0)$. The parallelogram has adjacent vectors $(2,1,0)$ and $(0,1,-2)$, whose cross product has length $2\sqrt6$, its area. The intersections are $X=(4/3,2/3,2)$ and $Y=(2/3,4/3,0)$, obtained by solving the two line equations on the top and bottom faces. Hence $XY=\sqrt{4/9+4/9+4}=2\sqrt{11}/3$.

statement: Four distinct lines form two pairs of parallel lines. Describe the locus of points for which the sum of the four perpendicular distances is a prescribed constant $C$.
solution: First suppose the two directions differ. Let $u,v$ be signed perpendicular coordinates from the midlines of the pairs, and let $a,b>0$ be their half-separations. The distance sum is $2\max(|u|,a)+2\max(|v|,b)$. Hence the locus is empty for $C<2(a+b)$, the closed parallelogram $|u|\le a,|v|\le b$ for equality, and for $C>2(a+b)$ it is the boundary of the octagon $\max(|u|-a,0)+\max(|v|-b,0)\le C/2-a-b$. If all four lines are parallel, use a common signed normal coordinate with offsets $c_1<c_2<c_3<c_4$. The minimum sum is $c_4+c_3-c_2-c_1$; below it the locus is empty, at it the locus is the strip $c_2\le u\le c_3$, and above it the locus consists of the two parallel lines whose coordinates solve $\sum_i|u-c_i|=C$.
ratingReason: Signed distance coordinates turn the geometric locus into a piecewise linear level set; the minimum is a filled region, a case that must not be mistaken for only its boundary.
notes: Statement restated in original wording. Official CMS paper checked; original independent proof supplied because no worked solution is linked in the official archive.

statement: (a) Maximise $x^2y-y^2x$ for $0\le x,y\le1$. (b) Maximise $x^2y+y^2z+z^2x-x^2z-y^2x-z^2y$ for $0\le x,y,z\le1$.
solution: For (a), a positive value requires $x\ge y$. For fixed $y$, $xy(x-y)$ increases with $x$ on $[y,1]$, so its maximum is $y(1-y)\le1/4$, attained at $(x,y)=(1,1/2)$. In (b) the expression is $(x-y)(y-z)(x-z)$. After ordering the three values, its absolute value is $ab(a+b)$, where $a,b\ge0$ and $a+b\le1$ are the two consecutive gaps. Hence $ab(a+b)\le(a+b)^3/4\le1/4$. The positive maximum is attained, for example, at $(x,y,z)=(1,1/2,0)$.

statement: Find all triples of positive integers $(a,b,c)$ satisfying $(1+1/a)(1+1/b)(1+1/c)=2$.
solution: Assume $a\le b\le c$. We cannot have $a=1$, and if $a\ge4$ the product is at most $(5/4)^3<2$. Thus $a=2$ or $3$. For $a=2$, rearrangement gives $(b-3)(c-3)=12$, yielding $(b,c)=(4,15),(5,9),(6,7)$. For $a=3$, the inequality $(1+1/b)^2\ge3/2$ gives $b\le4$. Substitution yields $(b,c)=(3,8)$ or $(4,5)$. All permutations of these five triples work.
ratingReason: Ordering bounds the smallest denominator; completing both resulting factorisations is the main proof task.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the official paper. Difficulty is an individual AI estimate, not an official UKMT rating.

statement: Points $X,Y,Z$ are respectively the circumcentre of a triangle $ABC$, the midpoint of $BC$, and the foot of the perpendicular from $B$ to $AC$. Describe how to reconstruct the triangle.
solution:
If $X
e Y$, line $BC$ passes through $Y$ perpendicular to $XY$. Because $\angle BZC=90^\circ$, $YB=YC=YZ$. The circle centred at $Y$ of radius $YZ$ therefore recovers the unordered pair $B,C$. For each assignment with $Z
e B$, draw the circle centred at $X$ through $B$. If $C
e Z$, its second intersection with $CZ$ is $A$; if $C=Z$, instead use the line through $C$ perpendicular to $BC$. Retain all nondegenerate results. If $X=Y$, then $BC$ is a diameter of the circumcircle, so $\angle A=90^\circ$ and $Z=A$. Draw the circle centred at $X$ through $Z$ and choose any diameter $BC$ not passing through $Z$; these give all triangles in this exceptional family.
ratingReason: The altitude foot must first be recognised as lying on the circle with diameter BC; that recovers the unknown side before the circumcircle recovers A.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the compendium; the construction explicitly handles coincident X and Y and a right angle at C.

statement: A five-digit integer $n$ becomes the four-digit integer $m$ when its middle digit is removed. Find all $n$ for which $m$ divides $n$.
solution: Write $n=1000A+100d+B$ and $m=100A+B$, where $10\le A\le99$, $0\le d\le9$, and $0\le B\le99$. Thus $n=10m+100d-9B$. The final term lies between $-891$ and $900$, while $m\ge1000$. If $m\mid n$, it follows that $100d=9B$. Hence $d$ is a multiple of 9; $d=9$ would give $B=100$, so $d=B=0$. Exactly the numbers $n=1000A$, $10\le A\le99$, work.
ratingReason: The key is to bound the correction to ten times the shortened number below one full divisor, forcing the quotient exactly.
notes: Statement restated in original wording. Official CMS paper checked; original independent proof supplied because no worked solution is linked in the official archive.

statement: A nonempty set $S\subset\mathbb Q\setminus\{0\}$ is closed under quotients. Suppose some $q\in\mathbb Q\setminus S$, $q\ne0$, satisfies $\mathbb Q\setminus(S\cup\{0\})=qS$. Prove each $x\in S$ is a sum of two elements of $S$.
solution: Closure under quotients gives $1\in S$, inverses in $S$, and hence products in $S$. We have $q^2\in S$: otherwise $q^2=qs$ for some $s\in S$, forcing $q=s\in S$. Every nonzero rational is either in $S$ or $qS$, so every nonzero rational square belongs to $S$. In particular $9/25$ and $16/25$ lie in $S$. For any $x\in S$, both $y=9x/25$ and $z=16x/25$ belong to $S$, and $y+z=x$.
ratingReason: The two-coset hypothesis forces all rational squares into S; a rational Pythagorean identity then supplies the desired additive decomposition.
notes: Mathematical statement paraphrased from Mark Dukes’s UCD-hosted IrMO compendium. The solution below is independently written, not an official marking scheme.

statement: Find all real polynomials $f$ such that $f(x^2)=f(x)^2$ for every real $x$.
solution: The zero polynomial works. Otherwise write $f(x)=x^r g(x)$ with $g(0)\ne0$. Then $g(x^2)=g(x)^2$, and at zero this gives $g(0)=1$. If $g$ is nonconstant, let $cx^j$ be its lowest positive-degree term. The coefficient of $x^j$ in $g(x)^2$ is $2c$, while $g(x^2)$ has no positive-degree term below $2j$, a contradiction. Thus $g=1$, and all answers are $f=0$ and $f(x)=x^r$ for integers $r\ge0$.
ratingReason: After removing the zero root, comparing the first nonconstant coefficient gives a clean contradiction without needing to classify complex root orbits.
notes: Mathematical statement paraphrased from Mark Dukes’s UCD-hosted IrMO compendium. The solution below is independently written, not an official marking scheme.

statement: An integer sequence satisfies $u_0=1$ and $u_{n+1}u_{n-1}=ku_n$ for every $n\ge1$, where $k$ is a positive integer. If $u_{2000}=2000$, determine all possible $k$.
solution: None of the terms can be zero: a zero would force adjacent zeros and ultimately contradict $u_{2000}=2000$. Put $u_1=t$. Successive terms are $1,t,kt,k^2,k^2/t,k/t,1,t,\ldots$. Since $2000\equiv2\pmod6$, $kt=2000$. Integrality of $k/t$ is necessary and sufficient, so $t\mid k$, or equivalently $t^2\mid2000=2^4\cdot5^3$. Therefore $t=2^a5^b$ with $0\le a\le2$ and $0\le b\le1$, and $k=2000/t$. The values are $2000,1000,500,400,200,100$.
ratingReason: Finding the six-term period is only half the work: all intermediate terms must remain integers.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the official paper. Difficulty is an individual AI estimate, not an official UKMT rating.

statement: An integer-coefficient polynomial takes the value $5$ at four distinct integers. Prove that it cannot take the value $8$ at any integer.
solution: If the four integers are $a,b,c,d$, the monic polynomial $(x-a)(x-b)(x-c)(x-d)$ divides $f(x)-5$ in $\mathbb Z[x]$, by repeated division by monic linear factors. If $f(k)=8$, then the product of the four distinct nonzero integers $k-a,k-b,k-c,k-d$ divides $3$. But four distinct nonzero integers have absolute product at least $1\cdot1\cdot2\cdot2=4$, impossible.
ratingReason: Repeated integral factorization converts four equal values into a divisibility obstruction; the distinctness bound on the four factors is essential.
notes: Statement restated in original wording. Official CMS paper checked; original independent proof supplied because no worked solution is linked in the official archive.

statement: Find all monic polynomials $x^n+a_1x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n$ with every $a_i\in\{-1,1\}$ and all roots real.
solution: For $n=1$, both $x-1$ and $x+1$ work. For $n\ge2$, if the real roots are $r_i$, Vieta gives $\sum r_i^2=a_1^2-2a_2=1-2a_2$. Positivity forces $a_2=-1$, so the sum is 3. Also $\prod r_i^2=1$, and AM-GM gives $n\le3$. For $n=2$, the possibilities $x^2+x-1$ and $x^2-x-1$ both have real roots. For $n=3$, equality in AM-GM forces every root to be $1$ or $-1$. The coefficient restriction excludes three equal roots; the remaining polynomials are $(x-1)^2(x+1)=x^3-x^2-x+1$ and $(x+1)^2(x-1)=x^3+x^2-x-1$.
ratingReason: The first two coefficients bound the sum of squared roots, while the constant coefficient fixes their product; equality then classifies the cubic cases.
notes: Mathematical statement paraphrased from Mark Dukes’s UCD-hosted IrMO compendium. The solution below is independently written, not an official marking scheme.

statement: Call an increasing sequence of integers alternating if its terms have parity odd, even, odd, even, and so on. Count the empty sequence as alternating. Let $A(n)$ count alternating sequences drawn from $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Show $A(1)=2$, $A(2)=3$, and determine $A(20)$ with proof.
solution: Let $b_n$ be the number of nonempty alternating sequences ending in $n$. We have $b_1=b_2=1$. For $n\ge3$, compare the ways to append $n$ with those to append $n-2$: the additional possible penultimate element is $n-1$, giving $b_n=b_{n-1}+b_{n-2}$. Thus $b_n=F_n$, where $F_1=F_2=1$. Consequently $A(n)=1+\sum_{j=1}^nF_j=F_{n+2}$. In particular $A(20)=F_{22}=17711$.
ratingReason: A useful recurrence comes from comparing the sequences ending at successive largest elements; spotting the Fibonacci structure is the main hurdle.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the official paper. Difficulty is an individual AI estimate, not an official UKMT rating.

statement: A square $ABCD$ has side length $1$. Find the shortest straight segment which splits triangle $ABC$ into two regions of equal area, and determine its position.
solution: A cut joins two sides and separates a triangle of area $1/4$. If that triangle contains the right angle $B$, its side lengths $u,v$ satisfy $uv=1/2$, and its third side has squared length $u^2+v^2\ge1$. If it contains $A$ (or $C$), its angle there is $45^\circ$, so $uv=1/\sqrt2$. The squared cut length is $u^2+v^2-\sqrt2uv\ge\sqrt2-1$, with equality when $u=v=2^{-1/4}$. These distances fit on the two sides. Thus the minimum is $\sqrt{\sqrt2-1}$, attained by either of the two cuts taking equal distances $2^{-1/4}$ from $A$ or from $C$ along its incident sides.
ratingReason: Requires examining which vertex the smaller triangle contains, then optimising a chord with fixed area; the symmetry-axis cut is not optimal.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the official paper. Difficulty is an individual AI estimate, not an official UKMT rating.

statement: One endpoint of a segment of length $4$ lies on $y=x$, and the other lies on $y=2x$. Find the equation of the locus of its midpoint.
ratingReason: If the midpoint is (x,y), the endpoints are (4x−2y,4x−2y) and (2y−2x,4y−4x). The length condition gives (2y−3x)²+(3y−4x)²=4.

statement: Does a function $f:\mathbb Z_{>0}\to\mathbb Z_{>0}$ exist with $f(n)=f(f(n-1))+f(f(n+1))$ for every $n\ge2$? Prove your answer.
solution: No. Since the right side is a sum of two positive integers, $f(n)\ge2$ for $n\ge2$. Let $m=\min_{n\ge2}f(n)$ and choose $r\ge2$ with $f(r)=m$. If both $f(r-1)$ and $f(r+1)$ were at least 2, the defining equation would give $m\ge2m$, impossible. Thus one is 1. Only the argument 1 can have value 1, so necessarily $r=2$ and $f(1)=1$. But now $f(2)=f(1)+f(f(3))\ge1+m$, again contradicting $f(2)=m$.
ratingReason: The equation is unavailable at one, so a global minimum argument needs a separate minimum over arguments at least two and a careful boundary case.
notes: Mathematical statement paraphrased from Mark Dukes’s UCD-hosted IrMO compendium. The solution below is independently written, not an official marking scheme.

statement: For a positive integer $c$, define $u_1=1$, $u_2=c$, and $u_n=(2n+1)u_{n-1}-(n^2-1)u_{n-2}$ for $n\ge3$. Determine all $c$ for which $u_i\mid u_j$ whenever $i\le j$.
solution: Since $u_3=7c-8$ must be divisible by $c$, we have $c\mid8$, so $c\in\{1,2,4,8\}$. For $c=8$, $u_3=48$ and $u_4=312$, which violates divisibility. For $c=1$, the next terms are $-1,-24,-240,-2280$, and $-240\nmid-2280$. If $c=2$, direct induction gives $u_n=n!$. If $c=4$, induction gives $u_n=(n+2)!/6$. Each surviving sequence has the required divisibility, so $c=2$ or $4$.
ratingReason: Early divisibility constraints reduce the parameter to four cases; the surviving factorial sequences still need discovery and induction.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the official paper. Difficulty is an individual AI estimate, not an official UKMT rating.

statement: Find the largest positive integer $n$ for which some real $x$ satisfies $2^k<x^k+x^{k+1}<2^{k+1}$ for every $k=1,\ldots,n$.
solution: The value $x=3/2$ satisfies the inequalities for $k=1,2,3$, so $n\ge3$. Suppose $n\ge4$. The first two lower inequalities force $x>1$, and the first upper inequality gives $x^2+x<4$. Hence $x^3<4x-x^2=4-(x-2)^2<4$. Therefore $x^4+x^5=x^3(x+x^2)<16$, contradicting the lower inequality for $k=4$. Thus the answer is $3$.
ratingReason: The useful contradiction combines the first upper bound with the fourth lower bound; independently estimating each power would obscure this short relation.

statement: Positive real numbers $x,y,z$ satisfy $\frac13\le xy+yz+zx\le3$. Find the possible values of $xyz$, and separately the possible values of $x+y+z$.

The expression $t^2+2p/t$ varies continuously from infinity down to $3p^{2/3}\le3$ and back to infinity, so it takes the value $3$. Also $(x+y+z)^2\ge3(xy+yz+zx)\ge1$, hence the sum is at least $1$. Given any $s\ge1$, set $x=y=t,z=s-2t$ with $0<t<s/2$. Then $xy+yz+zx=2st-3t^2$ takes every value between $0$ and $s^2/3$ on $0<t\le s/3$, so it can equal $1/3$. The ranges are therefore $(0,1]$ and $[1,\infty)$.

statement: Let $p>3$ be prime and $m=(4^p-1)/3$. Prove $2^{m-1}\equiv1\pmod m$.

statement: Form all distinct strings containing $n$ copies of each symbol $1,2,\ldots,m$. For each string let $d$ be the sum of the absolute differences between adjacent symbols. Find the average value of $d$.

Two fixed adjacent positions contain distinct values $a,b$ with probability $n^2/[mn(mn-1)]$ for each ordered pair $(a,b)$. Thus the mean total is $(mn-1)\frac{n^2}{mn(mn-1)}\sum_{a,b=1}^m|a-b|=\frac nm\cdot2\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}k(m-k)=\frac{n(m^2-1)}3$. The same argument is a double count of all adjacent ordered pairs, so no probabilistic assumptions are needed.

Thus equality holds everywhere.

statement: A function on positive integers satisfies $f(1)=1$, $f(2n)=f(n)$, and $f(2n+1)=f(2n)+1$. Find the maximum of $f(n)$ for $1\le n\le1989$, and count the arguments attaining it.
solution: The recurrences identify $f(n)$ as the number of ones in the binary expansion. Eleven ones first occur at $2047>1989$, whereas ten ones occur at $1023$. Thus the maximum is 10. Every number below $2048$ with ten binary ones is $2047-2^j$ for $j=0,\ldots,10$. It is at most 1989 precisely when $2^j\ge58$, that is, $j=6,7,8,9,10$. Therefore five arguments attain the maximum.

statement: For real $x,y,z$ satisfying $xy+yz+zx=-1$, find the least possible value of $x^2+5y^2+8z^2$. Does a greatest value exist?

Equality holds at $(x,y,z)=(-3/2,1/2,1/4)$ and its negative, which satisfy the constraint. statement: Let $p$ be an odd prime. Prove that there is exactly one positive integer pair $(x,y)$ with $x^2=y(y+p)$, and express it in terms of $p$.
solution: If $p\nmid y$, then $y$ and $y+p$ are coprime and their product is a square, so $y=a^2,y+p=b^2$. Thus $(b-a)(b+a)=p$, giving $a=(p-1)/2,b=(p+1)/2$. This yields $y=(p-1)^2/4$ and $x=(p^2-1)/4$. If $p\mid y$, write $y=pk$; then $p\mid x$ and $(x/p)^2=k(k+1)$. Coprimality would make $k$ and $k+1$ both squares, impossible for positive $k$. The displayed pair is therefore unique.
ratingReason: Separate the two possible gcds of the factors; one case forces consecutive squares and the other a prime difference of squares.

statement: Each of $n$ club members starts with a different piece of information. During a telephone call only one participant speaks and may convey everything they know to the listener. Find the minimum number of calls needed for everyone to know every piece.
solution: For $n=1$ no calls are needed. In general, have one member collect information from the other $n-1$ people and then pass all information to each of them, using $2n-2$ calls. For the lower bound, consider the first moment anyone knows everything. At least $n-1$ calls have occurred: the information ancestry of that person must connect all $n$ initial holders, requiring at least $n-1$ edges. Immediately after this first completion, every other person still lacks something, and each requires a later call in which they listen. At least $n-1$ further calls are therefore necessary.
ratingReason: The first person to know everything provides a useful time cut; a connectivity lower bound before that moment must be combined with separate recipients afterwards.

statement: Triangle $ABC$ has circumradius $R$ and satisfies $AB^2+AC^2=BC^2-R^2$. Prove that its angles are uniquely determined and find them.
solution: Let $A,B,C$ be the angles. The cosine rule gives $2AB\cdot AC\cos A=-R^2$, so $A$ is obtuse and $-8\cos A\sin B\sin C=1$. Since $\sin B\sin C\le\sin^2((B+C)/2)=(1+\cos A)/2$, we obtain $1\le-4\cos A(1+\cos A)\le1$. Equality in the last bound forces $\cos A=-1/2$, and equality in the sine-product bound forces $B=C$. Therefore $(A,B,C)=(120^\circ,30^\circ,30^\circ)$.
ratingReason: The cosine rule and extended sine rule convert the identity into a sharp bound on a product of sines, forcing equality throughout.

statement: An interior point $P$ of triangle $ABC$ has distances $x,y,z$ from $A,B,C$, and perpendicular distances $p,q,r$ from $BC,CA,AB$, respectively. Prove $xyz\ge8pqr$, and show equality forces $ABC$ equilateral.
solution: Write $\angle PAB=u$, so $r=x\sin u$ and $q=x\sin(A-u)$. The product-to-sum identity gives $qr\le x^2\sin^2(A/2)$. Cyclically, $rp\le y^2\sin^2(B/2)$ and $pq\le z^2\sin^2(C/2)$. Multiplying and taking positive square roots yields $pqr\le xyz\sin(A/2)\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2)$. Since $\log\sin t$ is strictly concave on $(0,\pi)$, the product of these three sines is at most $\sin^3(\pi/6)=1/8$, with equality only at $A=B=C$. This proves the claim and the required equality consequence.
ratingReason: Each vertex distance must be related to the product of two perpendicular distances; multiplying the three inequalities exposes a sharp half-angle product bound.

statement: A finite connected friendship network has three kinds of friendship, each person having exactly one friend of each kind. (i) Prove its size is even and greater than two, and construct such a network for every even size greater than two. (ii) If all friendships crossing from a chosen group to its complement are removed, prove that the three numbers removed, one for each kind, have the same parity.
solution: Each friendship type is a perfect matching, so the number of people is even. Three distinct friends per person require at least four people. For any even $n\ge4$, take an $n$-cycle, colour its edges alternately with the first two types, and join each vertex to the opposite vertex with the third type. This is connected and gives exactly one edge of each type at every vertex. For a group $S$, count incidences of one friendship type: $|S|=2e+f$, where $e$ counts internal friendships of that type and $f$ those crossing the boundary. Thus $f\equiv|S|\pmod2$ for each of the three types.
ratingReason: Viewing each friendship kind as a perfect matching makes both parity claims transparent, but a connected construction for every even size is still required.

statement: For positive real $a$, define $b=\sqrt[3]{a+\sqrt{a^2+1}}+\sqrt[3]{a-\sqrt{a^2+1}}$, using real cube roots. Prove $b$ is a positive integer exactly when $a=\tfrac12 n(n^2+3)$ for a positive integer $n$.
solution: If the two cube roots are $u,v$, then $uv=-1$ and $u^3+v^3=2a$. Therefore $b^3+3b=2a$. The function $t\mapsto t^3+3t$ is strictly increasing and vanishes at zero, so $b>0$. Thus integer $b=n$ gives the stated formula for $a$. Conversely that formula makes $n$ the unique real solution of $t^3+3t=2a$, hence $b=n$. The quantity $n(n^2+3)$ is always even, so this a is indeed an integer.
ratingReason: Cubing the sum cancels the nested radical, but monotonicity is needed to prove the converse without extraneous solutions.

The product of these $n$ positive summands is $(1-x^2)^{n(n-1)/2}$, so AM-GM bounds their sum below by $n(1-x^2)^{(n-1)/2}$. This is the desired inequality. The endpoints follow directly, with the case $n=1$ simply an equality.

For an equilateral triangle, any inscribed rectangle has a side on a triangle side: two of its four vertices share a triangle side, and they cannot be opposite rectangle vertices since the other two would lie on opposite sides of that line. All three base choices give the same minimum, so equality is attained. The answer is $4\sqrt3/7$.

statement: Let $b(k)$ be the number of ones in the binary expansion of a nonnegative integer $k$. Prove $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{2^n-1}(-1)^{b(k)}k^n=(-1)^n2^{n(n-1)/2}n!$ for every positive $n$.
solution: For a polynomial $f$, let $\Delta_hf(x)=f(x+h)-f(x)$. Expanding $\Delta_1\Delta_2\cdots\Delta_{2^{n-1}}f(0)$ gives $\sum_{k=0}^{2^n-1}(-1)^{n-b(k)}f(k)$, because each subset of the binary place values has a unique sum. Each difference lowers the degree by one and multiplies its leading coefficient by the former degree times $h$. For $f(x)=x^n$, the resulting constant is $n!\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}2^j=n!2^{n(n-1)/2}$. Multiply by $(-1)^n$ to obtain the result.
ratingReason: Binary subset expansion turns the sum into an iterated finite difference of a degree-n polynomial.

statement: Find the point $P$ inside a triangle $ABC$ maximising the product of its perpendicular distances to the three side lines.

Those quantities are twice the three subtriangle areas, so equality means those areas are equal, which uniquely identifies the centroid.

statement: Prove no proper fraction $m/n$ with positive denominator $n\le100$ has a decimal expansion containing the consecutive digit block 167.

ratingReason: A block anywhere in the expansion can be shifted to the decimal point; its narrow interval lies too close to one sixth for a small denominator.

statement: Show that for positive integers $n$, $2\cos(n\theta)$ is a polynomial of degree $n$ in $2\cos\theta$. Deduce that if $k$ is rational, then $\cos(k\pi)$ is either $0,\pm1/2,\pm1$ or irrational.

The angle-addition identity gives $P_n(2\cos\theta)=2\cos(n\theta)$, and $P_n$ is monic of degree $n$ with integer coefficients for $n\ge1$. If $k=a/b$, then $t=2\cos(k\pi)$ satisfies $P_{2b}(t)-2=0$. If $t$ is rational, the rational-root theorem makes it an integer. Since $|t|\le2$, the five stated cosine values are the only rational possibilities.
ratingReason: The cosine recurrence gives monic integer polynomials; combining periodic angles with the rational-root theorem gives the classification.

statement: For a positive integer $n$, determine every root of $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}(-1)^{r-1}\frac{x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)}{(x+1)(x+2)\cdots(x+r)}=\frac12$.

statement: A publisher has unlimited copies of four different books and gives each of $n$ friends exactly two different books. Every book must be given to someone, and the four sets of recipients must be pairwise distinct. Prove the number of distributions is $12(3^{n-1}-1)(2^{n-2}-1)$.
solution: There are $6^n$ unrestricted assignments. Requiring all four books to appear gives $6^n-4\cdot3^n+6$ by inclusion-exclusion. If two books have the same recipient set, every friend receives either that pair or the complementary pair. Thus the bad all-used assignments correspond to one of the three partitions of the books into two pairs, with both pairs chosen at least once: $3(2^n-2)$ assignments. Different partitions cannot give the same all-used assignment. Subtracting gives $6^n-4\cdot3^n-3\cdot2^n+12=12(3^{n-1}-1)(2^{n-2}-1)$.

statement: For $n>1$, prove a circular necklace with $2n^2$ beads in $2n$ colours can have every pair of distinct colours appearing on adjacent beads. Prove $2n^2-1$ beads cannot suffice.

At least $n$ extra edges are required, so at least $\binom{2n}{2}+n=2n^2$ beads are needed. Conversely add a second copy of every edge of a perfect matching to $K_{2n}$. The resulting connected graph has all degrees even, so an Euler circuit reads off a necklace with exactly $2n^2$ beads and every required adjacency.

statement: Prove $x^2-3y^2+5z^2-7t^2=0$ has only the zero integer solution. Prove $x^2-3y^2-5z^2+7t^2=0$ has infinitely many positive integer solutions, no two with the same ratio $x:y:z:t$.
solution: For the first equation, reduction modulo 4 forces either all variables even or all odd. If all are odd, their squares are 1 modulo 8 and the left side is $1-3+5-7\equiv4\pmod8$, impossible. Thus all are even, and dividing by 4 repeatedly excludes any nonzero solution. For the second equation set $z=t=1$. Define positive integers $x_k,y_k$ by $x_k+y_k\sqrt3=(1+\sqrt3)(2+\sqrt3)^k$ for $k\ge0$. Conjugating gives $x_k^2-3y_k^2=-2$, so these solve the equation. The $x_k$ strictly increase, and the final two coordinates are fixed at 1, so no two ratios agree.
ratingReason: The first quadratic form yields a parity descent; the sign change in the second permits a Pell family.

statement: Seven points lie in the closed unit disc, with every pair at distance at least $1$. Prove one of the points is the centre of the disc.
solution: Assume no point is the centre and order the seven polar angles. Some consecutive angular gap is at most $2\pi/7<\pi/3$. If the corresponding radii are $r,s\in(0,1]$, their squared distance is $r^2+s^2-2rs\cos\theta<r^2+s^2-rs\le1$. The last inequality holds because, for fixed $s$, the convex quadratic in $r$ is at most the greater of its endpoint values $s^2$ and $1+s^2-s$, both at most 1. This contradicts the assumed separation.
ratingReason: Six angular sectors give the bound, but equality on sector boundaries requires a careful angular-gap argument.
notes: Historical paper: statement paraphrased from the official scan. Difficulty is an individual AI estimate, not an official UKMT rating.

statement: For $m\ge1$, let $f_m(\theta)=\sum_{j=0}^{2m}\binom{2m}{j}\cos(j\theta)=(2\cos(\theta/2))^{2m}\cos(m\theta)$, and let $g_m(\theta)=\sum_{j=0}^{m}\binom{2m}{2j}\cos(2j\theta)$. For real $\alpha$ with $\alpha/\pi$ irrational, determine when $\lim_{m\to\infty}g_m(\alpha)/f_m(\alpha)=1/2$.
solution: Filtering the even terms gives $g_m(\alpha)=(f_m(\alpha)+f_m(\alpha+\pi))/2$. The supplied identity shows $f_m(\alpha+\pi)/f_m(\alpha)=(-1)^m\tan^{2m}(\alpha/2)$. The irrationality condition ensures the denominators do not vanish and excludes $|\tan(\alpha/2)|=1$. Therefore the required limit holds exactly when $|\tan(\alpha/2)|<1$, equivalently $\cos\alpha>0$.
ratingReason: The even-term filter uses a shifted angle; the resulting ratio simplifies to a geometric sequence despite the oscillating cosine factor.

statement: Let $S=\{3\cdot4^k,-2\cdot4^k:k\ge0\}$. Prove every positive integer outside $S$ is a sum of two or more members of $S$.
solution: We prove the stronger assertion that every nonnegative integer is a sum of distinct members of $S$, allowing the empty sum for zero. For $n>0$, select $d\in\{0,1,-2,3\}$ congruent to $n$ modulo 4. Then $m=(n-d)/4$ is a nonnegative integer smaller than $n$. By induction represent $m$, and multiply its representation by 4. Add nothing for $d=0$, the terms $3,-2$ for $d=1$, the term $-2$ for $d=-2$, or $3$ for $d=3$. The added terms have a new scale, so remain distinct. If $n\notin S$, a representation cannot contain just one term, completing the proof.
ratingReason: A signed base-four expansion supplies the representation; the two generators at each scale cover all four residues.
notes: Historical paper: statement paraphrased from the official scan. Difficulty is an individual AI estimate, not an official UKMT rating.

statement: A $16\times16$ matrix $M$ has entries $1$ on its main diagonal and throughout its bottom row; all other entries are $1/2$. Find $M^{-1}$.
solution: Let $Mx=y$ and $S=\sum_{i=1}^{16}x_i$. The last row gives $S=y_{16}$. For $i\le15$, $y_i=(S+x_i)/2$, hence $x_i=2y_i-y_{16}$. Therefore $x_{16}=S-\sum_{i=1}^{15}x_i=16y_{16}-2\sum_{i=1}^{15}y_i$. Thus the upper-left $15\times15$ block of $M^{-1}$ is $2I$, its first fifteen entries in the last column are $-1$, its first fifteen entries in the last row are $-2$, and its bottom-right entry is $16$.
ratingReason: The dense-looking matrix has a simple row-sum structure, so solving Mx=y reveals the inverse directly.

statement: Let $X,Y$ be the perpendicular feet from a point $P$ to the lines $CA,CB$ of triangle $ABC$, with $PX=PY$. The line through $P$ perpendicular to $AB$ meets $XY$ at $Z$. Prove that $CZ$ bisects $AB$.
solution:
Choose coordinates $C=(0,0)$ and $P=(p,0)$. Since $P$ is equidistant from the two side lines, write $A=(a,ta)$ and $B=(b,-tb)$, allowing signed $a,b$ to cover both angle bisectors. The perpendicular feet have first coordinate $p/(1+t^2)$, so $Z=(p/(1+t^2),z)$.

The direction of $AB$ is $(b-a,-t(a+b))$. Since $PZ\perp AB$,
$$(b-a)\left(\frac{p}{1+t^2}-p\right)-t(a+b)z=0,$$
whence
$$Z=\frac{p}{(1+t^2)(a+b)}\,(a+b,t(a-b)).$$
The midpoint of $AB$ is $((a+b)/2,t(a-b)/2)$, proving the required collinearity with $C$. The nondegeneracy implicit in the defined intersection $Z$ rules out the zero denominators.
ratingReason: The equal distances put P on an angle bisector at C. Coordinates along that bisector make XY a line of constant first coordinate; the perpendicular condition then identifies CZ as the median. The construction must be followed carefully, but the resulting calculation is short.
notes: Corrected against the official 1974 scan: the perpendicular through P meets XY at Z, and CZ bisects AB. An earlier bank transcription incorrectly introduced an extra point Q and changed the conclusion. Reassessed from the corrected problem.

statement: Prove that the cube roots of three distinct primes cannot be three terms, even nonconsecutive terms, of an arithmetic progression.
solution: If the three numbers occur in an arithmetic progression, there are nonzero integers $a,b,c$ such that $a\sqrt[3]p+b\sqrt[3]q+c\sqrt[3]r=0$. Set $x=a\sqrt[3]p,y=b\sqrt[3]q,z=c\sqrt[3]r$. The identity $x^3+y^3+z^3=3xyz$ when $x+y+z=0$ shows $3abc\sqrt[3]{pqr}$ is an integer. But $\sqrt[3]{pqr}$ is irrational, since the three primes each occur with exponent one. This is a contradiction.

statement: Design a finite algorithm, with a detailed flow chart, that prints every positive integer at most 100 of the form $a^2-b^2-c^2$, where $a,b,c$ are positive integers and $a\ge b+c$. Repetitions and non-increasing output order are allowed.

For each pair loop over integers $a$ from $b+c$ to $\lfloor\sqrt{100+b^2+c^2}\rfloor$, and print $a^2-b^2-c^2$. These bounds are finite, each output is positive and at most 100, and the preceding inequalities show every eligible triple is visited. A flow chart consists of these three nested loops and the print step.

statement: For positive $a,b,c,d$, prove $\frac{a+c}{a+b}+\frac{b+d}{b+c}+\frac{a+c}{c+d}+\frac{b+d}{d+a}\ge4$, and determine equality.
solution: Write $T=a+b+c+d$. Since $1/u+1/v\ge4/(u+v)$ for positive $u,v$, the first and third terms sum to at least $4(a+c)/T$, and the other two to at least $4(b+d)/T$. Adding proves the result. Equality requires $a+b=c+d$ and $b+c=d+a$, equivalently $a=c$ and $b=d$.
ratingReason: Pairing opposite denominators exposes two reciprocal-sum inequalities with the same total.

statement: In a group of $n$ people, friendship is mutual. Friends have no common friend, while strangers have exactly two common friends. Prove everyone has the same number of friends. If this number is $5$, determine $n$.
solution: Let $u,v$ be friends. Put $A=N(u)\setminus\{v\}$ and $B=N(v)\setminus\{u\}$. For each $a\in A$, the strangers $a,v$ have common friend $u$ and exactly one other common friend in $B$. Similarly every vertex of $B$ has exactly one neighbour in $A$. Thus these edges give a bijection, so $\deg u=\deg v$. Any two strangers are joined by a two-edge path, hence the graph is connected and all degrees are equal, say $k$. Fix a vertex. Its $k$ neighbours have $k(k-1)$ edges to the other $n-k-1$ vertices; each such vertex has exactly two neighbours among them. Thus $k(k-1)=2(n-k-1)$. For $k=5$, this gives $n=16$.
ratingReason: A local matching between the neighbours of adjacent vertices proves regularity; a second count determines the population.
notes: Historical paper: statement paraphrased from the official scan. Difficulty is an individual AI estimate, not an official UKMT rating.

statement: Let $a=BC,b=CA,c=AB$ for a triangle $ABC$. Determine the locus of points $P$ in three-dimensional space satisfying $aPA^2+bPB^2+cPC^2=kabc$, first for $k=1$ and then for other real $k$.
solution: Let $T=a+b+c$ and $I=(aA+bB+cC)/T$, the incentre. The weighted variance identity gives $aPA^2+bPB^2+cPC^2=TPI^2+(ab\,AB^2+bc\,BC^2+ca\,CA^2)/T=TPI^2+abc$. Hence $k=1$ gives just $I$; $k>1$ gives the sphere centred at $I$ with radius $\sqrt{(k-1)abc/T}$; and $k<1$ gives no points.
ratingReason: A weighted centroid identity turns the three squared distances into one; recognising the centre as the incentre completes the locus.
notes: Historical paper: statement paraphrased from the official scan. Difficulty is an individual AI estimate, not an official UKMT rating.
